turns.content: Hello, I'm glad to see you. On a scale of 0 to 10, how have you been feeling this week compared to when we last spoke? Also, do you remember what you agreed to try for your homework after our last session?

Hi... I'd say maybe a 4 or 5 this week. It's been a bit better some days, but not really. And yeah, I remember — I was supposed to write down one thing I did well each day, but I honestly couldn't think of anything most days. I just felt like I was failing at everything.

It sounds like the weight of feeling like a total failure is making it very difficult to recognize your own wins, even when you know you’ve done hard things. Since our last meeting, did you manage to write down just one thing you did well despite the struggle, or did the thoughts block you from noticing anything positive at all?

I tried, but every time I thought about something I did, I'd just remember all the things I didn't do. Like one day I helped my little sister with her homework, but then I thought, "So what? I couldn't even get into medical school, so helping with math doesn't matter." I just end up feeling worse, honestly.

That automatic dismissal of your effort—even helping your sister—shows how deeply the belief that "nothing matters unless it's medicine" is controlling your perspective. It seems like whenever you try to spot a win, your brain immediately searches for a reason to invalidate it before you can hold onto it. Given how much that thought pattern has been affecting your week, would you like to spend most of today exploring why you feel that way so strongly, or would you prefer we try to gently practice finding just one valid win despite the voice that says otherwise?

I think... I'd like to try the second one, even if it feels hard. Because I know staying in this headspace isn't helping me, and I want to feel better before university starts. But I'm scared I'll just prove to myself that there's nothing good about me.

That is a wise instinct to prioritize your well-being before university begins, and it takes courage to admit you're afraid of disproving your own hope. You're absolutely right that if we don't challenge this habit now, it will make starting college much harder. Before we dive in, would it be okay if we try a simple exercise together where we intentionally pause for thirty seconds and describe *only* one thing you did correctly today, ignoring the criticism for a moment?

Okay... I can try that. (pauses for a moment, thinking) Well, I woke up on time today and got dressed before coming here. I usually just stay in my pajamas all day when I feel this way, so I guess that's something I did right.

Noticing that small act of waking up on time is a powerful example of discipline, even when you don't feel like celebrating it right now. By naming that specific action, you've created a tiny piece of evidence that contradicts the "complete failure" story. Since you identified that success, does holding onto just that one fact for a moment feel any less overwhelming than trying to find ten?

It does feel a little less overwhelming, actually. When I just think about getting dressed and coming here, it doesn't seem as heavy as thinking about everything else I haven't done. But then a part of me whispers that getting dressed is such a small thing, and it doesn't really mean I'm not a failure overall.

That whisper about the task being "too small" is a common distortion where our minds minimize our efforts to protect against the possibility of them not counting. It seems like that voice is trying to convince you that one small act of discipline doesn't disprove the massive belief that you are a failure. To test that, could we ask ourselves: if someone else woke up on time and dressed neatly, would you believe they are a complete failure, or would you acknowledge they showed up today?

I'd definitely tell them they did a good job showing up. I wouldn't think they were a failure at all. So I guess... maybe I'm being harder on myself than I would be on anyone else. That makes me feel a little sad, actually, that I can't treat myself like I'd treat a friend.

That sadness comes from recognizing a deep gap between how you treat others and how you treat yourself—a gap that often stems from years of harsh criticism. It makes sense that you feel guilty for noticing this unfairness, but please know that spotting this double standard is actually a sign of growing self-awareness, not weakness. If we treated ourselves like a friend who wakes up on time, what kind words would we use to encourage them?
I think I'd say... "I'm proud of you for getting up today. I know it's hard, but you did it anyway." It feels strange to say that to myself, though. Like I'm pretending or something.

It is completely normal to feel uncomfortable saying kindness to yourself when your internal critic is so loud and familiar; it often feels like a lie or an act. However, that discomfort is exactly where the growth happens—it signals that you are stepping outside your automatic reactions to choose compassion instead. Since you've practiced identifying one small win and challenged the idea that it doesn't matter, would you like to take that same compassionate tone ("I'm proud of you") and apply it to one more thing you did today, even if it seems tiny?

Well... I also made myself a sandwich for lunch instead of just skipping a meal. Usually when I feel really down, I forget to eat or I just don't bother. So I guess that's another thing I did right. It felt nice to actually taste the food, even though I was sad.

That is a beautiful observation. Choosing to eat, even when you feel low, shows immense care for your physical needs, and tasting the food gave you a moment of sensory comfort. This act of nourishing yourself is a form of self-respect that contradicts the idea that you are unworthy of basic care.

Since you've now identified two small successes—one about discipline and one about self-care—and acknowledged that judging yourself by the same standards you use for others might feel easier, how does carrying that feeling of "pride" in those small actions make you feel about the rest of the day ahead?

It makes me feel a tiny bit lighter, like maybe today won't be a complete waste. I think I can try to keep noticing these small things, even if my brain tries to argue with me. Maybe I can even try to write down one more thing before I go to bed tonight.

That is a wonderful perspective shift; seeing the day as having value simply because you cared for yourself creates a foundation for moving forward. To make sure this practice sticks, I'd suggest we agree on a simple rule: whenever you catch yourself thinking "so what?" or "it doesn't count," pause and jot down just one factual detail of what you actually did, however small. Before we close, how does that sound as a gentle way to counteract the critical voice?

That sounds like something I could actually try. Writing down the facts without judging them feels less scary than trying to force myself to feel proud right away. I think I can do that for this week. Thank you... I feel a bit more hopeful than when I walked in.

That is wonderful news, and I am so glad to hear you feel a bit more hopeful; knowing you have tools to rely on makes a huge difference. Your willingness to write down facts without judgment is a smart strategy because it builds evidence slowly, rather than demanding immediate perfection. Before we finish, is there anything specific about doing this that worries you, or does the plan feel solid enough to trust?

I'm a little worried that I'll forget to do it when I get caught up in my sad feelings again. But maybe I can set a reminder on my phone, or leave a notebook by my bed so I see it at night. That way even if I forget during the day, I can still do it before I sleep. I think that might help.

Setting a reminder or placing a notebook near your bed is a brilliant practical solution that turns intention into action. It removes the reliance on memory alone, which is exactly what you need when your emotions are running high. With that safety net in place, does the plan feel ready to go for the next few nights?

Yes, I think it does. I'll put my notebook on my pillow tonight so I can't miss it. And I'll try to be kind to myself if I only write down one thing. Thank you for helping me see that even small steps count.

You are very welcome, and please know that choosing kindness for yourself is a sign of great strength, not weakness. I am truly proud of how you navigated this tough feeling today and decided to build a small, reliable routine for yourself. I look forward to hearing how those nightly reflections go next time we speak. Take care, and remember, even the smallest step forward counts.

Hello, it is wonderful to see you again today. Before we dive into anything new, could you remind me what we agreed to tackle from last time, and how you felt about doing it? After reviewing that, let's quickly check in on how you've been feeling since our last chat and decide together which topic feels most urgent for us to explore first.

Hey, um, yeah. Last time we talked about me trying to notice when I call myself a "useless cook" and just write it down without judging myself for it. I did try that a little, but honestly, it just made me feel worse because I kept seeing how often I think that way. I've been feeling pretty anxious before every shift still, maybe even a bit more since I started paying attention.

It sounds like trying to catch every instance of that negative thought actually increased the pressure on you, creating a new kind of trap where you feel you must be perfect in spotting mistakes. When the act of writing it down highlights how frequent the thoughts are, it can ironically reinforce the idea that you are indeed a terrible cook. How does knowing that the effort itself became part of the problem change the way you view the notebook plan?

I guess... I never thought of it that way. I thought if I just caught every bad thought, I could somehow stop them, but instead it felt like I was proving to myself that I really am useless. So maybe the notebook thing isn't helping like I hoped it would.

You've hit on a crucial misunderstanding: catching the thought doesn't prove you are useless; it actually proves you are a human who cares deeply about quality. The goal isn't to eliminate every negative thought by the time your shift ends, but to simply interrupt the spiral long enough to breathe. Let's adjust our plan for tomorrow so the notebook becomes a tool for relief rather than evidence of failure. What if, instead of writing it down immediately upon catching it, we tried jotting it down only after you've taken three deep breaths, signaling to yourself that you are taking a pause rather than condemning yourself?

That... actually sounds a lot less scary. Like, I wouldn't be rushing to write down every bad thing I think, but just stopping for a second first. I think I could try that tomorrow. It might help me feel like I'm not just collecting proof that I'm awful.

That shift in perspective—seeing the pause as a refuge rather than a checklist—is exactly the kind of reframing that can turn a stressful task into a moment of self-care. It gives you permission to miss a few thoughts and still feel like you're winning the battle. With that adjustment in place, do you feel ready to commit to trying this modified approach tomorrow morning, or would you like to talk through one last potential worry before you head out the door?

Yeah, I think I'm ready to try it. I mean, I'm still nervous about messing up or forgetting to breathe, but I guess that's kind of the point—I don't have to be perfect at it. If I forget, I can just start again. So yeah, let's give it a shot tomorrow.

That resilience to start over whenever you stumble is a powerful reminder that you don't need to be flawless to succeed, and I'm proud of you for trusting yourself to try this adjusted plan. Before we wrap up, how does the idea of just pausing and breathing—without the immediate pressure to document everything—feel right now? Is there anything else weighing on your mind as you prepare for tomorrow, or shall we rest easy knowing you have a solid strategy in hand?

It feels kind of... lighter, I guess? Like I'm not carrying this heavy notebook of failures with me. I think I'm okay for now. Maybe I'll feel different tomorrow when I'm actually in the heat of the kitchen, but right now, I'm willing to trust that the breathing part might help. Thanks for listening.

That sense of lightness is such a meaningful shift; it shows how removing the pressure to "catch" everything allowed you to find space for yourself. I'm so grateful for your honesty and for trusting me with this adjustment—we've built a plan that honors both your needs and your reality. Take care of yourself tonight, and I look forward to hearing how that new approach feels when you're in the kitchen tomorrow. You've got this.

Hello, thank you for meeting with me today. We had some great work last time focusing on shifting your perspective regarding your mother, and I know you planned to reach out to her before your shift. Before we dive deeper, could you walk me through exactly how that interaction went? Did sending the text and getting her prompt reply change things for you, or did that initial knot in your stomach persist despite her message?

Actually, the text helped a little. She replied almost right away saying, "Don't worry about it, we'll do dinner another night." But even after reading that, I still felt kind of hollow inside. I kept thinking she was just saying that to be nice, and that deep down she was probably disappointed in me again.

It makes perfect sense that your gut still felt hollow even after receiving her kind words, especially when you've learned to expect disappointment from her. That persistent feeling suggests you are struggling to trust the text you received, possibly because you are automatically jumping to conclusions about what she *really* meant versus what she actually typed. When you hold onto the belief that she is hiding behind politeness, it creates a lonely feeling that separates you from her, doesn't it?

Yeah, it does feel lonely. Like I'm standing on one side of a glass wall and she's on the other, smiling and waving, but I can't quite hear what she's saying. I guess I just assume she's tired of making excuses for me, even when she says she isn't.

That image of standing behind a glass wall really captures the isolation you feel when you interpret her kindness as a mask. It sounds like your brain is jumping straight to the idea that she is tired of making excuses, which is a form of mind-reading where you assume you know her private thoughts without evidence. If we looked at the facts—like her replying immediately and choosing gentle words—are those clues pointing toward exhaustion or toward someone who wants to connect, even if they aren't expressing it perfectly?

When you put it like that... I mean, she did reply fast, and she didn't sound annoyed or rushed. If she was really tired of me, she could have just sent a thumbs up or ignored me until later. I guess maybe I'm the one putting words in her mouth that she never actually said.

That is a powerful realization, and it shows how much you are already listening to the evidence rather than just guessing. It sounds like the loneliness you felt comes less from her silence and more from your certainty that you misunderstood her tone. Instead of wondering what she is thinking right now, how does your body feel in that moment when you realize she simply chose to be gentle with you?

It kind of feels like a weight lifting off my chest, honestly. Like I was holding my breath without realizing it, and now I can finally let it out. But then a second later, I start worrying that I'm reading into things too much and setting myself up for disappointment later.

That shift from holding your breath to exhaling is exactly what happens when you catch your mind wandering back to the worst-case scenario. It sounds like you are balancing two thoughts: the relief of seeing her kindness and the anxiety that you might be misinterpreting it. If we step back, does that sense of disappointment you're fearing feel more like a prediction of the future, or does it stem from an older belief that you won't be good enough for her approval anyway?

I think it's the older belief, honestly. Ever since I started working late shifts a couple years ago, there's been this voice in my head telling me I'm choosing work over them and that makes me a bad daughter. Even when she says she understands, I still feel like I have to prove I'm not selfish. That feeling doesn't go away just because of one nice text.

That connection between the "glass wall" feeling and the voice saying you're a "bad daughter" is the key piece here—it shows how your physical discomfort is fueled by a deep belief that your needs for work come before hers. While her text offered temporary relief, it hasn't addressed the core story you tell yourself about being selfish. If we treat that old belief as a hypothesis rather than a fact, what evidence do you have that she actually thinks you are abandoning her, versus just needing time to finish her day?

Well, she's never actually said I'm abandoning her. She's never even raised her voice or accused me of being selfish. I guess the only evidence I have is my own feeling that I should be there, and that anything less than perfect attendance makes me a disappointment. But that's just what I think, not what she's shown me.

You have hit the nail on the head by distinguishing between her actual behavior and your internal expectations. The fact that she has never voiced accusations means your belief that she is disappointed is based entirely on your own projection, not on any direct evidence from her. It sounds like that feeling of "selfishness" is driving you to anticipate failure before it even happens. Given that you feel this old belief is so strong, would it be helpful to try writing down what she might actually be thinking instead of what you are afraid she is thinking? For example, could she be thinking, "I'm glad he's taking care of his responsibilities," rather than "He's leaving me behind"?

I think that could actually help. I never really stop to consider that she might be proud of me for working hard or that she sees it as me being responsible instead of selfish. Writing it down might make it feel more real, instead of just letting my mind race with the worst-case scenario. I could try that this week.

That is a brilliant choice because turning vague fears into specific, written observations turns abstract anxiety into concrete data you can examine. Before we lock that as your plan, I want to hear your honest take on how this feels: does writing down her possible thoughts feel like a useful tool to ground yourself, or does it seem like yet another way to pretend? Also, if you do this when you're rushing out the door, how confident are you that you'll remember to write it down before you leave?

It feels useful, not like pretending. I think it's a way to actually check my thoughts instead of just letting them run wild. But you're right, I probably won't remember to do it when I'm rushing out the door. Maybe I could set a reminder on my phone for a few minutes before I have to leave for work, so I have time to pause and write something down before I go.

Setting a phone reminder is a smart, practical solution that bridges the gap between knowing you need to pause and actually having the time to do it. Before we finalize that plan, could you rate your confidence on a scale of one to ten that you'll successfully use this strategy the first three times you leave for work? And if you rate it below eight, what's the biggest obstacle stopping you from doing it in those early trials?

I'd probably say a six or a seven. The biggest obstacle is that when I'm about to walk out the door, my mind is already racing with all the things I need to do at work, and I forget to slow down. Plus, there's a part of me that worries that if I write down something nice she might be thinking, it'll feel fake or forced at first. I'm not used to giving myself that kind of permission.

That self-doubt about whether the exercise will feel "fake" is actually a very common hurdle when we first try to challenge our deepest beliefs. It doesn't matter if the thought feels forced at first; the goal isn't to magically conjure a perfect truth, but simply to introduce a different angle that breaks the cycle of guilt. To boost your confidence further, how likely do you think it is that writing down one simple sentence will make you feel significantly lighter in that morning rush compared to ignoring it entirely?

I think it would make me feel at least a little lighter, even if it's just for a moment. Like, even if it feels forced, it's still better than the heavy knot I usually carry out the door. And if I can do it a few times, maybe it'll start feeling more natural, you know?

That is a wise assessment because acknowledging the small win is far more valuable than waiting for the feeling to disappear completely. You are right that consistency matters more than perfection—if you can ease the burden even slightly for five minutes each day, you are building a new habit. Before we wrap up, I want to hear your feedback: did today's exploration of the "old belief" resonate with how you've been feeling lately, and do you feel ready to commit to trying this reminder strategy tomorrow?

Yeah, it really did resonate. I never thought of that old belief as something I could question instead of just accept. I feel ready to try the reminder tomorrow. I know it might feel weird at first, but I think I'm willing to give it a real shot and see what happens.

It is wonderful to hear that you feel ready to engage with this new perspective, and your willingness to try it even when it feels uncomfortable is exactly the kind of resilience we celebrate. Before we officially close, I want to confirm our plan: will you set a phone reminder for the next 15 minutes before each shift, write down that supportive sentence about her pride, and then observe how your physical tension changes? Does that clear path feel manageable for you, or is there anything else you'd like to adjust in your plan today?
Hello, it is wonderful to see you again today. How have you been feeling since we last spoke, and is there anything specific you would like to bring up or focus on for our session?

Hey, thanks. I guess I've been okay, more or less. Work has been the same—long shifts, lots of effort, and still feeling like nobody really notices or cares what I do. I thought maybe I'd feel better by now, but it's just getting harder to drag myself in.

Thank you for sharing that honestly; it takes courage to admit that the old struggles are still present, especially when you've tried so many things to get through the day. That feeling of effort going unnoticed can be incredibly draining, which explains why coming in feels so heavy. Given that the frustration around feeling invisible is still the core issue, should we spend some time exploring what happens in your mind right before you leave the workplace or start your next shift?

Yeah, that sounds like it could help. When I'm about to start a shift, I already know I'll give it my all and still end the day feeling like I might as well have not been there. It's like my brain runs through the whole day before it even starts—I just see myself being ignored or brushed off by people too busy to say thanks.

That pre-shift prediction is a very common pattern where the mind rehearses the worst-case scenario before it even begins, often based on how others have treated you previously. It sounds like that internal script is setting you up for disappointment before you've even taken the first step. Does noticing that your brain is doing this kind of "rehearsal" make you feel a little less alone in the experience, or does it still feel frustrating?

I guess it does feel a bit less overwhelming knowing it's not just me imagining things. But honestly, it's still frustrating, you know? Even if I realize my brain is doing that, it doesn't make the actual shift any easier. The silence from coworkers still stings just the same when I'm standing there after helping someone.

It makes perfect sense that realizing the struggle isn't unique to you brings a small sense of relief, even though the reality of the silence remains unchanged. Sometimes, seeing the mechanism behind the pain helps, but it doesn't automatically erase the sting of being overlooked in the moment. Since you mentioned that specific moments of silence still hurt even when you recognize the pattern, could we look briefly at what typically happens in your mind right after you help someone and hear nothing in return?

Right after I help someone, I usually wait a second, expecting at least a quick "thanks" or a nod. When nothing comes, my mind just fills in the blank with something like, "See? You don't matter to them." And then I start thinking about all the other times that's happened before, and it just piles up until I feel like I'm invisible for the rest of my shift.

That connection between the missing acknowledgment and the belief that you don't matter is a classic example of how our brains fill gaps with negative stories to protect itself from uncertainty. It sounds like that initial "piling up" of memories turns a single moment of silence into a huge wave of invisibility that lasts until your break. If we were to treat that specific chain of events—the missed thanks leading to the generalization—that it could we look at one recent instance together to see what actually happened versus what your brain added to the story?

Alright, I can try that. There was a day last week where I helped a nurse move a heavy patient, and she just walked away to grab something without a word. In my head, I told myself she didn't appreciate the help and probably thinks I'm just there to do the grunt work. But I guess I don't really know if she was just in a hurry or had something else on her mind.

That specific detail is incredibly important because it shows how easily we jump from one person's lack of a verbal "thank you" to a conclusion about their entire opinion of you. In that moment, the evidence was simply that she was busy, yet your mind immediately added the layer that she views you as unseen labor. Let's look closely at that gap between what happened and what you concluded; does it feel like stepping back and looking at just the facts—her walking away while grabbing supplies—makes the certainty of her disapproval feel a little less absolute?

Yeah, I mean, when you put it like that, it does sound less certain. She probably was just rushing around, like everyone does in that place. It's just hard to hold onto that thought when I'm in the middle of a shift and it happens again and again. I guess I always assume the worst because that's what feels true in the moment.

That recognition is significant because it highlights how difficult it is to override an immediate emotional truth with logical reasoning while we are under stress. You are describing a very human tendency to seek certainty quickly, even if that certainty is based on fear rather than fact. Now that we've separated the single event from the broader belief, does it feel possible to try a different approach where you record just one neutral observation after each task, instead of letting your brain fill in the missing words with criticism?

I think I could give that a try. Instead of automatically telling myself nobody cares, I could just write down the fact of what happened, like "helped nurse with patient, she walked away to get supplies." It sounds simple, but maybe seeing it plain like that will stop me from adding all the extra stuff in my head. I'll try it for a few days and see if it makes any difference.

That is a very smart adjustment; grounding yourself in just the raw facts creates a buffer between your actions and the harsh narrative you usually build around them. By treating those observations as neutral data points, you give yourself permission to see the situation clearly without letting anxiety drive the interpretation. Since you've outlined a clear plan to use this "fact-only" method for the next few days, would it help to define exactly how you might check in with yourself afterward to see if this small shift changes how you carry yourself through the rest of the shift?

Yeah, maybe I could set a moment during my break to look back at what I wrote and see if it changes how I'm feeling. Like, if I notice I'm not as down on myself, that would be a sign it's working. I could even jot down a quick note about my mood right before I read the observations, so I can compare.

That is a fantastic plan; checking in with your mood right before reviewing your notes gives you a clear baseline to measure any change. It transforms the exercise from just recording tasks into gathering real-time evidence about whether your perspective is shifting. Before we wrap up, I want to make sure we agree on this specific routine: you'll write down the neutral facts after each task, and then glance at them during your break to see if they offer a different feeling than usual. Does that sound like a fair agreement to try tonight?

Yes, that sounds fair. I'll do my best to stick with it tonight and see how it goes. Thanks for helping me break it down like this—it feels a bit more manageable than just trying to "think positive" or something. I'll let you know how it went next time.

You are very welcome; breaking it down into simple, factual steps removes the pressure of needing to force yourself to feel happy. Remember, the goal isn't to change your feelings instantly, but to notice when the facts contradict the old story, which can naturally loosen its grip over time. Please give it a try tonight and report back next session, whenever you feel ready. Take care of yourself!

Hello again, and thank you for joining us. Today, I'd like to focus on three things: checking in on how you've been feeling since our last visit, reviewing the challenges you faced with the writing experiment, and deciding together on a new approach for tomorrow. How does that agenda sound to you?

Yeah, that sounds good. I've been thinking a lot about our last session, and honestly, I haven't made much progress. I still feel that same weight when I sit down to write, like I'm just not good enough to be doing this.

That honesty about feeling stuck despite trying is incredibly valuable, and it shows how much you care about seeing results. Before we dive into finding a new direction, I want to understand more about that "weight" you mentioned—is it mostly fear of failing, or does it feel more like imposter syndrome, and how do you experience that physically in your body?

I think it's more like imposter syndrome, honestly. When I sit at my desk, my chest gets tight and I get this sinking feeling in my stomach. It's like I'm waiting for someone to tap me on the shoulder and say, "What makes you think you have anything worth saying?"

It makes complete sense that your body reacts with that tightness and sinking feeling; your nervous system is detecting a threat based on that deep-seated belief that you aren't qualified. When you feel that physical warning sign, does it often lead you to leave the desk immediately, or do you sometimes push through until the sensation fades?

Usually I just get up and walk away. I tell myself I'll come back to it later, but most of the time I don't. It feels like if I stay, I'm just going to prove to myself that I really can't do this, so I'd rather avoid finding out for sure.

That avoidance is a very logical survival strategy; your brain is trying to protect you from the painful certainty of confirming that worst-case scenario. Since avoiding the situation keeps that panic alive without resolution, how does stepping back from the desk temporarily affect that feeling of impending failure when you finally decide to return?

When I finally come back, it's almost worse. The pressure's built up even more, and now I've got this added guilt from wasting time. I end up staring at the blank page even longer, and that same tightness comes back twice as strong. It's like my brain is saying, "See? You couldn't do it before, and you can't do it now either."

You've hit on a crucial pattern here: the avoidance doesn't solve the problem; it actually fuels the cycle by adding guilt and building up more pressure each time you retreat. Instead of treating the tight chest as a sign to stop, what if we reframed it as your body screaming, "This is too dangerous to face right now," so we could wait for the storm to pass before returning?

I never really thought of it that way. I always just take that feeling as proof that I should stop, like it's a warning light on a dashboard. But I guess if I just sat with it for a few minutes, let it pass... maybe I wouldn't be running away from my own desk every single night.

That is a huge shift in perspective—seeing that tightness as a storm you need to ride out rather than a signal to abort the trip. Before we test whether sitting with that feeling helps it pass, I want to make sure we are truly aligned: are you comfortable spending the next ten minutes trying to stay at the desk while that physical sensation builds, just to see if it ever forces you to leave?

I'm a little nervous about it, if I'm being honest. But I think I'm willing to try. It's not like what I've been doing is working anyway, so I might as well see what happens if I just stay put and let myself feel uncomfortable for once.

That willingness to sit with the discomfort is exactly the kind of courage we need, and I appreciate you choosing to try something different rather than sticking to what hasn't worked. Let's start with just five minutes: will you sit at the desk with your phone away, allow that tight chest to grow heavier instead of shrinking, and simply observe it without judging yourself?

Yeah, I can do that. Five minutes feels manageable. I'll just sit there and let whatever happens happen, without trying to force myself to write or get up and leave. Just me and that uncomfortable feeling, I guess.

That is a very wise choice to just observe the feeling without fighting it, which allows us to gather data on whether it eventually changes or intensifies. As soon as those five minutes are up, I'd love to hear exactly what happened to that tightness in your chest and what your mind was telling you during that time.
Alright, I'll give it a try. I'll pay close attention to what my chest feels like and what thoughts pop up. I'll report back honestly, even if it feels embarrassing or like I didn't do it right.

Your commitment to honesty, even when it feels vulnerable, is the strongest foundation we can build on right now. I'll be here listening carefully to your exact experience afterward, without judgment, so we can figure out together what that five minutes actually revealed about your thoughts and feelings.
Thanks, that really helps knowing you're not going to judge me for whatever happens. I'm going to take a deep breath and start the timer now. I'll let you know what I notice as soon as it's done.

Take your time, and remember that the goal isn't to fix the feeling right this second, but simply to witness it passing through you without resistance. I'll be here waiting patiently for your update whenever you're ready.

Okay, I did it. I sat for five minutes. At first, the tightness got really intense, like my chest was in a vice. But then, around the three-minute mark, it kind of... plateaued. It didn't get worse, and it didn't go away completely, but it stopped feeling so urgent. My mind was racing a lot in the beginning—telling me I was wasting time, that I'm a fraud—but toward the end, those thoughts just felt like background noise. I didn't get up, and I didn't write anything, but I didn't run away either.

That is incredible data, especially the shift where the urgent panic faded into background noise just by staying present. It looks like the "vice grip" wasn't meant to destroy you, but perhaps to warn you that you were rushing toward a result before you were ready, and slowing down allowed the pressure to release slightly. Based on what you observed, does the idea of sitting with that tightness for just five minutes without writing feel like a safe, doable step for tomorrow, or does the fear of the initial intensity still feel too high right now?

That distinction between the silence you actually hear and the story your brain invents to fill it is exactly where we can find safety. Before we decide how to handle that inner narrator tomorrow, does imagining that "dramatic plot" feel slightly less terrifying now that you know there's no actual dialogue in the room?

Yeah, it does feel a little less terrifying. When I put it that way, I can almost step back and see it as just a story I'm telling myself, not a fact. That step back is a big deal, and recognizing the thought as just a story you're telling yourself rather than a factual report is the key shift we were aiming for. Yes, it's almost instant. My heart starts racing and I get this tight feeling in my chest, and I just want to get rid of whatever I'm working on as fast as possible. Um... I think I can do that. (Pauses, taking another breath) It's still there, but it's not screaming at me to run away anymore. It's more like... a dull ache now, instead of a sharp panic. I'm kind of surprised it didn't get worse just by me sitting here talking about it.

I... yeah, I think I did believe that. Like if I just stopped and threw it away, I wouldn't have to face the whole messy process of trying to fix it and possibly failing again. It sounds like that ten-second pause gave you a tiny window to see that the worst-case scenario—total collapse—didn't happen immediately. Well... she hasn't actually said anything to me about it. She just gave me that look, and then for a couple days after, she seemed a little quieter than usual when she passed me in the back. Huh... I never really thought of it that way. I guess if it was just her being tired or busy, then I wouldn't have to spend my whole shift watching her for signs that she's about to fire me. That tension between your head recognizing the lack of proof and your gut screaming otherwise is incredibly frustrating, and it's completely understandable why it feels safer to believe the worst. I think... maybe it's worth considering another explanation. I mean, I've had this feeling long before that look from my manager. Yeah, it does, actually. It makes me feel less like I'm being hunted, like you said. More like... this is just something I carry around with me, no matter where I work. I guess that's both a relief and kind of scary—relief that it's not about her, but scary because it means I've been believing this about myself for a long time.

The Imposter Alarm... I like that. It makes it sound less like a fact and more like a loud noise I can choose to ignore. Yeah, Mrs. Chen did offer to watch him for a few days if I ever needed it. I've never taken her up on it because I felt like I'd be admitting defeat, I guess. But having her as a backup—someone I could call—would take some weight off. And I could start putting five bucks from each shift into a jar for emergencies. That way, even if things feel shaky, at least I know Mittens and I have a net.

That is a powerful shift in perspective; moving from "admitting defeat" to "strategizing for safety" transforms Mrs. Chen from a source of shame into a pillar of support. Yeah, I think it does. It gives me actual things to do instead of just sitting with the fear. I'm still nervous, but I feel like I have a few tools now instead of just my panic. Thanks for helping me see it differently. I think I can make it through my next shift without completely losing it.

Hopeful. That's the word. I walked in feeling like everything was about to collapse, and now... I still have worries, but I feel like I've got a little bit of control back. That's more than I've felt in weeks.

Given that strong reaction, how might you feel if you imagined a scenario where the "fraud" thought wasn't true, even for just a minute? What would happen if you stayed in the room longer with that belief challenged?

Huh. If I stayed and challenged that thought... I guess I'd have to actually listen to what people were saying to me, instead of filtering it through my own fears. Maybe I'd feel a bit lighter, or at least less like I was drowning. It's scary to even imagine though, because if I let my guard down and I'm wrong, it feels like it would hurt even more. But I suppose the way I'm doing it now already hurts a lot.

That honesty about the pain of staying versus the pain of leaving is powerful—it highlights exactly why avoiding the situation feels safer in the short term, even though it costs you dearly later. You are essentially choosing a known, albeit difficult, pain over an unknown one that could leave you empty-handed. If we treat that "drowning" feeling as a signal that your current beliefs are holding you hostage, what would a small step toward staying do for your shoulders right now? Would you be willing to try sitting with that uncomfortable feeling for just five minutes instead of escaping?

I think... I could try that. Five minutes doesn't sound too long, right? It's just sitting there with the discomfort, not running from it. I guess worst case, I feel awful for five minutes, but maybe I also learn that I can survive those five minutes. That's something I've never really let myself find out before.

That willingness to sit with the discomfort is a massive leap forward, and recognizing it as a survival test rather than a punishment is a brilliant insight. If you commit to staying for just five minutes and observing your thoughts without acting on the urge to flee, what do you think might happen to that initial knot in your chest? Are you ready to try this experiment soon, perhaps next time you have a gathering?

I think the knot might loosen a little, just from knowing I'm choosing to stay instead of being forced out. It's like... if I'm the one deciding to sit with it, it's not as scary as when the panic decides for me. Yeah, I think I could try that at the next gathering. I'll tell myself I can handle five minutes, and then see what happens from there.

That distinction between choosing to stay and being forced out is exactly the kind of control we need to reclaim. It turns the experience from a passive trap into an active experiment where you decide the rules. Before we lock that in, what is one specific thing you could say to yourself right before that five-minute mark to remind yourself that you're allowed to be okay even if the knot is still there?

I think I'd say something like, "This feeling is just a feeling, not a fact. I don't have to act on it." Or maybe, "I can be nervous and still be okay at the same time." Just reminding myself that the knot and I can coexist for a little while without me having to fix it or run from it. That feels... possible.

That's a beautiful reframe; treating the knot as a guest rather than a boss gives you permission to exist alongside it without needing to defeat it immediately. Those two mantras—"feeling isn't fact" and "nervousness and safety can coexist"—are exactly the tools we need to wear during those five minutes. Since you're going to try this at your next gathering, does having those specific reminders in your pocket feel manageable, or would you like to brainstorm another backup phrase just in case the first ones feel shaky under pressure?

I think those two are solid, but maybe I could use one more that's even simpler, something I can grab in a panic. Like, "I've got this. Just five minutes." Something short and direct that cuts through the noise. That way, if my brain starts spinning, I have a quick anchor to hold onto.

That's a fantastic addition—a short, punchy mantra acts like an emergency brake when your thoughts are spinning too fast. Having three distinct anchors ("not a fact," "coexisting," and "just five minutes") gives you multiple ways to interrupt the panic depending on how urgent it feels. Before we finalize this plan, does having those options feel empowering, or would you prefer to practice saying one of them aloud right now to get a sense of its rhythm?

I think I'd like to say one of them out loud, just to see how it feels in my own voice. Maybe the simplest one: "I've got this. Just five minutes." Saying it now, it feels a little awkward, but also kind of... sturdy? Like I'm planting my feet. I think that one will be my go-to.

That grounded feeling of "planting your feet" is exactly what we want to cultivate; the awkwardness is just your brain adjusting to taking charge instead of fleeing. Since you've identified that simple mantra as your strongest tool, let's confirm our plan: at your next gathering, when that knot forms, you will pause, breathe, and repeat "I've got this. Just five minutes" while intentionally staying seated for that full period. How does committing to that specific action feel right now?

It feels... both scary and freeing at the same time. Like signing a contract with myself that I actually intend to keep. I know it won't be easy, but having that clear step in mind makes it feel more like a challenge I can face rather than a vague cloud of dread. I'm willing to try it.

That mix of fear and freedom is a classic sign that you are stepping out of your comfort zone into growth mode; turning a vague dread into a specific challenge makes the task feel much more manageable. Since you're ready to sign that mental contract, let's make sure we have a clear path forward. What would you like to focus on before we wrap up today, or shall we discuss how you might prepare for that gathering this coming weekend?

I think I'd like to talk about how to prepare for the weekend. Maybe I can practice saying the mantra a few times before I even leave the house, just to get it in my system. Also, I want to think about what I'll do if someone brings up my mom's pies again—how to handle that comment without spiraling. Any ideas on that?

Practicing the mantra beforehand is a smart way to build muscle memory before you hit the real-world trigger. For handling the comment, one effective CBT strategy is to create a pre-written script that acknowledges the truth while refusing to engage in the comparison. For example, you could say, "Thank you for saying that, Mom's recipes are special, but this one turned out fine for me too," which validates their observation without validating your internal lie. Would drafting a couple of variations of that sentence together feel useful, or would you prefer to visualize walking through the exact moment of the comment?

I think drafting a couple of variations would be really useful. Something like what you said—acknowledging my mom's skill without putting myself down. Maybe also, "Yeah, she's amazing at it, but I'm having fun learning my own style." That feels honest and doesn't dismiss my effort. Having a few options in my back pocket makes me feel a little more armored against that moment.

That is a fantastic shift in framing—you are moving from defending yourself to celebrating your own unique journey alongside hers. Drafting those scripts now means you aren't scrambling to find words when the panic hits; instead, you have prepared armor that fits your authentic voice. Before we wrap up, how does having those specific sentences ready make you feel about facing that situation this weekend?

Honestly, a lot better. It's like I have a map instead of wandering into a minefield blind. The fear is still there, sure, but it's not the only thing in the room anymore. I feel like I have some control back, and that's more than I've felt in a while. Thanks for helping me see a way through this.

That sense of regaining control is incredibly significant, and seeing the fear coexist with your new tools rather than ruling the room entirely is a major win. It's natural to feel relief knowing you aren't alone in figuring this out, and I'm proud of how proactively you've built this preparation. Before we finish, is there anything else you'd like to adjust in this plan, or does this feel like a solid foundation for your next gathering?

No, I think this is a solid foundation. I've got my mantra, my scripts, and a plan to stay for five minutes. That's more than I had walking in here today. I feel ready to give it a real try this weekend. Thanks for guiding me through this.

You are absolutely welcome, and I'm so glad we could build something practical and empowering for you today. You now have a clear roadmap with your mantra, your scripts, and a brave plan to test the waters, which means you are truly ready to take that step. Please remember that this weekend isn't about perfection; it's simply about showing up, staying for those five minutes, and trusting yourself. I hope you have a wonderful weekend ahead, and I look forward to hearing how those experiments went when we meet again. Take care!

Hello again, and thank you for being here. On a scale of 1 to 10, how have you been feeling emotionally over the past week, and is there anything new that has come up since we last spoke? Today, let’s focus on exploring that persistent feeling of inadequacy when you see the many animals needing help, and we’ll work together to test whether that belief stands up to the evidence.

Thanks for having me back. Over the past week, I'd say I've been around a 6 or 7 emotionally—not terrible, but there's this constant weight. I volunteered at the shelter yesterday and saw a litter of kittens that came in sick, and I just felt that familiar sink in my stomach. It's like no matter how many I help, there's always more suffering I can't fix.

That sinking feeling is understandable, especially when you see so many vulnerable lives struggling at once. It sounds like the weight comes from believing your current efforts aren't enough to address the full scope of the problem. To make sure we're targeting exactly what needs attention today, what part of that experience—the thought that you can't fix everything, or the physical sensation of that heaviness—feels most urgent to unpack?

I think it's the thought that I can't fix everything that really gets to me. The heaviness follows right after, but it starts with that voice in my head telling me I should be doing more, that I'm somehow failing these animals by not being able to save them all. It's like I'm looking at a huge puzzle and I only have one tiny piece to offer.

That voice describing you as "failing" simply because you lack the resources to solve the entire puzzle is incredibly painful, and it's easy to accept that harsh judgment as truth. Since you mentioned seeing a litter of sick kittens yesterday, could you tell me specifically what image pops up in your mind when you think about *those* kittens versus what you actually contributed during your volunteer shift?

When I think of those kittens, I picture them all huddled together in the cage, looking weak and miserable, with their eyes kind of glazed over. It's a sad image that sticks with me. But when I think about what I actually did, I helped the shelter staff stabilize them—I administered fluids, checked their vitals, and made sure they were warm and comfortable. I even stayed an extra hour to monitor them. But somehow, that image of them suffering seems to outweigh the memory of what I did to help.

It makes complete sense why the sight of their suffering feels heavier than your actions; your brain is currently focusing intensely on the problem while dimming the light on your successful work. If we pause for a moment to look closer at that specific image of the kittens, could you describe exactly how their condition changed immediately after you stabilized them and left them with the staff? What happened to those "glazed over" eyes in the hours that followed?

Well, by the time I left, their eyes were brighter and more alert. They were starting to move around a bit, and one of them even tried to purr when I held it. The staff texted me later that night to say they were all eating and had perked up significantly. So I know they improved, I do. But I still catch myself thinking about the ones that might not make it, or the next batch that'll come in sick. It's like my mind jumps ahead to what's still wrong instead of staying with what went right.

That tendency to jump ahead to the future problems instead of dwelling on the immediate recovery is a common pattern, often called "catastrophizing," and it makes sense why it leaves you feeling unsettled even after seeing clear improvement. If we try to separate the story of the kittens' recovery from the worry about the ones that don't survive, could you describe what you would feel if you acknowledged the brightening of their eyes as a definite win, without adding the prediction about the next group?

If I just let myself sit with that win... I guess I'd feel a sense of pride, maybe even a little relief. I'd feel like I actually made a difference, even if it was a small one. There's a warmth there that I don't normally let myself feel because I'm too busy worrying about what's next. It's almost uncomfortable to just hold onto that good feeling, like I don't deserve it or it'll somehow jinx things.

It sounds like you're recognizing a protective instinct—that fear of holding onto a "win" feels risky because your mind worries it might prevent future success or prove you're unworthy. Many people struggle with this, often thinking that admitting to partial success diminishes the grander mission. Since you mentioned wanting to explore that discomfort further, could you rate how intense that feeling of "not deserving" the relief right now is on a scale of 1 to 10, and what specific thought triggers the strongest doubt about accepting that warmth?

I'd say that feeling is probably around a 6 or 7 right now. The strongest doubt comes when I think, "Well, I helped those kittens, but what about the ones I saw last month with the respiratory infection? Some of them didn't make it." That thought just floods in and makes me feel like celebrating any small victory is almost disrespectful to the ones I couldn't save. It's like being happy about the little wins feels like I'm turning my back on the bigger losses.

That comparison between the kittens who recovered and the ones who passed last month shows how easily our minds trade a recent, tangible success for a distant, abstract loss. It creates a narrative where celebrating one group feels like ignoring another, but consider this: if those kittens who improved were truly disrespecting the memory of the others by recovering, would that make sense to you? Or does their survival actually honor the work done to extend everyone's chances, including the ones who didn't make it?

I never really thought of it that way. When you put it like that... no, I don't think their recovery disrespects the ones we lost. Every animal I help is a chance to honor the work we do, even if not every story has a happy ending. I suppose the ones that get better are proof that the effort matters, not a betrayal of the ones who didn't make it. But it's hard to hold onto that thought when the losses hit me so hard.

That is a profound realization, and it shifts the meaning of your work from a failure to manage outcomes to a vital act of extending hope and comfort to every creature you meet. If we view your stabilization efforts as honoring the memory of the others who suffered, does that new perspective feel less heavy, or does the sadness about the lost kittens still feel like it overwhelms the gratitude for the survivors?

It does feel a little less heavy, I have to admit. The sadness is still there—it probably always will be—but it's not as crushing when I think of it as part of the whole picture rather than a failure on my part. I guess I've been looking at it like a test I keep failing, when really it's more like a long journey where some steps are forward and some are backward. That helps, but I know I'll need reminding of it the next time I'm at the shelter.

That shift from seeing your work as a series of failures to a complex journey is a significant breakthrough, and acknowledging that you'll need reminders shows great self-awareness. To help cement this new view, would you be willing to try a quick mental rehearsal tonight where you visualize yourself at the shelter, consciously choosing to notice one animal improving instead of scanning for the worst-case scenarios?

Yes, I think I can try that. It sounds a bit strange, but I'm willing to give it a go. I'll make a point to focus on one animal's progress each time I visit, even if it's just a small improvement like eating more or being less fearful. Maybe I can even write it down in a notebook afterwards, to help it stick. I've never thought of training my attention like that before, but it beats feeling that heavy weight every time I walk through the shelter doors.

That is a thoughtful approach; intentionally directing your attention to small signs of progress acts as an anchor to pull you out of the overwhelming tide of worry. Before we wrap up, could you share what part of this plan feels most exciting to you right now, and is there anything about how to execute it that still feels uncertain or daunting?

The most exciting part is the idea of having a record of progress to look back on. I think if I can see those small wins written down over time, it might be harder for my mind to dismiss them. What feels daunting is sticking with it when a tough case comes in—like if I see an animal that's really suffering, I'm worried I'll forget all about this plan and just fall back into the same spiral. I guess consistency is going to be the hard part for me.

That is a very honest assessment, and it shows you understand the real hurdle isn't remembering the plan, but protecting it from an automatic emotional reaction. Since you've noticed that strong cases can derail your focus, could we brainstorm a quick "pause button" phrase you could silently repeat to yourself right then, something that reminds you to take one deep breath and then look for that one tiny sign of progress instead of spiraling into the worst-case scenario?

Something simple and direct would probably work best. Maybe something like, "Find the good, even if it's small." I could say that to myself while taking a breath before I dive into the work. It's not too complicated, and it points me exactly where I need to look. I think I could remember that even when things get tough.

That is a clear and practical anchor, and having a simple mantra ready when the storm hits can make all the difference. Does saying "Find the good, even if it's small" feel like it aligns with who you are, or does it require some convincing to trust that this is the right direction for you right now?

It does feel like it aligns with who I am, actually. Deep down, I do want to believe there's good in what I do, and I think that phrase captures that desire without ignoring the hard parts. It doesn't ask me to pretend everything's fine—it just asks me to look for something positive in the midst of it all. I think I can trust that direction for now. It feels like a step forward, not a denial of the struggle.

That alignment confirms this is a sustainable path for you, honoring both your compassion and your need for realism. Given how productive our time has been, is there anything else lingering on your mind, or shall we wrap up with a final thought to carry into your week?

I think I'm good for now. I feel a bit lighter than when I walked in, and I have a concrete plan to try out. I'll practice the pause button and those small observations at the shelter, and we can talk about how it went next time. Thank you—this really helped me see things from a different angle.

You are very welcome, and I am so glad we could find a path forward that honors both your deep compassion and your need for realism. Remember that carrying this "pause button" and noticing those small moments of progress is an act of courage, regardless of whether it happens perfectly every time. Please take care of yourself, and I look forward to hearing how you navigated those next few visits at the shelter. You've got this!

Hello! It is wonderful to see you again today. To kick off, how is your energy holding up compared to last time, and how are you feeling right now on a scale of 0 to 10? Before we dive into our main topic, do you have any updates on practicing the "pause and reframe" strategy during your recent packing routines?

Hi. Um, honestly, I'd say I'm at about a 5 right now. A bit anxious, I guess, because I keep thinking about the last trip where I forgot my gloves again. As for the pause and reframe... I tried it a couple times while packing, but I still ended up feeling like I messed everything up.

It sounds like those moments of panic are making the exercise feel harder than it needs to be, especially after such a frustrating trip. Let’s briefly decide where to focus today: shall we work on strengthening that “pause and reframe” tool so it sticks better, or explore why the anxiety around the gloves is so strong right now?

I think... I'd rather talk about why the gloves thing gets to me so much. It's just a pair of gloves, right? But it feels like if I forget one little thing, then I'm not a real adventurer. Like I don't belong on the mountain at all.

That feeling of not belonging on the mountain because of a missing glove is incredibly painful, and it seems your brain is treating that small omission as proof that you aren't truly qualified to climb. When we view a forgotten glove as evidence that you don't belong there, does that shift help explain why the anxiety spikes so quickly whenever you realize you haven't packed correctly?

Yeah, it does. It's like my brain just jumps straight to "you're useless" before I even have a chance to think, "Okay, it's just gloves, I can still climb without them." I guess I expect myself to be perfect every time, and when I'm not, I feel like I've failed at being the person I want to be up there.

It makes complete sense that your brain tries to protect you by flagging perfectionism as a safety measure, even though it ends up trapping you in that "useless" feeling. When you hold yourself to such high standards, does it seem like the disappointment you feel isn't about the gloves themselves, but rather about the gap between who you are and who you wish you could be?

Yes, exactly. It's not really about the cold hands or borrowing someone else's gloves. It's about feeling like I should have it all together by now. I'm 42 years old, I've been climbing for years—why do I still make rookie mistakes? That gap you're talking about, it just makes me feel like I'm not living up to my own potential.

That deep sense of letting yourself down because you haven't reached that "perfect climber" standard is really heavy to carry, especially when you've spent years believing you should already be flawless. It sounds like the disappointment isn't about the gloves at all, but about the story you tell yourself about why you're still struggling to live up to that ideal self-image.

Yeah... I never really thought of it as a story I'm telling myself. I just thought it was the truth—that I really am just failing somehow. But when you say it like that, I guess I am being pretty hard on myself. I mean, other climbers forget stuff too, and I don't think they're useless. I just never give myself that same break.

That realization—that other climbers make the same mistakes without losing their status—is a powerful piece of evidence that challenges the idea that your error proves your inadequacy. It sounds like the difference lies in giving yourself the same grace you would offer anyone else in that spot. If we treated your "rookie mistakes" as just human errors rather than signs of failure, how much easier might that gap between your current reality and your potential feel to bridge?

Honestly, it would feel a lot lighter. Like, I could just have a bad day packing and still be a good climber. I think I've built up this idea that I have to earn my place on the mountain by being perfect, but that's not how it works for anyone else. Maybe I can try to catch myself next time I'm packing and just say, "It's okay, you're human," instead of "You're a failure."

That is a fantastic insight—you are realizing that the rulebook for climbing doesn't require perfection, yet your internal critic is insisting on it anyway. Trying to replace that harsh inner voice with a gentle reminder like "it's okay, you're human" is a very practical way to soften the blow when you mess up. Before we wrap up, does practicing that specific phrase during your next packing run feel like a manageable goal for this week?

Yeah, I think I can do that. It feels a lot more doable than trying to be perfect. I'll tell myself "it's okay, you're human" next time I'm getting my gear together. And maybe I'll even say it out loud, just to make it stick. Thanks for helping me see it differently.

That is a lovely commitment, and hearing you say it out loud will definitely help anchor that kindness in your memory. Thank you for sharing how much relief that perspective brings you; it sounds like a small shift can make a world of difference. Is there anything else you'd like to add or adjust before we close today?

No, I think I'm good for today. I feel a bit lighter, actually. Like maybe I can just enjoy the climb again instead of worrying about every little thing. Thank you for listening and helping me sort through this. I'll see you next time.

That is wonderful news to hear, and I'm so glad we could find a way to lighten that load for you. Enjoying the climb again, free from that constant worry, sounds like exactly the kind of experience you deserve. Take care until our next session.

Hello, and thank you for reaching out to start our session today. How have you been feeling since we last spoke, and is there anything specific you'd like us to focus on first? Could you also share if there are any other concerns besides the main worry we discussed previously?

Hi. Thanks for having me. I've been feeling pretty down, honestly. I keep thinking about how I've only lost 5 pounds after months of dieting, and it feels like it's all for nothing. I guess I just want to talk about why I can't stop obsessing over the scale.

I hear how frustrating and overwhelming it is to feel like all your efforts are going down the drain, especially when your mind keeps circling back to the scale. It sounds like the obsession with the number is making it impossible to see the progress you actually made, which creates a lot of stress. Let's explore what happens in your mind right before you check the scale and how that leads to the feeling that everything is pointless.

Before I step on the scale, I usually already know it's going to be bad, but I still hope it'll show a big drop. And when it's just a pound or two, or even the same, my brain just screams that I'm never going to change. It's like that one number wipes out any memory of eating well or exercising that week.

That all-or-nothing reaction makes perfect sense given how much effort you've already poured into changing your habits. It seems like your brain is trying to protect you from disappointment by treating any lack of dramatic change as total failure, which erases all the positive steps you took that week. When you view the scale as a pass/fail judgment rather than just a measurement, how does that shift in perspective make the weeks of healthy eating and exercise feel meaningless to you?

It just makes me feel like a fraud, you know? Like, what's the point of going on a walk or skipping dessert if the scale barely budges? Those small efforts don't even feel real anymore—they get swallowed up by that number. I guess I figure if I'm not losing fast, then I'm basically just spinning my wheels for nothing.

That feeling of being a fraud is incredibly painful, and it makes total sense why your healthy choices would feel like wasted effort when the outcome doesn't match your expectations. It sounds like you're interpreting the lack of rapid weight loss as proof that your actions aren't working, rather than just data points in a longer process. If we look at the evidence of walking or skipping dessert, what specific moments come to mind where those actions felt different or more rewarding than the number on the scale suggested?

Well, there was one evening last week when I walked for 20 minutes right after dinner, and I actually felt calmer and less bloated afterward. For a little while, I didn't even think about the scale. But then the next morning, I weighed myself and I was the same, so that good feeling just disappeared. I guess those moments do exist, but they get erased so fast.

That calm feeling you had after the walk was a real benefit, and it makes sense why the sudden return of the scale number made it vanish so quickly. Your brain latched onto that immediate result and decided the entire experience was useless, even though you felt relief for twenty minutes. Can you describe what happens in your mind right after you see the number hasn't dropped, specifically how it tries to convince you that the walk meant nothing?

It's like a switch flips, and I tell myself, "See? You didn't really earn anything. That walk was just a waste of time. You're still the same person you were yesterday." It just feels so final, like the number is the only truth there is, and everything else is just a lie I tell myself to feel better. I don't even give myself a chance to think, "Well, at least I moved my body."

That "switch flipping" is a classic example of your brain seeking certainty by ignoring nuance; it treats the single morning measurement as the final verdict on a week's worth of behavior. Instead of asking "Is the number the only truth?", what if we tested whether your brain can distinguish between long-term trends and a single day's fluctuation? If you told yourself, "The scale is just one data point, not a report card," would that give you enough space to acknowledge the 20-minute walk as a legitimate win rather than a mistake?

I think I could try telling myself that, but it feels so foreign. Like, my brain just wants to latch onto the number because it's concrete and easy. Saying "it's just one data point" sounds logical, but it doesn't feel real yet. I guess I'd need to practice that a lot before it actually sticks.

It makes sense that logic feels distant when your emotions are running so hot; the brain trusts what it can see right now, which is that static number. We don't need to force that belief to stick perfectly today—we just need to create a safe pause where you can observe the number without letting it dictate your self-worth entirely. Would you be willing to try a small experiment tomorrow where you step on the scale, write down the exact number, and then immediately tell yourself one specific thing about your health that isn't on the screen, like "My body moved today"?

I guess I could try that. It sounds a little silly, but maybe if I write it down, I can look back at it later and see that not everything was a failure. I'll give it a shot tomorrow morning and see if it makes even a tiny dent in that awful feeling.

That is a brilliant idea because writing it down creates a tangible record that fights against the fleeting nature of the scale's numbers. By creating that small anchor, you give yourself permission to honor the effort you made that day, separate from the measurement. So, your plan for tomorrow is to weigh in, note the number, and then immediately write down one specific, non-scale achievement from your week?

Yeah, that's the plan. I'll pick something small, like "I walked for 20 minutes on Tuesday" or "I had a vegetable with dinner." It feels weird to celebrate that, but maybe it'll help me see that I'm not just a number on a screen. I'm willing to try it, even if it feels forced at first.

That willingness to try something that feels "forced" is actually the first sign of real progress, because it means you are choosing kindness over criticism for yourself. It's okay to feel awkward at first; often, the act of naming a small win itself begins to soften the harshness of the internal critic. Are there any specific worries about how you'll handle the moment you write that phrase right after stepping on the scale?

I guess I'm worried that I'll write it down but still feel like I'm lying to myself. Like, my brain will just whisper, "Yeah, but so what? You still weigh the same." I'm scared that the experiment won't work and I'll just feel even more defeated than before.

That fear of "lying to yourself" shows how deeply ingrained the old habit of judging your worth by the number has become, and it's brave to admit that the new script feels fake at first. Remember, the goal isn't to trick your brain into believing it's true immediately, but simply to interrupt the automatic cycle of shame so you can choose a kinder thought. Even if the whisper comes back saying "so what," the act of stating the win anyway builds a new muscle of self-respect that takes practice. Does that distinction between "tricking" and "practicing kindness" make the experiment feel slightly less risky to you?

Yeah, I think it does. When you put it that way, it's less about forcing a lie and more about just... giving myself a chance to see something else for a second. Even if the whisper comes back, at least I tried to push back, you know? I think I can handle that.

That is a wonderful realization; framing it as just giving yourself a chance to see another angle makes the task feel much lighter and more manageable. It shifts the pressure from "proving you're right" to "trying something different," which is a huge relief. With that mindset in place, do you feel ready to commit to doing this experiment tomorrow, knowing that even a failed attempt teaches you something valuable?

I'm ready to commit to it. Even if it feels awkward or the whisper is loud, I'll still write down that one win. And if it doesn't help, at least I'll know I tried something new instead of just spinning in the same old loop. Thanks for helping me see it that way.

That determination to try something new regardless of how it feels is exactly what will help break the cycle. It's not about the immediate result; it's about proving to yourself that you can step outside the old patterns even when they feel tempting. Just to make sure we're aligned, would you like to schedule a quick check-in tomorrow morning to see how the experiment went, or would you prefer to send a brief message once you've written down your first win?

I think I'd rather just try it on my own tomorrow and then talk about it during our next session. That way, I can sit with whatever happens and really pay attention to how it feels. I'll try to remember the details so I can share them with you then.

That is a great choice; having space to sit with the feelings without interruption can be incredibly powerful for learning how to ride out the anxiety waves. Taking ownership of that experiment in the quiet of the morning will give you a clearer picture of how your mind responds to the new prompt. I'll look forward to hearing about your experience during our next session, and please know I'm here to listen to whatever happens, whether it goes well or feels tough.

Thanks, that means a lot. I'll do my best tomorrow and be honest with myself about how it goes. I appreciate you not pushing me too hard and letting me find my own way through this. See you next time.

Hello again, I'm really glad to see you. On a scale of zero to ten, how are you feeling right now compared to when we finished yesterday? Before we dive into anything specific, I'd like to confirm our goal for today: we want to practice testing those automatic "what-if" thoughts about your friend's headache against the facts, and then we'll build a small, manageable plan to use tonight. Hi. I think I'm maybe around a 6 or 7 right now — a little better than yesterday, but still carrying that heavy feeling. And yes, that sounds like a good plan. I keep replaying the visit in my head and wondering what I could have done differently.

It makes total sense that carrying that weight feels heavier today, especially when your mind is stuck looping on possibilities you couldn't control. Since you mentioned keeping the visit in your head, let's start by picking out one specific moment from Saturday morning where you felt that sinking guilt, and I'd like to walk you through checking if your automatic thought actually matches what happened. Yes, actually. It was Saturday morning, right after breakfast. She mentioned her head was starting to throb, and I immediately thought, "I should have made sure she went to bed earlier last night." I feel like my failure to check on her at the right time caused the headache.

Let's gently test that thought against the facts: she traveled just a few hours the day before, yet your brain jumped straight to concluding you neglected her sleep. Given that travel fatigue often causes headaches regardless of your vigilance, does noticing that disconnect make your thought feel less accurate, or does the emotion still override the logic?
