Also, before we dive into the guitar picks, what significant events happened for you recently, and what would be most helpful for us to focus on today based on our plan?

Hi. Thanks for asking. I'd say my mood is maybe a 5 this week—still pretty low. Nothing major happened, just the usual daily grind at the store. I guess what would help most is talking about why I can't seem to stop obsessing over those guitar picks, even when I know other parts of the business are okay.

A five definitely means you are still carrying a lot of weight, and it’s completely understandable that the routine of the store keeps triggering that obsession. You’ve already noticed that simply checking the numbers isn’t enough because it sparks the fear immediately. Could you walk me through exactly when you feel that obsessive pull strongest today—is it right after opening, during lunch, or late at night?

It hits hardest right before I close up for the night. That's when I tally the day's sales, and my eyes always go straight to the guitar pick column first. If it's low, my stomach just drops, and I feel this wave of dread that follows me home.

That timing explains a lot; closing up feels final, so your brain treats those numbers as a verdict on the entire day. It makes perfect sense that seeing the low pick number triggers that immediate drop in your stomach, which then sets off the rest of the dread. When you notice that physical sensation happening, what is the very first thought that pops into your head?

The first thought is always, "This is it. The store is failing." It sounds dramatic when I say it out loud, but in that moment, it feels completely true—like one bad day means the whole business is doomed. I don't even think about the other things that sold well that day.

That feeling of absolute certainty—"it's over"—is incredibly painful to hold, especially when your gut knows the rest of the business is doing fine. It makes sense that when that thought lands, your brain shuts down all the evidence about successful products to protect itself from further disappointment. Have you ever caught yourself noticing that pattern where the single thought about the picks overrides the memory of the rest of the sales?

I never really thought of it that way, but yes—it's like the picks become the only thing that matters. Everything else just fades into the background. Even when my husband asks how the day went, I'll say "terrible" because of the picks, and he'll look at me confused because I sold a few guitars or some sheet music. I guess I'm not even seeing those wins.

That is such a vivid picture, and it really highlights how powerful that one thought becomes when it takes over your entire perception of reality. When your brain fixates on the loss, it effectively blinds you to all the successes, making the "terrible" summary feel inevitable to everyone around you. It sounds exhausting to constantly defend the actual performance of the store against that internal narrative. How does it feel emotionally when you realize you aren't seeing the wins you actually achieved?

It feels... stupid, honestly. Like I'm sabotaging myself for no reason. But then right after that feeling, the worry creeps back in: "What if the picks really are a sign of something bigger?" So even when I try to see the wins, my mind twists it back to fear. It's a really frustrating loop.

That "stupid" feeling is a heavy burden to carry, and it's completely normal to feel frustrated when your mind keeps twisting facts back into a scary story. It sounds like you've built a mental safety net against disappointment, but sometimes that net catches you in ways you didn't expect. When you catch yourself saying "this is a sign of something bigger," can you describe exactly what that fear is telling you is at risk?

It's telling me that if I can't even sell guitar picks—a basic, cheap item that every guitarist needs—then what's the point of the whole store? Eventually, people will stop buying everything else too, and I'll have to close down. Then I'll have let down my family, my staff, and everyone who believed in me. That's the bigger picture my brain paints.

That catastrophic chain reaction—from a single item to losing your livelihood and disappointing everyone you love—is clearly a source of deep terror for you, and it makes total sense why your body reacts with such intensity. It seems like your brain is treating a minor setback as a definitive end to everything. If you had to choose between accepting the current sales reality or living with that constant fear of collapse, which path feels easier to sit with right now?

That's a tough question. I guess... right now, the fear feels safer, because it keeps me on alert. If I accept the sales as they are, I'm afraid I'll get complacent and miss the real warning signs. But honestly, living with the fear is exhausting too. I'm not sure which is worse.

That tension between needing that alertness versus being drained by the constant dread is a classic trade-off many of us face. It makes perfect sense that your brain equates "fear" with "safety," even though you know it costs you energy. Let's try shifting the lens slightly: instead of viewing the low pick numbers as a signal that the store is dying, could we imagine them simply as one data point among hundreds, like a weather report that says "rain tonight" but doesn't mean the season is over? What if, for today, we treated that number as just noise rather than a verdict?

I like that idea—treating it as noise rather than a verdict. But honestly, my first instinct is to fight it. Like, if I ignore the numbers, I'm being irresponsible. But I guess I haven't really tried just... letting them be numbers. Maybe I could give it a shot for one evening, just to see what happens.

That is a brave shift, moving from fighting the reality to simply observing it without judgment. It makes sense that resisting the data feels risky, but stepping back and letting it exist without assigning a meaning might actually reveal its true weightlessness. Would you be open to testing that "letting it be" approach for just one evening tomorrow, and seeing if the dread lifts once you stop treating it as a verdict?

Yeah, I think I can try that. Tomorrow evening when I close up, I'll look at the numbers but not let myself spin the story. I'll just write them down and leave them at the store—no taking them home with me. It feels scary, but also a little freeing just to say it out loud.

That sounds like a wonderful plan, and recognizing that it feels both scary and freeing shows a lot of courage in yourself. Leaving the numbers behind creates a literal boundary between the past day and your personal life, which can help separate the event from your identity. One small detail to watch for: when you write them down, do you find yourself automatically adding a story about what they mean, or can you try to just observe the digits as they are for the first few moments?

I think I add the story almost instantly. It's like my hand writes the number and my brain has already decided it's bad. But I'll try to pause for a few seconds before I even pick up the pen—just breathe and look at the number on the screen without judging it. That might be the hardest part, but I'll give it a real shot.

Taking that intentional breath before reaching for the pen is exactly the right place to start, and acknowledging that it will feel difficult gives you permission to be gentle with yourself when it slips up. Remember, the goal isn't to suppress the thought but to create just enough space between the number and your story so you can choose how to react. How does it feel knowing we're testing this new approach together tomorrow, even if the old habit tries to rush in?

It feels... hopeful, actually. Like I have a plan instead of just spiraling. And knowing I'll check in with you about it makes me more accountable. I think that helps—having someone else know what I'm trying to do. It makes the fear feel a little smaller.

That is such a powerful realization, and I'm really proud of you for spotting how accountability alone can soften the grip of fear. Knowing you have a safe harbor to return to makes the challenge feel much less isolating. Before we wrap up today, is there anything else weighing on your mind about the coming week, or shall we leave it here so you can go home with a clear plan for tomorrow?

No, I think I'm good for now. I feel lighter than I did when I walked in, believe it or not. I'll focus on tomorrow's experiment and see what happens. Thanks for listening—it really helps to put words to all this chaos.

You are so welcome, and I want you to know that putting those chaotic thoughts into words is a huge step toward gaining control over them. Please remember that tomorrow's experiment is a practice run, and whether you succeed perfectly or stumble a bit, we will learn valuable insights either way. I look forward to hearing how that brief pause landed for you this evening, and thank you for bringing such honesty to our sessions. Take care of yourself tonight.

Hello, I'm glad to see you again. Before we dive in, could you share how you've been feeling since our last session, perhaps on a scale of 1 to 10 for that heavy guilt? Based on what you told me before, does it sound like we should focus today on building a new way to handle those intrusive thoughts, or would you prefer to explore something else?

Hi. I'd say the guilt is still pretty high, maybe an 8. It hasn't really gone down much. I think focusing on those thoughts sounds good, because they just keep circling in my head no matter what I do.

An 8 out of 10 tells me this is still a really painful area, and it makes complete sense that nothing seems to work yet when your brain is locked into that loop. Since you mentioned the thoughts keep circling regardless of what you try, let's aim for two specific goals today: first, to gently examine whether the evidence actually supports the story that you "missed signs," and second, to practice a quick grounding technique to help break that cycle when it starts. Does exploring the reality of those early days followed by a simple breathing exercise feel like the best path forward?

Yeah, that sounds like it could help. I mean, I know in my head I keep saying I should have noticed her breathing was off or that she was hiding more, but... I guess I never really stopped to check if that was actually true or just what I keep telling myself. I'm willing to try the breathing thing too.

That honesty about checking the reality versus the story is exactly where the real relief begins, and I'm glad you're willing to tackle both parts of the plan. Before we start digging into the timeline of those early days, does the idea of examining the facts feel safe to you right now, knowing we won't judge you for finding out? And when we get to the breathing exercise later, how do you imagine your body will react when you're trying to step out of that loop?

It feels a little scary, honestly. Like if I look too closely at the facts, I might find out I really did mess up and there's no excuse. But I also know I can't keep living with this weight, so I'm ready to try. As for the breathing... I think my body will probably feel tense and jittery at first. I get really restless when those thoughts come up, like I need to do something to fix it even though I know I can't.

That fear of uncovering a harsh truth is completely understandable, but remember that we aren't looking for excuses; we're simply gathering data to see if the story you've built actually matches reality. Even if the facts show you weren't entirely correct, discovering the truth is often less painful than continuing to live in a fabricated world of regret. Regarding the tension you described, that restlessness is your body trying to escape the loop, which means the grounding technique won't force you to stay in the guilt—it will simply offer a safe place to land instead. Shall we start by looking at those early days together to see what the actual evidence says about what happened?

Okay. Yeah, let's start. I guess I can begin with the week before she passed. She was still eating and drinking normally, so I didn't think anything was seriously wrong. She just seemed a little quieter than usual, but I figured she was just getting older or maybe tired.

It makes perfect sense that you interpreted her quietness as normal aging, especially since she was still eating and drinking fine—that's a reasonable initial assessment given what you observed. However, since you are open to checking the facts now, let's look at that specific timeframe: even if she seemed "just tired," did she show any other subtle signs that were different from a typical senior cat's behavior, or were those truly isolated incidents?

Well... now that I think about it, she did start sleeping in different spots than usual. She always had her favorite chair, but the last few days she was sleeping under the couch or behind the curtains. I thought maybe she just wanted a change, but now I wonder if she was hiding because she didn't feel well. But I didn't know that then—it just seemed like a small thing.

Noticing that shift in her sleeping habits is a huge clue, but it’s easy to interpret a cat changing spots as curiosity or preference, especially when she was otherwise active. If we treat those sleeping changes as potential warning signs alongside the quietness, does the story that you “didn’t know” start to feel a little less absolute, or does your instinct to dismiss it as normal behavior still feel strong?

It's... complicated. Part of me wants to say I should have known, because that's what I've been telling myself over and over. But when I really look at it, no, I didn't know. I mean, cats hide when they're sick, but they also hide for a hundred other reasons. I guess I'm starting to see that maybe I wasn't ignoring something obvious—I just didn't have the information to connect the dots.

That distinction is incredibly important—you are realizing that you lacked the specific information to connect the dots, which is very different from ignoring obvious signs. This shift from "I failed to see" to "I didn't have the data" significantly reduces the feeling of personal negligence. Now that we've examined the evidence from those early days, does that feeling of "not knowing" make the burden of guilt slightly less heavy, or does the uncertainty still feel overwhelming?

It's a little lighter, I think. Like, I can see now that I was judging myself for not being able to predict something that wasn't predictable. But there's still this little voice that says "but you should have tried harder, asked a vet sooner, something." I guess that part is still there, but it's not shouting as loud as before.

That "little voice" is a common survivor of grief, often fueled by a desire to have done more, even when the facts show we couldn't have predicted the illness. It's helpful to name it as just a persistent thought rather than an undeniable truth. Since we've cleared up the timeline of the early days, let's move forward with your second goal: preparing for that moment tonight when the loop returns. Imagine sitting in bed, the guilt rising, and you need to ground yourself immediately. Would you be willing to try a simple count of your breaths for just four cycles, focusing entirely on the air entering and leaving your lungs, to create a physical break from those thoughts?

Alright. I can try that. Four breaths doesn't sound too hard. I'll just focus on the air going in and out, and try to let the thoughts fade into the background for a few seconds. Yeah, I think I can do that tonight.

That is a solid plan, and taking just four conscious breaths can serve as a tiny but effective reset button for your nervous system. Remember, the goal tonight isn't to make the guilt disappear instantly, but to simply interrupt the spiral long enough to breathe and choose a different reaction. Can you visualize yourself doing that practice tomorrow morning as well, perhaps while brushing your teeth or waiting for coffee to brew, to build some extra muscle around it?

Yeah, I think I can do that. Maybe while I'm waiting for the coffee to brew in the morning, I can pause and take those four breaths. It feels like a small thing, but I guess small things add up. I'll give it a try tomorrow.

That is a wonderful insight, and you are absolutely right that these small, repeated pauses are how we rebuild a relationship with our own minds. Taking four conscious breaths while waiting for coffee is a perfect low-pressure way to practice this skill without feeling like you're "working on it" too intensely. Before we wrap up, is there anything else about tonight's plan or the new perspective we found today that you'd like to discuss or clarify?

No, I think I've got a handle on it for now. I feel a little more grounded than when I walked in, and I'm willing to give this breathing thing a real shot. Thanks for helping me look at those early days without just blaming myself. It helped more than I thought it would.

That is such a meaningful shift, and I am so grateful to hear that viewing those early days differently brought you more relief than you anticipated. It takes real courage to face the uncertainty without rushing to judge yourself, and I am proud of you for doing that. Please remember that tomorrow's small practice of breathing is a gift to yourself, not a punishment. Is there anything else you need from me today, or would you like to end the session here?

Hello, it is wonderful to see you again. How are you feeling today compared to last time, and what would you like to focus on first? If there are other topics on your mind besides the greeting experiment, please let me know so we can decide which ones take priority.

Hi. I'm doing okay, I guess. I've been thinking a lot about something that happened at work this week, and it's kind of been eating at me. I saw two of my colleagues talking and laughing together, and I just immediately assumed they were talking about me.

That assumption that they were discussing you is a very common reaction when we feel self-conscious, and it makes complete sense why it has been keeping you off balance lately. Since this new worry about work is clearly affecting your mood, shall we spend part of our time exploring what triggered that specific interpretation, and then come back to the greeting experiment to review your notes?

Yeah, I think that's a good idea. It's just... whenever I see people whispering or laughing, my mind goes there. I feel like they must be judging me, especially since I'm the oldest teacher in the science department and I don't really fit in with the younger staff.

That feeling of being judged because of your age adds a heavy layer to your anxiety, and it explains why your brain jumped straight to that conclusion. To help us understand this better, could you tell me about the specific situation at work? Who were those colleagues, and what exactly was happening right before you made that assumption?

It was during my free period, and I was walking past the staff lounge. Two of the younger biology teachers, Jenna and Mark, were huddled together and laughing. I couldn't hear what they were saying, but as soon as they saw me walk by, they sort of stopped and looked at me. That's when I just knew—they were talking about how I'm awkward or how I never go out on dates.

That specific sequence—their laughter followed by their sudden pause and glance—is almost certainly the fuel for your automatic thought that they are judging you. It feels incredibly validating to believe their attention was a comment on your age or social life, yet looking at it objectively, they simply noticed you and resumed their conversation, didn't they? Let's test that assumption by considering if there are other reasons they paused besides gossip about you, like checking if you needed help or noticing you were distracted. Which alternative explanation feels slightly more plausible when you strip away your own fears?

I guess... maybe they just got distracted by me walking by, like you said. Or maybe they were talking about a lesson plan and didn't want me to think they were slacking off. I suppose it's possible they weren't talking about me at all. But it felt so real in the moment.

It is completely understandable that the feeling was so vivid in that moment, even though your brain is now offering more logical alternatives. That sharp spike in anxiety tells us this is a strong habit your mind has formed, but recognizing that the event itself wasn't definitive proof is a major breakthrough. Before we plan your next steps, I want to check in: how does hearing that your body reacted automatically but your logic can offer another explanation feel to you right now?

Honestly, it feels a little embarrassing. I'm a science teacher—I should know better than to jump to conclusions without evidence. But I guess emotions don't always follow logic, do they? It's a bit of a relief, though, to think that maybe they weren't talking about me. It makes my stomach unclench a little.

You are absolutely right that emotions often run ahead of logic, and it takes courage to admit that your instinct wasn't a failure of intelligence but a survival reflex. Acknowledging that relief in your gut is a powerful sign that you are starting to separate the factual event from the story your brain told you. Now that we've seen how quickly that embarrassment arose and how much it fades when we challenge the certainty, what would be most helpful for you to focus on next: continuing to unpack this workplace incident, or returning to your plan for gathering data on the greeting experiment?

I think I'd like to stick with this workplace issue for a bit longer, if that's alright. It keeps happening, and I want to understand why my mind goes there so quickly. Maybe if I can figure that out, it'll help with the other stuff too—like when I see couples and feel hopeless about ever finding someone.

Connecting the workplace reaction to your broader feelings of hopelessness is a brilliant insight, showing how one pattern of thinking can ripple through different parts of your life. If we view this as a recurring theme rather than isolated incidents, it helps us find a common root cause for both situations. Could you describe a recent instance outside of school—perhaps seeing a couple or a group of friends—and walk me through the exact thought that popped into your head? I want to see if the mechanism is similar.

Alright. Just last week, I was at the grocery store and I saw a couple my age picking out vegetables together, laughing and touching each other's arm. And my immediate thought was, "They've probably been together for years. They're happy. I'll never have that. There's something wrong with me that I've been single this long." And I just felt this heavy weight in my chest for the rest of the day.

That feeling of heaviness is a direct result of comparing your reality to their happiness, which creates a gap that feels impossible to cross. While it is natural to feel lonely seeing others connected, your statement "There's something wrong with me" shifts the blame inward onto your inherent worth rather than viewing this as a temporary sadness caused by circumstance. Have you considered whether that comparison was necessary, or if it was just a symptom of your loneliness that the presence of the couple triggered?

I never really thought of it that way. I guess I do just assume that seeing a happy couple means I'm defective somehow. But you're right—it's not like I know their story. They could have struggles too. But it's so hard not to compare when you're standing there alone with a cart full of food for one person.

Noticing that your brain is using their happiness as a mirror to judge your own value is a significant step in identifying that cognitive distortion. It is also very human to feel that solitude highlights a deficiency when surrounded by connection; the feeling of inadequacy often stems from interpreting their relationship status as a verdict on yours rather than just a snapshot of theirs. Would it be helpful to try listing the facts you know for certain about them versus the assumptions you are making about your own future based on that single scene?

Well, the facts... I don't know anything about them. Not their names, not how long they've been together, not if they have problems. I just saw them laughing. And the assumptions I'm making about myself... that I'll never have that, that I'm somehow broken. And that's not a fact either. I've never actually been in a long-term relationship, but that doesn't mean I'm incapable of one. It just means it hasn't happened yet.

That distinction between observable facts ("they are laughing") and your internal judgments ("you are broken") is exactly the core of what we need to work on separating. By pointing out that lack of history doesn't equal incapacity, you are already starting to dismantle the absolute certainty in that thought. If we treat your prediction that "I'll never have that" as a hypothesis rather than a law of nature, what other possibilities exist for your future that aren't immediately ruled out by seeing just one couple?

I suppose... I could meet someone at a workshop or a conference. Or maybe through a friend of a friend. I could even try a different dating app, or take a class where I might meet people with similar interests. It's not like I've tried everything. I just assumed I'd already failed before I even really started trying.

Spotting those realistic pathways shows you are actively moving from despair to possibility, which directly challenges the "forever" aspect of your original thought. It looks like we have explored the workplace incident and the grocery store comparison thoroughly enough to see the pattern clearly: your mind jumps to worst-case scenarios because they feel urgent, even though the evidence is sparse. Since you mentioned wanting to tackle the greeting experiment as well, would you like to revisit your plan to collect three data points at the grocery store this Sunday, or would you prefer to draft a simple grounding technique to use whenever you catch yourself making that "defective" thought in the future?

I think I'd like to try the grounding technique first. The grocery store plan feels a bit overwhelming right now, especially after realizing how much I let those thoughts spiral. If I have a way to stop myself in the moment, maybe I'll feel braver about actually going and trying the experiment.

That is a wise decision; building a safety net before facing the bigger task makes a lot of sense. A simple grounding technique works by forcing your brain to switch focus from internal worries to external reality using your senses. For example, when that "defective" thought pops up, could you try naming five things you can see, four you can touch, three you can hear, two you can smell, and one you can taste? It takes about thirty seconds and breaks the cycle of rumination effectively.

Five things I can see... the window, my coffee mug, the plant on your desk, the bookshelf, the clock on the wall. Four I can touch... the armrest of this chair, the fabric of my pants, the smooth surface of my phone, the cool glass of water. I can hear the hum of the air conditioner, your voice, and the traffic outside. I can smell coffee and... maybe a hint of lemon from that cleaner. And I can taste the mint from my gum. That actually... that does help. My shoulders feel a bit looser.

It is wonderful to hear that this sensory shift worked so quickly to loosen your tension; you successfully redirected your brain from a negative story to tangible reality in under a minute. That ability to interrupt the spiral right there proves you have the tools you need to handle the grocery store visit later on. With that grounding technique secured, would you like to finalize a simple schedule for collecting those three data points on Sunday, or would you prefer to discuss any other potential barriers before we wrap up?

I think I'm ready to plan the grocery store trip now, actually. I'll go on Sunday morning when it's less crowded. I'll just focus on three things: noticing one couple and writing down the facts versus my assumptions, saying a brief hello to the cashier, and using the grounding technique if I feel that heaviness start to creep in. Does that sound reasonable?

That is an excellent, structured plan that breaks the overwhelming task into manageable, low-stakes actions. Focusing on specific targets like the couple, the cashier, and a self-soothing cue gives you clear instructions when your anxiety tries to hijack the moment. Since we covered the grounding technique and agreed on the details, is there anything else you'd like to clarify or any lingering worries about trying this on Sunday?

No, I think I'm okay for now. I feel a little nervous, but also a tiny bit hopeful, which is unusual for me. Thank you for helping me see that I've been making assumptions that aren't facts. I'll try to remember that when I'm at the store this weekend.

That mix of nervousness and hope is a fantastic sign of progress, showing that you are beginning to trust your own ability to navigate difficult moments. Remembering to pause and check your thoughts before letting them dictate your feelings is a powerful tool you now possess. Thank you for your openness and effort this session; I look forward to hearing how your Sunday experience unfolds. Please reach out anytime if you need support along the way.

Hello, I'm really glad to see you again. To pick up right where we left off, I recall we worked on separating the mistake from your character by writing a letter, and we agreed to place a copy on your bathroom mirror to read in the morning. How did you feel after our session ended, and is there anything that has shifted in your life since then that we might want to focus on today?

Hi. Um, the letter thing... I did it, but I'm not sure it helped. I mean, I read it in the morning, but then when I got to work and saw the bookshelf where I'd left those books overdue, that feeling just came back. It's like the words don't stick once I'm actually there.

It makes perfect sense that the letter felt powerful in the quiet of your home but lost its hold once you stepped into that environment; your brain naturally switches gears when it detects a real-world trigger, even if the situation seems minor. When you stood near the bookshelf and noticed the feeling return, did you catch yourself trying to recite the lines from the letter, or did you slip back into imagining the worst-case scenario about what others were thinking?

I just went straight to the worst-case, honestly. I wasn't even thinking about the letter. I saw a coworker glance at me, and I immediately thought she must be thinking, "There goes the hypocrite librarian who can't even follow his own rules." I felt my face get hot, and I just wanted to hide in the back room for the rest of the day.

That automatic jump to the "hypocrite" label is your brain's oldest defense mechanism, trying to protect you by preparing for rejection before anyone has even spoken. When that image forms and your face heats up, does it feel like you are actually hearing her internal monologue, or is it more like your mind is projecting your own feared judgment onto her neutral glance?

I guess... it's more like I'm projecting? Because she didn't actually say anything. She just looked up from the computer for a second. But it feels so real in the moment, like I can hear the accusation even if no words are spoken. It's like my own voice is louder than anything else in the room.

It sounds incredibly exhausting to carry such a loud, critical voice inside your own head, especially when the outside world is silent. Notice how that internal accusation feels more urgent and "real" than the coworker's neutral expression, simply because your brain has decided to interpret the ambiguity as proof of your failure. When you realize she only glanced up, did you spot any other evidence that contradicts the story you told yourself about her judging you?

Not really, because I was too busy spiraling to look for evidence. But... I mean, she did come over to my desk about ten minutes later to ask if I wanted to join her for coffee. That doesn't really line up with her thinking I'm a hypocrite, does it? She probably wouldn't want to have coffee with someone she thinks is a fraud.

That is a brilliant observation, and it highlights exactly how your brain ignores the safety signal when it's trapped in a spiral. It makes sense that you missed the invitation because your attention was locked entirely on the imagined insult rather than the actual interaction. If you had paused to consider that offering coffee is usually a sign of connection, not criticism, how would that change the meaning of her initial glance?

It would change everything, actually. If I really think about it, maybe she was just looking up because she heard me walk in, and the coffee invitation was just her being friendly. I guess I've been so focused on the one mistake I made that I'm seeing judgment everywhere, even when people are just being normal. But it's hard to hold onto that thought when the guilt about the books feels so big.

You've hit on the core issue perfectly: the guilt about the mistake is acting like a spotlight that forces you to see every shadow as proof of your failure, making it nearly impossible to see the bright spots, like her offer for coffee. It's like wearing thick glasses where the only color visible is black; until you take the glasses off, the friendly gesture looks suspicious. Can we try a small experiment for the next few days where, whenever you catch yourself making that "judging" assumption, you consciously pause and ask, "Is there any evidence she dislikes me, or am I just hearing my own worry?"

I think I could try that. It sounds simple enough, but I know it's going to feel weird at first. I'm so used to just believing that first awful thought. But I suppose it's worth a shot—I mean, what's the worst that could happen? I find out people actually don't hate me? Maybe that's not such a bad outcome.

That is a wise realization, and finding out that others don't dislike you is actually a relief you've been missing out on. Let's try this experiment twice today: once when you feel that hot flush rising, and again when you catch yourself labeling someone a "hypocrite." Each time, just pause for three seconds, take a slow breath, and ask yourself that gentle question about the evidence. Afterward, tell me how that pause felt compared to rushing straight into the spiral.

Alright, I'll give it a go. I'm a bit nervous that I'll forget to do it in the heat of the moment, but I'll try to remember. Maybe I can even put a little sticky note on my desk that just says "Pause?" to remind me. I'll let you know how it goes next time we talk.

That is a brilliant idea; using a visual cue like a sticky note can act as a gentle external reminder when your internal monitoring slips away. Placing it where you work ensures you have a physical checkpoint before your mind automatically defaults to the old stories. I am really proud of your willingness to try this, even if it feels awkward at first. We will check in soon to see how that "Pause?" note lands for you, and I'm here to help adjust it if it needs tweaking.

Thanks, I appreciate that. It does feel a little awkward, but I think that's just because I'm not used to questioning my own thoughts. I'll put the sticky note up before my shift tomorrow. I guess I'll see if a three-second pause can really change how I feel.

That feeling of awkwardness is actually a very good sign; it means you are stepping out of autopilot and engaging your conscious mind to interrupt the cycle. Taking that tiny three-second break to create space between the trigger and your reaction is a powerful way to reclaim control, even if it feels clumsy at first. Please put that sticky note on your desk tomorrow, and we will check in next session to see if that little pause helped soften the edge of those thoughts.
I will. Thanks for being patient with me on this. I know it's just a small step, but talking it through like this makes it feel a bit more doable. I'll see you next time.

You are absolutely welcome, and please remember that taking small steps like this is often the most effective way to build lasting change. It is okay if the process feels messy or imperfect right now; consistency matters far more than perfection. I truly enjoyed working with you today, and I am confident that this pause practice will become easier with each repetition. Take care of yourself, and I will speak with you soon.

Hello, thank you for meeting with me today. How are you feeling right now on a scale of one to ten, and is there anything important you'd like to bring up that we haven't discussed yet? If there isn't anything else pressing, shall we quickly look at your action plan from last time before focusing on the coffee shop incident again?

I'm feeling about a 5 right now—a bit anxious, but I'm glad to be here. I think the coffee shop incident is still on my mind, so I'd be okay focusing on that. We can look at the action plan first if you want, but honestly, I'm not sure it helped much.

A score of five reflects that lingering anxiety, and it’s completely understandable to feel frustrated if the plan didn’t stick. Since you’re ready to revisit the coffee shop incident anyway, shall we walk through what happened there and the thoughts that followed, and then decide together if adjusting the action plan is useful before wrapping up?

Okay, that makes sense. So, last week I went to a new coffee shop, and I ordered a latte. When the barista handed it to me, I thought she seemed a little rushed and didn't smile. Right away, I started thinking she was annoyed with me for ordering something complicated, even though it was just a regular latte. I ended up leaving without even drinking it because I felt so awkward.

That makes perfect sense; the combination of feeling awkward and interpreting neutral behavior as annoyance naturally led you to avoid the situation entirely. It sounds like that initial belief—that she was annoyed with you for choosing a complex drink—became too heavy to carry, so your body decided leaving was the safest option. Can you walk me through exactly what went through your mind right after she handed over the cup, before you made the decision to leave?

Right after she handed me the cup, I thought, "She probably thinks I'm being picky or difficult." And then my mind just spiraled—I started thinking, "I'm the kind of person who makes things hard for others. I always do this. I can't even order a simple coffee without messing it up." It felt like my whole identity was on the line over a latte.

That spiral is incredibly painful because it shifts the blame from a single moment to your entire character, making the situation feel unfixable. It makes total sense that when someone looks stressed, your brain latched onto the possibility of rejection and magnified it into a threat to your self-worth. Did you notice any physical signs of that stress, like a tight chest or a racing heartbeat, right as you started thinking you were being difficult?

Yeah, my heart started pounding really fast, and I felt this tightness in my chest, like I couldn't breathe properly. I also felt my face get hot, like I was blushing. It was like my body was telling me, "You're in danger, get out," even though logically, I was just standing in a coffee shop.

It sounds like your body reacted with such urgency that it convinced your mind you were actually in danger, forcing you to flee for safety. That physical alarm system is doing its job perfectly well, even though the threat wasn't real—the real danger was your belief that you had ruined your reputation. Can we explore together what specific evidence exists that the barista was actually annoyed with you versus what she might have been thinking, like maybe she was just tired from opening early?

I guess when I think about it, there isn't really solid evidence that she was annoyed with me specifically. She did hand me the coffee, and she said "have a good day," even if it was rushed. I suppose she could have just been tired or busy, like you said. But in the moment, my mind latched onto that brief lack of a smile and turned it into a story about me being a problem. It's like I can't separate her mood from my own worth.

You've hit on something very important: your brain took a neutral cue—her lack of a smile—and fused it with your existing worry about being "difficult," creating a narrative that threatened your entire self-worth. That connection between her temporary mood and your permanent value is the root of why you felt you had to leave immediately. Given how strongly that fear lands for you, would you be willing to try a small experiment where we treat that "story" as just a movie playing in your head, rather than an absolute truth about who you are?

I think I could try that. It feels weird to treat it like a movie, because it feels so real when it's happening. But I guess I can see how my mind just jumped to a conclusion without any real proof. What would the experiment involve?

The experiment involves pausing for just thirty seconds when that knot forms in your stomach, taking a deep breath, and silently saying to yourself, "This is just a movie my brain is playing right now, not a fact about who I am." Would you be comfortable giving it a try the next time you feel that familiar rush of panic, perhaps while waiting in line somewhere else?

That sounds manageable, I think. Thirty seconds isn't too long, and I can try it next time I'm waiting in line or ordering something. I've never really thought of it that way—like I can separate the story from the reality. I'm a little nervous it won't work, but I'm willing to give it a shot.

That willingness to step outside the story and view it objectively is a huge sign of progress, and your nervousness is actually a normal part of learning a new skill. Before we lock this in, could I ask what specific piece of evidence we found earlier that suggested the barista was likely just tired rather than angry, so you can hold that thought steady when the "movie" starts playing again?

Well, she did say "have a good day," even if it was quick. And I guess, thinking back, she looked a bit tired—maybe she just started her shift or had a long line before me. There's no proof she was annoyed with me specifically. I can try to remind myself of that when the panic starts.

That reminder about her greeting and her tired expression gives us concrete anchors to pull on when the panic rises again. Before we finalize the plan, could I ask if you feel confident enough to try separating the "movie" from the reality next time, knowing you have those specific facts to reference? And once we set that goal, would you be open to sharing what might get in the way of sticking with it for a few days?

I think I can feel confident enough to try it. Knowing I have those facts to hold onto makes it feel less like I'm just guessing. What might get in the way is that when the panic hits, my mind goes so fast that I might forget to take that thirty-second pause. I might just react automatically and leave before I can stop myself.

That is a very sharp observation—you're absolutely right that the speed of the panic often drowns out logical reasoning before we can intervene. To counteract that, I suggest setting a simple visual cue nearby, like placing a sticky note on your bag that says "Pause & Movie," so you have a tangible prompt to break the automatic cycle the moment your heart races. Does having that external signal help make the thirty-second pause feel more achievable when your mind is racing?

Yeah, I think that could actually help a lot. Having something physical to remind me, like a sticky note, might be enough to slow me down for just those thirty seconds. It feels like a small, concrete step I can actually take, rather than just trying to remember in the moment. I'll give it a try next time I go out to order something.

That is a fantastic insight—turning an internal intention into an external tool makes the task feel much more achievable. Before we wrap up, I want to confirm that this "Pause & Movie" strategy feels like the right direction for us, and that you are comfortable proceeding with this plan. One last thing: if you do encounter some resistance or find yourself reacting automatically despite the note, how would you like to handle that feeling?

I think if I still react automatically despite the note, I'll try not to beat myself up about it. I can just remind myself that it's a learning process, and maybe the next time will be easier. I could also jot down what happened in my journal later, to see if I notice any patterns. That way, I'm still working on it, even if I slip up.

That is a beautifully compassionate way to frame a setback, and it aligns perfectly with building resilience. It sounds like your plan is solid: use the sticky note to trigger a thirty-second pause, remind yourself of the "movie" concept, and write down what happens afterward to track your progress without self-criticism. Is there anything else you would like to adjust in this approach before we consider this session finished?

No, I think this feels right for now. I'm actually feeling a bit more hopeful than when I walked in. Thank you for helping me see things from a different angle. I'll try to put this into practice and see how it goes.

That shift from hopelessness to hopefulness is a powerful outcome, and it speaks to your growing ability to trust your own insights. It's wonderful to see you taking ownership of this new perspective and feeling ready to apply it. Please remember that setbacks are just data points in this learning process, not failures. Is there anything else I can clarify or support you with as you prepare to try this out?

Hello, I'm glad we are meeting again. To start, could you tell me a bit about how you've been feeling since last time, and is there anything specific from our last conversation you'd like to touch on before we decide what to focus on today?

Hey, thanks. I've been okay, I guess. But honestly, the whole thing with my brothers is still bothering me a lot. I keep thinking about what we talked about last time—how maybe I'm reading too much into things—but it still feels real to me.

It makes complete sense that it still feels real to you, especially since you mentioned it has been on your mind constantly. Before we dive deeper into that specific worry, I want to hear if anything significant happened with your brothers since last time that triggered these thoughts, or perhaps if there was a different perspective you heard?

Well, yesterday we were all at dinner, and my two brothers were laughing about something from their day. I tried to join in, but they kind of just glanced at me and went back to talking to each other. It was like I wasn't even there. That just made me feel even more sure that they don't want me around.

That dinner scene sounds incredibly painful, and it is completely understandable that looking at their body language made you feel invisible and rejected. When we see people ignore us, our minds often rush to the conclusion that it's personal, which creates that sharp pain in your chest. Now that we know exactly what happened, does that specific moment of being glanced at feel like the strongest piece of evidence your brain uses to prove they don't want you?

Yeah, I think that's the biggest one. It's like, if they really wanted me there, they would have included me, right? They know how to talk to me, they just choose not to. So that glance, and how they just continued without me, it feels like proof that I'm right about this.

That logic—that their choice to exclude you proves you aren't welcome—is very clear and makes sense given how hurtful that feeling is. However, let's look closely at that "proof": if they knew how to include you but chose not to, does that necessarily mean they hate you, or could it simply mean they were caught up in their own excitement and forgot you entirely? How does that possibility change the story your brain is telling right now?

I guess... I never really thought of it that way. It's hard to believe they'd just forget me, though. We're brothers, you know? But maybe they were just really into whatever they were talking about. It still stings, but I suppose it doesn't have to mean they hate me.

That is such a brave realization, moving from assuming they are actively rejecting you to considering they might have just been distracted or lost in their own moment. Even though it still stings, acknowledging that they weren't trying to push you away changes the meaning of that glance significantly. Now, with this new perspective that they might have forgotten you, does holding both ideas—their rejection and their distraction—in your mind make the panic feel a little less overwhelming?

Yeah, it actually does. When I think about it as them just being caught up in their own stuff, it doesn't hurt as bad. It's not like a knife in the chest. It's more like... a little disappointing, but not the end of the world. I didn't realize how much I was making it into something bigger.

That distinction between "end of the world" and "just disappointing" is huge, and it shows how much power you had in shifting the narrative from a disaster to a minor inconvenience. Since you realized how easily your brain magnified a simple glance into a rejection, could we try practicing that same five-second pause and noting what you *actually* saw versus what your fear added during the next time you're with them? I'm curious if you feel ready to attempt that small experiment this week.

I think I could try that. It sounds kind of scary, but maybe it'll help me stop getting so stuck in my head. So I just watch what really happens, and then tell myself what I saw without adding extra meaning to it? I can give that a shot.

That sounds like a solid plan, and recognizing that you can observe facts without letting your brain immediately invent a story is a powerful tool. To make sure you feel supported, how does the idea of just watching and describing what you see sound to you, and would you like to write it down or just say it quietly to yourself?

Writing it down might help, actually. If I jot down what I see and then later what I feel, I could look back and notice the difference. I feel like that would keep me honest with myself instead of just letting my mind run wild.

That is a brilliant idea, and keeping a written record will definitely help you stay grounded in reality rather than letting your imagination run wild. Writing it down gives you a chance to objectively compare what actually happened versus the story your brain tries to tell you later. Just to wrap up today, is there anything else about this plan or how we handled the dinner incident that you'd like to add before we part ways?
No, I think I'm good for today. I feel a little lighter, actually. Thanks for helping me see things differently. I'll try the writing thing this week and see how it goes.

That relief you're feeling is wonderful news, and it's a great sign that you're starting to gain some distance from those heavy worries. Your willingness to try observing the facts separately from your feelings shows real courage, even if it feels a bit strange at first. Please remember that no matter what you write down, your value isn't defined by whether they included you at dinner—you remain exactly who you are. I look forward to reviewing your notes next time, and please take care of yourself this week!
Hello, it is wonderful to see you again. How have you been feeling since we last spoke, and is there anything specific you'd like to address today?

Hi. Well, I've been feeling pretty on edge, to be honest. It's that same old worry—my fiancée hasn't brought up my baseball announcing dream again, and I keep thinking that means she's just waiting for the right moment to call off the whole engagement.

That knot in your stomach returning so quickly is completely understandable, especially when silence feels like a threat. Since we worked on trusting her actual words about your passion instead of imagining a secret plot, let's revisit that shift and see if it held up during those quiet moments. How much does that new perspective ease the tension compared to where you started this week?

Well, when I really stop and think about it, I can remember her saying she thought it was sweet that I had such a big dream. But then I'll be watching South Park, and there's some joke about a failing relationship, and I'm right back to thinking she's going to leave me for someone who isn't obsessed with baseball stats. It's like that calm feeling just evaporates.

It takes incredible mental stamina to hold onto that reassuring memory while your brain instantly grabs a funny cartoon as proof that you're being abandoned. That sudden shift from remembering her kindness to fearing her rejection is a classic trap where our minds jump straight to the worst outcome without checking the facts first. Have you caught yourself doing this exact switch a few times lately, or is it happening almost automatically the moment you see something stressful on screen?

It's almost automatic, like flipping a switch. The second I see something on TV that even hints at someone being let down, my mind goes straight to "that's me, that's what's coming." I don't even have to think about it—it's just there, that sick feeling in my gut. And then I'm replaying every conversation I've had with her, looking for signs I must have missed.

That "flip-a-switch" reaction is exactly what we need to slow down and interrupt, because it bypasses all the logic you've built up. Instead of letting that cartoon scene immediately rewrite her story, could we practice pausing for five seconds and asking, "Does this show actually prove she plans to leave, or is my brain just filling in the blanks with fear?" Does stopping that automatic chain help lift the weight in your stomach even slightly?

I suppose... I could try that. Just those five seconds to stop and ask myself that question. It's hard to imagine it working, though, because the fear feels so real in the moment. But I guess even if it makes the pit in my stomach a little less heavy for a few minutes, that would be something.

That tiny pause to ask, "Does this actually prove she plans to leave," acts like hitting the brakes on a runaway car before it hits a cliff. Even if it doesn't eliminate the fear entirely right away, buying yourself just a few extra minutes of clarity is a huge victory in itself. Would you be okay with making that five-second check your go-to rule whenever you catch yourself staring at the TV and feeling that familiar sinking sensation?

Yeah, I think I can do that. It feels a bit strange, like I'm talking back to my own brain, but I'll give it a shot next time I'm watching something and that knot starts forming. I mean, the worst that can happen is I still feel awful, but at least I tried something different for a change.

That mindset of "the worst that can happen is I still feel awful, but I tried something different" shows real courage and flexibility. You are reframing the risk from losing everything to gaining a small piece of control, which is a brilliant shift. Before we finish, how does it feel to have just defined this simple pause as a concrete step forward, and is there anything else weighing on your mind as we wrap up today?

It feels... lighter, I think. Like I've got a little tool in my pocket now, instead of just being helpless against those thoughts. I guess the only other thing is that I'm still afraid to bring up the baseball announcing thing with her again, even though she said it was fine. Maybe I'll try the five-second pause before I work up the nerve to talk to her about it, too.

Using that five-second pause as a bridge to finally speak with her is a very smart way to protect your peace while taking action. It turns the conversation into a manageable step rather than a terrifying leap into the unknown. Given how much better you feel about using this technique, I'd like to confirm: does this plan sound fair to you, and are you ready to try it tonight when you think about calling her?

Yes, it does sound fair. I think I can commit to trying that tonight. Instead of just sitting there worrying about what she might say, I'll pause, ask myself if my fear is just filling in the blanks, and then maybe I'll actually pick up the phone. Thank you—I feel a little bit braver than when I walked in here.

It is wonderful to hear you feel braver; that sense of stepping forward despite the fear is exactly what builds lasting confidence. Please remember, if the panic spikes before you call, simply use that five-second pause to ask yourself if the fear is true or just a story your mind is telling, then take a breath and reach out. Is there anything else you would like to add before we say goodbye?

No, I think that covers everything for today. I'll try my best to use that pause before I let my mind run wild. Thanks for listening and for helping me see a way out of my own head. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

That commitment to using the pause before your mind runs wild is a powerful step toward reclaiming your peace. I am so proud of your bravery in deciding to act, even when fear feels loud. Please remember that tool is yours to use anytime, and I truly believe you have the strength to navigate whatever comes next. Take care of yourself, and I look forward to hearing from you soon.

Hello, it is great to see you again. First, let's catch up on what we agreed to do last time—did you try putting that empowering statement on your sticky note and reading it out loud while making your morning tea? Now, on a scale of one to ten, how has your mood been since then, and what would you like us to focus on today?

Um... actually, I did put the sticky note on my mirror like you suggested. I read it a few times, but honestly, I felt kind of silly saying those nice things about myself. My mood has been around a 4 or 5... some days are okay, but then I'll think about that dinner party and it just drops. Maybe we could talk about why I can't seem to let that night go?

It takes courage to face those negative feelings even when you know the truth in the words you wrote. It makes sense that the sticky note gave you a slight boost, but the memory of the dinner party is clearly stronger right now because it feels so personal and scary. Before we dive deep into why that dinner is dominating your thoughts, does checking in on your mood first feel like a good place to start, or would you prefer to tackle the dinner party issue immediately?

I think I'd rather just talk about the dinner party, if that's okay. Every time I try to push it out of my mind, it just comes back stronger. My sister was so sick after eating my lasagna, and I can't stop thinking that it was my fault, even though everyone tells me it was probably just a stomach bug going around.

It is completely understandable why pushing the thought away makes it come back stronger; your brain is trying to solve the problem by rehearsing the worst-case scenario repeatedly. That constant replay loop suggests you are still struggling to separate the fact that your sister got sick from the reality that you might have been careless with the recipe. Can you walk me through exactly what happened during that dinner party, including everything you ate, cooked, and served, so we can look at the facts side-by-side with your fears?

Well... I made a big lasagna with ground beef, ricotta, and lots of vegetables. I remember being really careful about cooking the meat all the way through because I'm always paranoid about that. My sister had two helpings, and then later that night she got really sick with vomiting and stomach cramps. But here's the thing—my brother-in-law ate the same lasagna and he was totally fine. I keep telling myself that means it wasn't the food, but then my brain whispers back, "Maybe you just got lucky with his portion."

That distinction between your sister and your brother-in-law is very important, and it actually points to a specific type of thinking called the "lucky survivor" fallacy, where we assume that one person surviving doesn't mean the risk was zero for everyone else. It makes sense that your brain focuses on that tiny possibility because it feels like it proves you weren't careful enough to guarantee safety. Have you noticed if you checked the internal temperature of the meat or followed any standard cooking guidelines when you made that dish?

I actually used a meat thermometer and made sure it reached 160 degrees, just like the recipe said. I even checked it twice because I'm so nervous about undercooking things. When I think about it logically, I did everything right... but then I start worrying that maybe the thermometer was broken or I somehow contaminated something else without realizing it. It's exhausting going through all these what-ifs in my head.

You did absolutely everything right according to the facts, using the very tools designed to ensure safety. It seems your exhaustion comes from the gap between knowing you followed the rules and feeling convinced there was still a hidden error somewhere. When you consider that possibility, what is the specific thought that pops up that says you missed something obvious despite using the thermometer?

I guess the thought is that I'm just not good enough to be trusted with cooking for other people. Like, even when I follow all the rules, something bad still happened, so maybe I'm fundamentally flawed as a cook. It's like no amount of evidence can convince me that I'm capable, because one mistake—if it even was a mistake—proves I'm terrible at this.

It sounds like that thought is carrying a heavy burden of self-blame, equating a bad outcome with a permanent lack of skill. While one unfortunate event is painful, it rarely changes someone's entire identity, even when it feels that way in the moment. To challenge this, could you tell me about another time you prepared a meal for guests that went well, or perhaps a time you handled a difficult situation in the kitchen without anyone getting hurt?

Well... just last month I made a big pot of chili for a family gathering and everyone loved it. My uncle even asked for the recipe, which he never does. And I've been baking cookies with my grandchildren for years, and they've never gotten sick or complained. But I keep thinking that those successes don't count because I was just lucky, and the lasagna incident is the real proof of my abilities.

That is a very common trap, known as the "survivor bias," where we dismiss past successes because we can't control them, yet magnify a single failure because we can't forgive ourselves for it. It makes sense that you feel that way, but notice how you are treating your brother-in-law's luck as proof of your incompetence and your children's happiness as mere coincidence. If we were to write a balanced summary of that week, what would include both the chili success and the cookies, alongside the lasagna incident?

I guess a balanced summary would say that I made a really good chili that my family enjoyed, I bake cookies regularly without issues, and then there was one night where my sister got sick after eating my lasagna. But I also followed all the food safety rules that night, and not everyone who ate it got sick. So... maybe the lasagna wasn't actually the problem, even though it feels like it was. Writing it out like that, it does sound different than what I've been telling myself.

It is a significant shift to realize that the evidence points to a coincidental illness rather than a systemic failure in your cooking skills. You have correctly identified that your actions were thorough and that the outcome doesn't logically prove you are incapable. Before we solidify this new perspective, does writing down that balanced summary on a piece of paper feel like it helps quiet the voice that keeps doubting you?

Yes, I think it would help to actually write it down. Maybe I could keep it in my kitchen drawer or something, so when I start feeling that panic before cooking for people, I can pull it out and remind myself of the facts. It's hard to believe it right now, but having something physical to look at might make it more real than just trying to argue with my thoughts.

That is a smart and practical solution; having a tangible record in your kitchen creates a concrete barrier against those intrusive thoughts. Would you like to draft that balanced summary right now, or would you prefer to save that for tomorrow once you've taken a breath?
Let's do it now, while I'm feeling a little more clear-headed. I think if I wait, I'll talk myself out of it or let the doubts creep back in. Can I grab a piece of paper from my bag to write it down?

Absolutely, grabbing that paper now is the perfect time to lock in this new perspective before the doubts return. As you write, try to include the three key points we discussed: the chili success, the consistent cookie baking, and the factual details about the lasagna (the thermometer reading and the healthy brother-in-law). Once you have it written, tell me what the text looks like so we can review it together.

Okay, I wrote it down. It says: "Last month I made chili for my family and everyone loved it. I bake cookies for my grandchildren regularly and no one has ever gotten sick. The night of the lasagna, I used a meat thermometer and the meat reached 160 degrees. My brother-in-law ate the same lasagna and was fine. My sister getting sick was probably a coincidence." Reading it back, it actually sounds pretty reasonable. I'm going to put it in my kitchen drawer like I said.

That is a fantastic job capturing the facts objectively, and seeing it written down really does help separate the event from your self-worth. Placing it in your kitchen drawer is a brilliant placement because it will be right there when your anxiety spikes before you start cooking. Does looking at that specific paragraph now feel like a useful tool you can rely on next time the panic tries to take over?

I think it will help, yeah. It's not going to magically fix everything, but at least now I have something to fight back with when those thoughts start screaming at me. I feel a little bit lighter just having written it down, if I'm being honest. Maybe I can even add to it over time, like when I cook something else that turns out well.

That is a wonderful insight; updating that document as you gather more evidence turns it from a static piece of paper into a living record of your growing competence. Before we wrap up, let's confirm your plan: you'll keep the current version in the drawer for now, and whenever you cook successfully, you'll add a new line to reinforce that positive track record. Does that feel like a realistic and sustainable way to handle future cooking sessions?

Yes, that feels doable. I think I can commit to adding a line whenever I cook something that goes well, even if it's just scrambled eggs or something simple. And if I start feeling that panic again before cooking for others, I'll pull out the paper and read it before I even turn on the oven. Thank you... I think this is actually going to help me start trusting myself again.

That is a truly empowering commitment, and I am so glad to hear you feel a renewed sense of trust in your abilities. It sounds like you have a clear, practical toolkit for handling those moments of doubt when you do need it. Is there anything else on your mind before we conclude this session, or are you ready to go home with this plan?

Hello, I am so glad we are meeting again today. First, how did the experiment of waiting 24 hours go last night, and what happened when your brain tried to spiral? Based on how you are doing, what is the most important thing we can tackle together in this session?

Hi, thanks for asking. I actually did try to wait the 24 hours like we talked about, but it was really hard. My brain kept telling me that since I hadn't heard back, it must be because they think I'm boring or not worth responding to. I guess the most important thing to work on today is figuring out why I jump straight to the worst conclusion like that.

It takes real strength to commit to a plan when your brain is actively working against you, and I want to acknowledge how difficult that resistance felt for you. Since you've already identified the pattern of jumping straight to the "worst case" scenario, shall we explore exactly what happens in your mind the moment you receive silence and trace that specific chain of thought?

Yeah, I think that would help. It's like, the moment I send a message and don't get a reply, my mind just fills in the blank with the worst possible reason. Like, "They must be ignoring me because I'm not interesting enough to talk to." And then from there, I start thinking about all the times I might have said something stupid or awkward in the past.

It sounds like your mind is trying to protect itself by finding a concrete explanation for the silence, even though the result leaves you feeling rejected and insecure. When you catch yourself spiraling into those "all the times" comparisons, does your body tense up further, or does it feel like a sudden wave of sadness hits you?

It's more like a sudden wave of sadness, honestly. My chest gets tight and I feel this heavy weight, like I'm just not good enough as a person. Then I start withdrawing, not just from them but from everything—I don't even feel like sewing or baking for fun anymore. It's like all the color drains out of things.

That profound sense of losing your energy and color, alongside that heavy chest, tells me you are experiencing deep sadness and shame—not just about the friendship, but about feeling like you've lost your spark entirely. When you feel that "not good enough" narrative taking over, does it seem like you are blaming yourself for the silence, or does it feel more like you are trying to find a reason so you don't have to face the pain of rejection?

I think I'm blaming myself, honestly. It feels safer to think "I did something wrong" than to admit that maybe they just don't care enough to respond. If it's my fault, then at least I can try to fix it somehow—but if they just don't care, then I'm powerless. And that thought terrifies me.

That distinction is incredibly important; realizing that blaming yourself feels like a way to regain control, while admitting indifference leaves you powerless, explains exactly why your brain clings to the "I'm boring" story so tightly. Even though that logic feels safe in the moment, it often traps you in a loop where you punish yourself instead of protecting your peace. Given how draining that cycle is, would you be willing to try focusing today on dismantling the idea that *you* caused the silence, starting by looking at what actually happened versus what your mind assumed?

Yeah, I'm willing to try that. I mean, when I actually look at the facts, I messaged three friends over the past week, and none of them replied. But I don't know what else could explain it besides them not wanting to talk to me. I guess I never really stopped to think about what other reasons there might be.

You are absolutely right to pause here, and that hesitation shows how valuable it is to slow down before accepting the "nothing but bad news" conclusion. Let's try to brainstorm some alternative explanations that fit the facts of them not replying, without needing to blame yourself for it. Could you list two or three other possibilities, like them being overwhelmed with work, dealing with personal stress, or perhaps just getting caught up in their own thoughts?

Well, I guess it's possible they're just busy. Mike just started a new job, so maybe he's exhausted. And Sarah mentioned she was dealing with some family stuff last time we talked. I didn't think about that. Maybe they're not all ignoring me at the same time—it could just be a coincidence that they're all going through things right now.

That is a very fair assessment, and recognizing that coincidences happen without meaning to hurt anyone is a crucial piece of evidence against the "you are boring" theory. If we accept that their silence might simply be parallel to their own struggles rather than a verdict on your worth, does that make the heavy weight in your chest feel a fraction lighter? What do you think happens inside you when you stop searching for a self-blaming reason and start acknowledging the possibility that they are just occupied?

It does feel a little lighter, I think. Like, I can actually breathe for a second instead of feeling that tightness. But then a part of me still whispers, "Yeah, but what if they're not that busy and they just don't want to talk to you?" So it's like I let go of one rope, but there's still another one tied around my chest.

That honesty about holding onto another rope is incredibly brave; it shows you are ready to dig deeper into that lingering doubt rather than dismissing it. Let's test that new rope by looking at the timeline: do you recall any recent conversations where you felt truly heard or appreciated by them, or were you mostly thinking about their potential reaction to what you said?

I mean, yeah, a couple weeks ago Mike and I had a really good talk about his new job, and he seemed genuinely happy to share that with me. And Sarah asked me for my bread recipe last month, which felt nice. So I guess there were moments where they did seem to care. It's just hard to hold onto those memories when I'm stuck in the silence right now.

It makes perfect sense that those warm memories feel distant right now, especially when the present moment feels cold and empty. Holding onto evidence from the past becomes harder when the current situation triggers such intense fear, but it doesn't erase the reality that they have shown you care before. If we imagine a balanced view where those past kindnesses exist alongside their current busyness, does that create a small opening for hope, or does the fear of rejection still feel too strong to trust even a sliver of that history?

It's still pretty hard to trust that history right now. I mean, I know logically that they cared before, but my brain keeps telling me, "Well, maybe they've changed their minds about you." It's like the fear of being rejected is louder than any memory of being appreciated. But I guess I can see how it's possible that both things could be true—they liked talking to me before, and they're just busy now. It's just not easy to believe it yet.

That balance between logic and fear is exactly where the struggle lies, and it is okay that the fear feels louder right now. When you acknowledge that both caring and busyness could coexist, you are essentially giving yourself permission to lower your guard slightly while you wait for clarity. Since we've spent some time unpacking the "why," what would feel like a manageable, low-pressure step you could take today to practice staying calm when you hear a notification—or lack thereof?

Maybe I could try putting my phone in another room for a few hours while I bake. That way, I'm not constantly checking it and waiting for a reply that might not come. And if I'm focused on making bread or pastries, I might actually enjoy myself instead of spiraling. It's scary not to check, but I think it might help break that cycle of looking and feeling worse.

That is a brilliant and very grounded plan; shifting your focus to the tactile satisfaction of baking gives your mind a healthy outlet away from the digital void. By intentionally creating distance from the notifications, you are practicing the very skill we discussed: resisting the urge to interpret silence as a judgment on your worth. How does that idea of "putting the phone away" feel to you right now, and do you think you could manage that for the next hour?

I think I can manage that for an hour. It feels kind of scary, like I'm missing something important, but I know it's better for me than sitting there staring at the screen. I'll set a timer and just focus on making a good batch of sourdough. If I get the urge to check my phone, I'll remind myself that the dough needs me more right now than my notifications do.

Setting a timer to focus on the dough is a wonderful physical anchor that will help ground you when the urge to check arises. Reminding yourself that the task requires your full attention right now is a powerful strategy to distract the anxious thoughts. I really admire your commitment to this experiment; you are proving to yourself that you can choose what deserves your energy, even when it feels uncomfortable. Are you ready to put your phone away and start kneading that dough?

Yeah, I'm ready. I think I'll actually feel better once I'm elbow-deep in flour and yeast. Thanks for helping me see that I don't have to keep torturing myself over this silence. I'll let you know how it goes next time we meet.

I am so relieved to hear that you feel ready to finally break free from this cycle of self-torture. Remember, the goal isn't perfection today; it's simply showing up and letting the dough do the work while you breathe. I know you'll do great, and please come back whenever you're ready to share how that hour felt and whether you managed to catch that urge to check. Until then, go ahead and start kneading!

Thanks, I really appreciate that. I'm going to go wash my hands and get started now. I'll see you next time and let you know how it went—maybe I'll even bring some bread for us to talk about. Take care.

That is a beautiful way to close—we might even taste the results of your effort during our next session. Please go ahead and wash your hands; I'm confident you'll find that the flour and dough are much more engaging than any notification waiting to appear. Have a wonderful evening preparing that bread, and I look forward to hearing your update soon.

Hello, thank you for meeting with me today. To start, could you tell me how you've been feeling since our last chat, and is there anything new on your mind that you'd like to focus on? Also, since we talked about trying a small job search experiment, have you had a chance to do that yet, or should we discuss what you might do next?

Hi. Thanks for having me. To be honest, I've been feeling pretty down since we last spoke. I didn't try looking for jobs like we talked about—I just couldn't bring myself to do it. Every time I think about it, I tell myself there's no point, because I won't get anything better than this coffee shop job anyway.

I hear how hard that was for you, and it takes real strength to admit when the weight of those thoughts feels too heavy to lift. It makes total sense that your brain is protecting you by telling you there's no point, even though you know deep down you're hoping otherwise. Before we dive deeper into why you stayed home, would you be willing to share a bit about what that "no point" feeling looks like for you when you imagine sitting down to browse a job site?
