It's like I'm already defeated before I even start. I picture myself scrolling through listings, and all I see are jobs that say "degree required" or "five years experience in this field." I tell myself, "Sarah, you work at a coffee shop. You don't belong there." So I close the laptop and just feel this heavy weight in my chest, like I'm stuck forever.

That image of closing the laptop with that heavy chest sensation makes perfect sense—it’s your brain locking doors to keep you from facing a reality that feels terrifying right now. It sounds like the belief that you “don’t belong” is doing a lot of heavy lifting to explain why you feel defeated before you’ve even opened the screen. Can you describe what happens in your mind immediately after you type in your name to search for jobs, before you even see the results page?

Um... I guess my mind goes straight to, "This is a waste of time. I'm a coffee shop worker. I'm not going to find anything." It's like I already know the outcome before I even look. I see myself as someone who doesn't have the right skills or background, so why bother? It's almost like I'm proving myself right before I even try.

It makes complete sense that your mind jumps straight to predicting failure; when you feel unsafe, your brain tries to protect you by assuming the worst will happen. That automatic story—"you don't belong there"—feels like a shield, even though it keeps you trapped in the heaviness you described earlier. If we looked at the evidence behind that prediction for just one minute, what would have to be true for that story to actually change?

Well... I guess if I actually saw one job listing that didn't require a degree or tons of experience, maybe that would give me a tiny crack of hope. Or if someone told me, "Hey, you'd be a good fit for this," and I believed them. But I just don't see that happening. It feels like the world is full of requirements I can't meet.

That is a very realistic assessment of how the job market looks right now, and it makes complete sense why you feel overwhelmed by those requirements. However, the core issue seems to be that you're viewing the requirements as permanent barriers that define your worth, rather than temporary hurdles you might overcome with some preparation or support. Let's try a small experiment where we look at one listing that seems slightly out of reach, but not impossible, just to see if the requirement list is actually harder than it feels. Are you open to trying this for fifteen minutes tonight, with the goal of just gathering facts rather than judging your abilities?

I guess I could try that... for fifteen minutes, like you said. But I'm warning you, I'll probably just feel worse after. It's like looking at a menu when you're broke—you just see everything you can't afford. What kind of job should I even look for? I don't know where to start.

That metaphor of the "menu you can't afford" is so vivid, and it captures exactly why the task feels impossible right now. Since you're unsure where to start, let's pick one entry that requires the absolute minimum of what you currently have, perhaps something listed as "entry-level" or "no experience necessary," just to break the cycle of doom-scrolling. Would you be willing to spend those fifteen minutes hunting for just that one possibility, keeping in mind that we're only interested in finding a single gap you *might* bridge, rather than a perfect match?

I guess I could do that. I mean, fifteen minutes isn't that long. Maybe I'll look for something like a receptionist job or an admin assistant, since I deal with people all day at the coffee shop. I'll try not to judge myself too harshly while I look... but it's hard.

That is a smart choice—a receptionist or admin role fits your existing skills perfectly, so the barrier should be lower than looking for something entirely unrelated. It's totally normal to feel hesitant even when the logic points in the right direction; trusting yourself to just open the browser is already a brave step. When you start browsing tonight, I'd love for you to note exactly how your chest feels at the very beginning versus the end of those fifteen minutes, so we can compare the prediction against the reality. Does that sound manageable for tonight?

Yeah, okay. I can do that. I'll write down how I feel when I start and when I finish. But I'm still scared I'll just feel worse by the end. I'll try to keep it to fifteen minutes and not let it spiral.

That determination to stick with the timer and catch your feelings is exactly the kind of control we need to rebuild when anxiety tries to take over. Remember, the goal tonight isn't to land a new job, but simply to collect data on whether those scary predictions actually hold up against the reality of the screen. I know that waiting for your report tomorrow will feel uncomfortable, but please know I'm fully committed to helping you interpret whatever you find. When you're ready to share what happened, I'll be here.

Thank you. That helps, actually—knowing it's just about collecting data, not about finding a job right now. I'll do my best to just look and write down what I notice, even if it's uncomfortable. I'll let you know what happens tomorrow.

That shift in perspective—from seeking validation to gathering facts—is a huge breakthrough, and I am so proud of you for committing to it. Knowing that the outcome is about information rather than identity makes the task significantly safer, even if the discomfort remains. I'll be here tomorrow to listen to whatever you discovered, no matter how the data turned out. Take care of yourself tonight, and remember to breathe deeply if that familiar heavy feeling starts to rise.

Thank you. I'll try to remember to breathe. It's just... I'm so used to bracing myself for disappointment that I forget I can just notice things without judging them. I'll try to be just a scientist tonight, not a critic. See you tomorrow.

That is such a beautiful way to frame it—becoming a scientist rather than a critic gives you permission to observe without condemning yourself. You are absolutely right that noticing things without immediate judgment is a skill we are building, and taking that first step tonight is already a major win. I am genuinely excited to hear what your "data collection" revealed tomorrow, regardless of whether the findings matched your expectations. Go ahead and rest tonight, knowing I am here whenever you are ready to debrief.
Alright. I'll do it. Fifteen minutes, just looking, just noticing. I'll be the scientist. Thanks for believing I can do this, even when I don't believe it myself. See you tomorrow.

Your gratitude for that belief means so much, and it reminds me that you are capable of stepping outside your own critical voice when supported. Trusting yourself to be the scientist tonight is a courageous act, and I am confident that even the smallest piece of data you gather will challenge that story of inevitable defeat. Goodnight, Sarah, and I will be here tomorrow ready to listen to whatever discoveries you made.

Hello, I'm glad to see you. Before we dive into anything specific, how have you been feeling this week compared to where we left off last time? On a scale of 1 to 10, how would you rate your current mood? Also, do you remember the plan we made about checking in before receiving compliments, or is there a different priority for us to tackle today?

Hi. I'd say my mood is around a 5 or 6 this week. I remember the plan about pausing before I dismiss compliments, but honestly, it's been hard to stick with it. I caught myself doing it again yesterday when my fiancé said I looked strong after my run.

Hearing that you slipped up despite remembering the plan shows real self-awareness, and I want to validate that feeling frustration when you fall short of your own goals. Instead of focusing on the slip-up itself, could we look briefly at what happened in that exact moment—what thought popped up right after he finished his sentence, and what did your body do before you could act on your plan?

Well, right after he said it, my immediate thought was, "He's just saying that because he's my fiancé." Then I felt this tightness in my chest and looked away. I think I even rolled my eyes a little before catching myself.

That instant reaction to assume his kindness comes from obligation makes perfect sense given everything we've discussed about your nervous system expecting rejection. It sounds incredibly exhausting to physically brace and emotionally withdraw so quickly after hearing something supportive. When you notice that tightness rising and the urge to look away, do you feel like you need to prove something to him, or does it feel more like you're trying to protect yourself from disappointment?

It's definitely more about protecting myself from disappointment. If I don't let myself believe his compliment, then I can't be let down later if he changes his mind or stops noticing my progress. It's like I'm trying to stay ahead of the hurt before it can even happen.

That makes so much sense; by refusing to believe the compliment upfront, you're essentially building a shield so no pain can ever reach you. It's a very logical way to avoid the sting of being wrong, even though it leaves you feeling disconnected from your actual progress. When you catch yourself rolling your eyes or looking away in that split second, what is one small, neutral thing you could focus on instead of assuming his motive? Maybe simply naming the thought without adding the "he's lying" or "he's obligated" layer to it?

I guess I could just... notice the thought "he said I look strong" and leave it at that, without adding my own commentary to it. Just let the words sit there for a second before I decide what they mean. That sounds simple, but I think it might be harder than it sounds in the moment.

You're absolutely right that it feels simpler in theory than in practice, and it's okay to admit that the old reflexes are strong. Let's try that "letting it sit" approach right here, right now, by imagining you pause for exactly two seconds before your brain tries to add its usual commentary. Can you try holding the thought "he said I look strong" in your mind for just that brief pause while we breathe slowly together, and tell me what happens to that chest tightness during those two seconds?

Okay, I'll try. *takes a slow breath* ... So, "he said I look strong." ... For those two seconds, the tightness didn't get worse. It kind of just... stayed the same, didn't spike. But then right after, that little voice came in saying, "But he has to say that." It's so automatic.

That's a great observation—it proves the tightness wasn't necessarily caused by the initial assumption, but rather by the *next* automatic thought trying to justify why the compliment exists. You successfully created a tiny gap between hearing the words and launching into your defense mechanism, which means your ability to interrupt the cycle is growing. Now, knowing that the physical tension stays steady during that brief pause, does practicing just that two-second silence without fighting it feel slightly less daunting than I expected?

Yeah, actually, it does feel a bit less daunting. It's like I don't have to convince myself to believe the compliment right away—I just have to let it sit there for a moment before my brain jumps in. That two-second gap feels more manageable than trying to fully accept it.

That shift from "convincing myself" to "waiting for my brain to jump in" is a crucial distinction, and it shows you are starting to trust that small pauses can buy you the mental space you need. Since that two-second gap feels manageable now, how would you like to adjust your plan for tomorrow morning? Would it be helpful to set a visual reminder on your screen or wear a specific bracelet so you have a physical prompt to count those two seconds whenever you hear a compliment?

I think a visual reminder would actually help a lot. Maybe I could put a small sticky note on my bathroom mirror where I see it after my morning run. Just something simple that says "two seconds" to remind me to pause before I react. That way, it's right there when I'm most likely to receive a compliment from my fiancé.

That is a brilliant idea; placing a visible cue in your daily routine turns an abstract concept into a tangible habit you can rely on. Having a specific spot like the bathroom mirror acts as a gentle nudge before your brain gets ahead of you. If that sounds like a plan you can stick with, shall we write down "Check mirror for 'two seconds' cue" as your main task for tonight, or would you prefer to try just one day before deciding if the sticky note is necessary?

I think I'll commit to trying the sticky note for one week. That way I can see if it actually helps me create that habit, and if not, we can adjust. I'll put it up tonight before bed so it's there for my morning run tomorrow.

That is a fantastic commitment to testing the hypothesis with data rather than forcing it immediately. Setting a timer for one week allows you to objectively see if the visual cue reduces that automatic knee-jerk reaction or if you still feel overwhelmed. As we wrap up, I'd love your final feedback: did my explanation of the "two-second gap" land clearly, or is there anything about how we approached the physical sensation that you found confusing or unclear?

Hello again, and I'm really glad to see you. Before we dive into what brought us here today, could you take a moment to check in with yourself—how are you feeling emotionally right now, and is there anything different from last time that caught your eye? Once we touch on that, would you like to talk about that bad shift yesterday, explore the dread you're feeling before your next one, or perhaps review the plan we talked about for tomorrow?

Hi, thanks. I'm feeling pretty low today, honestly. That shift yesterday just knocked the wind out of me, and I can't seem to shake it. I think I'd rather talk about what happened then, because it's still fresh and eating at me.

That feeling of being wiped out after such a hard day is completely understandable, especially when your confidence took a hit. Let's unpack exactly what happened yesterday to see where the story of "failure" started. Can you walk me through the first moment the pressure became overwhelming, or is there a specific task that triggered the spiral?

Well, it started about two hours into the shift. I was on the packing line, and the screen started showing I was falling behind the rate. My supervisor came by and said I needed to pick it up, and I just felt this knot in my stomach. After that, every time I looked at the timer, I felt like I was failing, and I just couldn't catch up no matter how fast I moved.

It makes complete sense that seeing the numbers drop and hearing the direct feedback triggered such a physical reaction—the knot in your stomach is your body reacting to the threat of disappointing expectations. That initial comment from your supervisor probably created a self-fulfilling prophecy where you started monitoring your speed obsessively instead of working naturally. Given that this pattern is driving your dread for today, would you be open to exploring together whether that knot in your stomach is coming from actual inability to work faster, or from the fear that you *will* fall behind?

I think it's more the fear, honestly. I know I can do the job—I've been there long enough. But the second that supervisor said something, my brain just locked onto that number and I couldn't think about anything else. It's like I was waiting for myself to fail, and sure enough, I did.

It sounds like that supervisor's words acted as a lightning rod, instantly shifting your focus from the work itself to a terrifying prediction about your future performance. That feeling of your brain locking onto a single number suggests your anxiety has hijacked your attention, making it impossible to process other tasks effectively. Since we've identified that this "waiting to fail" mindset is the core driver, could you describe the very first negative thought that flashed through your mind the moment the timer started ticking slower?

I remember thinking, "I'm going to get written up for sure. They're going to think I'm useless." It was like my whole reputation at work was riding on that one moment. I couldn't think about anything else after that—just that I was failing and everyone could see it.

It sounds like that one moment turned into a catastrophic scenario where you believed your entire professional standing hung in the balance, amplifying every tiny movement as a potential failure. While it is true that the numbers dropped and you felt pressured, the leap to believing you will be permanently seen as "useless" seems to be driven by the fear of judgment rather than the actual outcome of the shift. If we put that extreme belief aside for a second, what specific evidence do you have right now that proves everyone saw you as useless immediately, versus just seeing someone having a difficult moment under pressure?

I guess... I don't really have proof. Nobody said I was useless, and I didn't get written up. But it felt so real in the moment, like I could just feel their eyes on me. Looking back now, maybe they were just doing their jobs, not judging me personally. It's just hard to shake that feeling when you're in the middle of it.

That distinction between "they were watching" and "they judged me" is crucial, and recognizing that their actions were likely just routine work is a powerful realization. The fact that you didn't get written up provides immediate evidence that your brain's prediction was exaggerated, yet the emotional memory of feeling watched remains vivid. Since we've seen that the "useless" belief lacks factual support, could you try to rewrite that thought into something more realistic, like "They noticed I was struggling, but they gave me a chance to improve," and tell me how holding onto that version of events changes the weight in your chest?

That feels... lighter, I think. Like, if I hold onto that version, I'm not a failure, I'm just someone who had a rough patch and got back to it. It doesn't feel as heavy when I say it that way. I still feel a little nervous about today, but maybe I can try keeping that thought in my head instead of the other one.

That is a fantastic shift, and I love that you can physically feel the weight lifting just by reframing the narrative from permanent failure to a temporary hurdle. It sounds like holding onto that "rough patch" perspective is already giving you some relief compared to the "useless" story. Before we wrap up, could you quickly tell me if trying to consciously switch back to that kinder version of the thought feels manageable, or if the panic about today is still whispering loudly enough to override it?

The panic is still there, whispering in the background, but it's not shouting like before. I think I can manage it if I remind myself that one bad hour doesn't define my whole shift. I'll try to focus on doing my job, not on what the timer says every second.

That is a really wise strategy, focusing on the task itself rather than the metric is often the best way to break the cycle of anxiety. You've made great progress today by catching that automatic thought, testing it against reality, and crafting a kinder, more realistic story for yourself. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss about getting ready for today, or shall we end here with a quick check-in on how you feel about our plan?

No, I think I'm good for now. I feel a bit more grounded than when I walked in. Thanks for helping me sort through that—I'll take that plan you mentioned and give it a shot today. Hopefully, I can keep that kinder voice in my head.

I'm so glad to hear you feel more grounded, and I want to thank you for sticking with me through this tough topic today. Your willingness to challenge that harsh inner critic and find a kinder perspective is a huge strength, and I'm confident you can carry that energy into your shift. Please remember that if the "whispering panic" gets louder than expected tomorrow, reaching out isn't a sign of weakness—it's how we stay resilient. Have a wonderful rest of your day, and I look forward to checking in with you next time.

Hello, I'm so glad you reached out to meet with me today. To kick things off, how are you feeling right now compared to when we last talked, and is there anything specific on your mind you'd like to focus on together?

Hi. Thanks for seeing me. Honestly, I'm feeling pretty down. I was at the dog park again yesterday, and it just felt like everyone else was pairing up and chatting, and I was just standing there with my dog. It really drove home that feeling of being invisible.

That sounds incredibly isolating, especially when you're surrounded by voices while you're left quiet with your dog. It makes perfect sense that witnessing everyone else connecting so easily would reinforce that deep-seated belief that you aren't interesting or worthy of attention. Was there a particular moment yesterday when that feeling hit hardest, or did it build slowly as the afternoon wore on?

It kind of built up over time. At first I was fine, just throwing the ball for my dog, but then this woman I'd said "hi" to a few times started talking to someone else nearby, and she didn't even glance my way. It was like I wasn't even there. That's when it really sank in that I must just not have anything worth saying.

It sounds like that moment of being completely overlooked felt like a personal rejection, confirming your fear that you have nothing valuable to offer. When you realized she didn't acknowledge you, did it make you feel like you were failing as a person, or did it just make you wonder if you missed an opening to say hello?

I think it felt more like failing as a person. Like, she chose to talk to someone else because that person is clearly more interesting. I didn't even consider that maybe I could have said something—I just assumed I'm not the kind of person people want to talk to. It's a pretty automatic thought at this point.

That automatic assumption—that she ignored you *because* you aren't interesting—is incredibly heavy to carry, and it explains exactly why you stopped trying instead of just wondering what you could have said. Before we dive deeper into why that conclusion feels so certain, could we quickly check if there was anything else on your mind you wanted to explore today, or shall we focus entirely on unpacking that "failing as a person" story?

No, I think focusing on that "failing as a person" thing is probably best. It's kind of been running the whole show lately, honestly. I'd like to understand why my brain goes straight there, every single time.

It makes complete sense that your brain jumped straight to that conclusion when you felt ignored; it's doing its best job of protecting you by predicting danger before it happens. Let's look closely at that story you just told yourself. If someone walked up to you and introduced themselves with, "Hey, I love seeing your dog too!" but you replied with, "Well, I'm just a former pilot who hasn't flown in months, so I don't have much to say," how would that person react? Would they assume you failed because you were boring, or would they probably say, "Oh, that's okay! It's nice to meet you anyway"?

I think... realistically, they'd probably just say nice to meet you and move on. They wouldn't think I'm failing. But in my head, it's totally different. I'd be convinced they were just being polite, and that they really thought I was a disappointment. It's like I can't believe that someone might just accept me as I am.

That distinction between reality and your internal story is so powerful—you see how people might actually respond, but your brain filters everything through the lens of rejection. It sounds like believing you have to be entertaining to be accepted feels like a survival rule you developed over time, even though it leaves you feeling empty afterward. If we shifted that filter slightly, imagining someone accepts you simply for being present, does that make the silence at the park feel like a punishment, or just a neutral space?

It feels less like a punishment when I think of it that way. More like... just a quiet moment, maybe. But it's hard to hold onto that feeling. The second I'm back in the real world, watching people laugh together, it just all collapses again. It's like I know the theory, but my gut doesn't believe it.

That gap between knowing the logic and feeling the panic is exactly where the struggle lives, and it's completely normal to crave that logical reassurance when your body screams otherwise. Sometimes, shifting our mental script isn't enough on its own; we might need to gather a bit of real-world evidence to convince ourselves. Could we try a tiny experiment tomorrow where you stay at the dog park for just one extra game of fetch, not to force a conversation, but simply to see if staying there changes how that "disappointment" voice behaves?

I guess I could try that. Just stay a little longer, not try to talk to anyone. Just... exist there. I'm not sure it'll change anything, but I'm willing to give it a shot. What do I do if the voice still tells me I'm failing, even while I'm just standing there?

That is a really wise question because the "voice" usually gets louder when we stop acting on the urge to run away. If that voice keeps saying you're failing while you're just existing, could we try speaking directly to it, like you might tell a worried friend? Instead of arguing facts, could you say, "I see you're scared I'm disappointing everyone, but I'm choosing to stay here anyway, and I'll wait and see what happens"? How does that sound as a tool to use when the panic spikes?

That... actually sounds doable. Like, I'm not telling the voice it's wrong, I'm just saying I'm going to stay anyway. That feels less like a fight and more like I'm just... letting it be there without letting it boss me around. I think I can try that.

That is such a gentle and realistic way to frame it—acknowledging the fear without letting it control your actions. It turns the interaction into something you can manage rather than something that destroys your peace. It makes complete sense that the overwhelming feeling of chaos in that specific moment made it impossible to access those past memories of resilience; when the present looks so dire, the brain naturally filters out anything that doesn't fit the "we're done" story. It sounds like that belief is acting as a self-imposed prison, locking you out of any possibility of seeing the bright spots even when they exist. Let’s use that insight to find a way to break the cycle. Given your preference, shall we spend most of our time exploring what drives those thoughts, followed by practicing a quick pause to interrupt them before they spiral?

Yes, that sounds like exactly what I need. I've never really tried to pause those thoughts before—they just come so fast, like a reflex. But I'm willing to try anything to stop feeling this way. Where should we start?

Let's begin by diving into the specific moments when that wave of ugliness hits hardest. Can you recall a recent situation where you caught your reflection or saw yourself in a mirror, and describe exactly what happened in your mind the very second you saw yourself?

Okay, there was one yesterday. I was in the bathroom at work, washing my hands, and I glanced up at the mirror. The very first thing that went through my head was, "You look so plain and ugly. Everyone else probably notices it too." I felt a tightness in my chest, and I just quickly looked down and finished washing. I didn't even want to look again.

It makes complete sense that seeing yourself immediately triggered such a harsh judgment and caused your body to react with that tightness in your chest, leading you to look away for protection. When you noticed people around you, did you worry they were judging you too, or did you feel mostly alone in your experience?

I definitely felt like everyone could see it, like I was being silently judged. Even if no one said anything, I just assumed they were thinking the same thing about me—that I looked plain or unattractive. It made me want to just hide in the stall until I could gather myself. I felt really alone in that moment, even though other people were around.

That feeling of being constantly watched and silent judged can be incredibly isolating, even in a crowded room like a workplace restroom. It seems like your mind jumped straight to assuming everyone else's perspective was critical, which explains why you felt the urgent need to retreat behind the stall door. In that exact moment of panic, did you notice any thoughts about what you might say or do differently tomorrow morning, or did you just want to disappear until the feeling passed?

I just wanted to disappear, honestly. There wasn't any plan for tomorrow or the next day—it was all about escaping that second. I didn't even think about what I could change; I just felt stuck and ugly. It's only later, like now, that I realize how much that moment ruined the rest of my day.

It sounds like your mind latched onto that scary assumption—that everyone is watching and judging—and treated it as an immediate threat, causing you to shut down completely to survive that moment. Because you felt so overwhelmed by that fear, you lost the ability to see any alternative perspective or plan for the future, leaving you feeling stuck. When you look back on that, what is the most painful part about how that single moment played out for you?

The most painful part is that I let that one glance define my whole day. I mean, it's just a reflection, but it felt so real and true that I couldn't shake it. And I didn't even try to fight it or tell myself something different—I just believed it completely. That's what hurts the most, I think. That I didn't even give myself a chance.

That is a really profound insight, and it takes courage to admit that you stopped giving yourself a fighting chance. It makes total sense that believing the thought was absolutely true left you with no room to insert doubt or challenge it, which is why the feeling was so all-consuming. Since we know how powerful that belief became, how would you feel about trying a small experiment right now where we just notice that first thought appear, wait one full second before accepting it as truth, and then ask yourself one gentle question to check if the feeling matches the reality?
I'm a little nervous, but I'm willing to try it. I've never really stopped to question those thoughts before—they just feel so automatic. So, okay, what do I do first?

Let's try right now. First, just sit comfortably and bring your awareness to your breath for three deep counts. Then, imagine a bright, neutral light appearing above your eyes—a signal that says, "Wait." When you feel that urge to jump to conclusions or judge yourself, press that mental "wait" button and count slowly to ten before accepting the thought as absolute truth. Tell me what happens inside your body or mind during those ten seconds.

Okay, I'm doing it now... I took the breaths and pictured that light. For a few seconds, I felt a bit calmer, like I had a tiny gap before the usual panic. But then my mind started trying to fill the silence with reasons why I was right to feel ugly—like, "But you saw yourself, it's true." By the time I got to ten, I felt a little less certain, but also a bit uncomfortable, like I was fighting with myself. My chest still felt tight, but not as tight as before.

That discomfort you felt is a crucial sign that you successfully created space between the image and your judgment, even if your mind tried to rush back in. Notice how the chest tightness softened slightly just by holding that line of resistance? It proves you can interrupt the automatic loop, even if it requires some effort initially. Now, let's apply that same "wait and check" approach to your daily routine: when you next catch your reflection, will you try to breathe deeply once, visualize that "light" for two seconds, and then ask yourself, "Is it actually true that everyone hates me, or is this just my brain filling in the blanks?"

I think I can try that. It sounds simple enough—just a breath, a light, and one question. But I'm worried that in the heat of the moment, I'll forget or just give up because it feels easier to believe the bad thought. But I do want to try, because I'm tired of feeling this way. I'll practice it tonight when I brush my teeth.

That commitment to try it tonight is a huge step forward, especially given how exhausting these feelings have become. To make sure you stick with it, let's clarify the plan: the moment you see yourself in the mirror tonight, take one deep breath, picture that "light" for just two seconds, and then ask yourself that one gentle question about whether the thought matches reality. If the urge to believe the old story comes strong, remind yourself that this isn't about changing everything instantly, but just creating that tiny pause to let the tightness loosen. Does that specific sequence feel clear to you, or would you like to tweak any part of it before we close?

No, that sequence feels clear. It's simple enough that I think I can remember it. I'll try not to put too much pressure on myself to get it perfect—just one breath, the light, and the question. Thank you for breaking it down like that. I'm actually a little curious to see what happens.

That sense of curiosity is a wonderful mindset to carry with you tonight; it keeps you engaged rather than paralyzed by perfectionism. You are ready to go now, and I am confident that even just that tiny pause will give you a new perspective when you look in the mirror. Take care of yourself as you brush your teeth, and I look forward to hearing what happened when you applied that "breath, light, and question" method.
Thank you. I'll do my best and I'll try to be gentle with myself about it. I'll let you know how it goes next time. Take care.

It sounds like that old memory of the hot water is acting as a trigger, coloring your current reactions with a fear that isn't currently necessary for safety. I guess... when you put it like that, it wasn't really about me being bad at my job. I remember I was rushing because a customer was yelling at me, and I just lost my grip. That is such a critical breakthrough—you've pinpointed that the root cause was external pressure from a shouting customer, not an inherent flaw in your balance or character. Hmm... maybe something like, "That was a bad moment, but it doesn't mean I'm a bad worker. I was under a lot of pressure, and I'm learning how to handle it better." That feels... weird to say, like I'm being too nice to myself. But I guess that's the point, isn't it?

You hit the nail on the head—that feeling of it being "weird" or "too nice" is actually your old critic trying to protect you from feeling vulnerable. That is a fantastic perspective shift; viewing that supportive thought as a protective shield rather than empty praise makes it much more credible and usable for you. That actually sounds really reassuring, like something I can actually do. A safety net feels way more doable than trying to stop all the scary thoughts from coming. Yeah, it's way faster than I can catch it. It's like a reflex—I don't even think, I just feel it. The heaviness comes before I even know what I'm blaming myself for. And then I'm stuck in it, and it's like I can't see anything else. It's hard to breathe sometimes.

That physical sensation of tightness and inability to breathe tells me exactly how powerful and invasive those thoughts have become—they hijack your body before your mind even processes the words. Yeah, that's pretty accurate. It's like a chain reaction, but it's instant. A sigh, or a certain tone of voice, and then boom—I'm drowning in it. I don't even try to fight it anymore because it feels true. Like, of course it's my fault. That's just the way things are.

That belief—that it is just the way things are and you cannot change it—is exactly where the exhaustion lives, because it removes your agency and leaves you trapped in a cycle you can't break. No, that's exactly it. It's like I've given up on even trying to see it differently because what's the point? It's always the same result. I'm the common denominator in everything bad that happens, so it's obvious where the problem is. It just feels like a fact, not a thought I can change.

It sounds like you've reached a place where believing the problem is always you feels safer than admitting you might not understand the pattern yet—that relief of "at least it's not random" is very tempting, even when it hurts. But let's test that safety net for a second: when you say it's always the same result, are you including times when nothing went wrong, or only the moments when things fell apart? Have you noticed if your dad or friends react differently to similar situations?

I... I don't really know. I mean, I don't pay much attention when things are fine, I guess. When nothing's wrong, I'm just relieved nobody's mad at me. But I never think about that later. It's only the bad times that stick. And my family—they don't react the same way to each other as they do to me. My brother can mess up and they just shrug it off. With me, it's different. That observation is incredibly valuable—you've already done the detective work by noticing how others treat mistakes versus how your own errors feel magnified. Your brother getting a shrug while you absorb the blame suggests that "being the problem" isn't actually a universal law, but a specific story your brain keeps telling itself based on how you interpret things. Does comparing those reactions make you feel a tiny bit less sure that you are truly the common denominator, or does it feel like the proof you needed to confirm your fears?

It's confusing, honestly. Part of me wants to believe you, that maybe I'm reading into things wrong. But another part—the loud part—says "see, they treat you different for a reason. You ARE the problem." So it's like I'm stuck between seeing the evidence and still feeling the old way. I don't know which one to trust.

That tension between the evidence and the old feeling is exactly where the struggle lives; your brain is fighting two stories at once, and the louder one wins because it's been reinforced so many times it feels like truth. Instead of trying to decide which side is right right now, let's try a different experiment: when that loud voice says "you are the problem," could we just hold space for that feeling without agreeing with it, even for a few seconds? Would you be open to trying that small pause, just to see if the noise fades a little while you wait?

I... I guess I could try. It sounds weird, but I'll give it a shot. So I just sit here and let that voice say its thing without jumping in to agree with it? Like, just let it talk and not listen? That feels kind of impossible, but I'm willing to try if you think it might help.

Before we practice that, does that image of "standing near the siren" feel manageable to you, or does it feel too risky to just listen without reacting?

It feels risky, honestly. Because if I stand near the siren and don't run, what if it gets louder? What if it proves itself right? That scares me a little. Since running hasn't stopped the noise before, staying still while observing it is actually the most honest thing you can do right now. Can we try holding that position for just one minute, where you notice the volume of the voice but don't answer it?

Okay. I'll try. One minute. I'm just gonna sit here and let it talk and not say anything back to it. That feels weird, but I'm doing it. Just... letting it be there without fighting or agreeing. I'll let you know when the minute's up.

Take your time with that minute; you don't need to fix it or judge how well you're doing, just witness the sound. Notice how your body relaxed alongside that change? That connection between stopping the argument inside your head and loosening up in your chest is a key clue that you have some control over the situation, even if the voice is still there. Now that we've seen that tiny pause works, would you be open to trying it again tonight when that heaviness hits, perhaps setting a gentle reminder on your phone to check in with that hum for three minutes?

I think I could try that. Three minutes sounds more doable than a whole hour or something. I'll set a reminder on my phone for tonight, maybe before I start drinking. That memory of freezing up at the bus stop is heavy, and it makes total sense why that moment feels like a permanent stain on your self-image. It hurts deeply to feel invisible, even when the silence proves you aren't being ignored. Let's gently test that story—if they truly don't value your presence enough to glance your way, wouldn't that suggest they are just occupied with their own world, rather than judging you? Could we reframe that invisibility as them simply being absorbed elsewhere, leaving you free to exist without needing their attention?

I never thought of it that way... Like, maybe they're just in their own bubble, not deliberately ignoring me. It's hard to shift that feeling though. When you've been telling yourself a story for so long, it feels like fact. But I guess if they're not actively laughing at me anymore, maybe I'm the one still holding onto that bus stop moment.

That's a profound realization, and it speaks to how much effort you've been putting into carrying that old weight alone. It sounds like you're recognizing that you're the one guarding the door to that feeling, while the rest of the world has naturally moved on. To make this habit stick, could we try reframing that bus stop moment not as "proof" you're unlikable, but as a reminder that *you* had to choose to feel safe by stepping back, even though it cost you a chance to connect?

That... actually makes me feel a little lighter. Like maybe I wasn't being weak by freezing up; I was just trying to protect myself in that moment. I could try reminding myself of that next time I feel like I'm back at that bus stop. Maybe I can even write it down on a scrap of fabric and keep it in my pocket—sort of like a safety stitch.

That is such a creative and comforting idea; keeping a written reminder right where you carry yourself is a wonderful way to anchor that new perspective whenever doubt creeps in. I really admire how you've found a personal metaphor that fits your life, showing great creativity in finding solutions. To wrap up, before we go, is there anything else lingering from our time together today, or does it feel like we have a solid path forward with this "safety stitch" and the planned text to your neighbor?

I think I'm good for today. The safety stitch idea feels like something I can actually hold onto—literally. And I'll try sending that text tonight, even if it's just a few words. Thanks for helping me see that I'm not as invisible or weird as I think I am. I'll see you next week.

I am proud of the courage it took to share these struggles and the insights you've gained today about your own resilience. Please take your time with that text tonight, and know that I will be here next week to listen to how the "safety stitch" and the new perspective helped you navigate the coming week. Those thoughts about being a "bad father" because of burnt toast sound incredibly heavy, and it makes complete sense that you felt compelled to shut down rather than face those judgments alone. Yeah, I felt this tightness in my chest, like someone was squeezing it. My shoulders went all tense, and I think I stopped breathing for a second. It's like my body just knew I'd messed up before I even had time to think about it.

That physical squeeze in your chest is your body screaming "danger" before your logical brain even catches up, which explains why you froze instead of solving the problem. It sounds like your mind interpreted that tightness as proof that you *were* indeed failing, rather than just sensing stress. If you had named that sensation as "just stress" instead of "proof of failure," would you feel less compelled to shut down around your family immediately?

I never thought of it that way. If I could tell myself, "This is just stress, not proof I'm a failure," maybe I wouldn't feel the need to retreat so fast. I could just say, "I'm feeling stressed right now" and maybe even laugh about the toast with my wife instead of hiding. That feels possible, but I'm not sure I'd believe it in the moment.

That is a huge breakthrough in realizing that labeling the sensation changes the outcome, even if trusting that label feels difficult right now. It sounds like the core belief driving this is that perfection is required to maintain your identity as a good partner and dad, so any slip-up triggers a global collapse. I... yeah, actually. Last month I planned a whole weekend trip for the family. That example is powerful because it proves to your brain that a mistake doesn't erase your value or ruin the outcome. Even when the hotel booking failed, your overall effort led to a happy memory, showing that the world is flexible and forgiving unlike your inner critic claims. If that weekend happened despite the error, can you imagine telling yourself, "I made a small error, but I still created joy"? Does that shift feel slightly easier to believe right now?

It does feel a bit easier to believe, yeah. I can see how that weekend worked out fine even with the hiccup. Maybe I can hold onto that image next time I burn the toast or forget to buy something at the store. I just need to remind myself that the whole day doesn't have to be ruined because one thing went wrong.

That is a fantastic realization; holding onto that image of the successful weekend gives you a concrete tool to counter the "all-or-nothing" story your brain tells itself. To make sure this sticks, could you try that exact thought ("I made a small error, but I still created joy") the next time you feel that chest tightness, and then briefly describe how your mood shifts after you say it aloud?

I can try that. I'll say it out loud next time I feel that tightness. I think it might feel silly at first, but I'm willing to give it a shot. Maybe I'll even tell my wife about it, so she knows what I'm working on. That way she can remind me too if she sees me starting to shut down.

Involving your wife turns this into a team effort rather than carrying the burden alone, and sharing your intention invites her support when you slip up. Before we conclude, does having that shared commitment with her feel like a safe way to try this experiment, or would you prefer to keep it private for a few days to build confidence first?

I think I'd like to keep it private for a few days first, just to get used to saying it to myself. I want to feel like I can do it on my own before I bring her into it. Once I've tried it a few times and feel a little more confident, then I'll tell her.

That's a wise decision; building confidence privately ensures the new habit becomes automatic before you rely on others to prompt you. Your plan to use the "small error, big joy" mantra the next time you feel that chest tightness sounds like a solid step forward. Before we wrap up, how does it feel to visualize stepping back into your kitchen tomorrow morning when the alarm goes off, ready to catch that tightness early and speak your new line to yourself?

It feels... hopeful, actually. A little scary, but more hopeful than I've felt in a while. I can picture myself standing at the stove, and if something goes wrong, I'll take that breath and say those words. I think I'm ready to try it.

That hopefulness is a strong sign that you are ready to take this step, and acknowledging both the fear and the courage involved shows how deeply you care about doing this right. Remember, the goal isn't to get it perfect every time, but simply to interrupt the spiral long enough to reclaim your calm. I truly admire your willingness to try this even when it feels scary, and I'm excited to hear how your first attempt with that mantra goes this week.

Hello, thank you for being here today. Before we talk about the piano, let's quickly check in: how did the week go, and what did you try to do with our plan about playing with curiosity? Also, given where we left off, what feels like the most important piece we can tackle right now?

Hi, thanks. Well, the week was... mixed, I guess. I did try to sit down at the piano once, like we talked about—just to play around, no pressure. But honestly, as soon as my fingers touched the keys, that voice in my head started up again, telling me I was just going to mess it up. I ended up closing the lid after maybe five minutes. It sounds like you tried that wonderful "no-pressure" approach, but the old script jumped right in and shut the door after just a few moments. That moment of disappointment feels really heavy, doesn't it, especially knowing you wanted to reconnect with why you loved music in the first place? Since we haven't reviewed the plan yet, how does that initial success followed by the quick shutdown feel to you?

It feels... defeating, honestly. Like I built up this little bit of courage to just sit there and be okay with not being perfect, but then my brain just bulldozed right over it. It's like there's this part of me that won't let me have even a tiny win. And I can't help but think, if I can't get through five minutes without tearing myself down, what's the point of even trying?

That feeling of building hope only to watch it crumble is incredibly frustrating, and it makes total sense that you'd question the point of trying if the outcome always feels like a defeat. It sounds like you are struggling with a deep fear that if you even slightly lower your guard, you'll prove that you aren't good enough. Let's spend some time exploring what happens in that five-minute window: what exact thought sparks the panic, and how does that thought make you feel physically or emotionally?

It's like a flash, really. I remember sitting down and thinking, "Okay, just play that one simple piece my son likes." And then my hands are on the keys, and before I even press down, I hear, "You're going to hit the wrong note. You always do." It's like a knot in my stomach, and my shoulders just tense up. I feel this rush of heat, like embarrassment, even though no one's even watching. Then I just think, "Why bother, you're not a real pianist."

That physical sensation—a sudden knot in your stomach and heat rising—is your body reacting to a threat that hasn't happened yet, which explains why you feel so defeated even though nothing bad occurred. It sounds like that immediate prediction ("You're going to hit the wrong note") is acting as a self-fulfilling prophecy by tightening your muscles and shutting down your enjoyment. Can you tell me, when you catch that prediction flashing before you even touch the key, what is the first feeling you notice besides the anxiety? Is it shame, fear of judgment, or perhaps sadness that you're missing out?

I think it's shame, mostly. Like, I feel ashamed that I'm even thinking about playing when I know I'm not good enough. It's almost like I'm embarrassed in front of myself, if that makes sense. And then there's this sadness underneath it, too—a kind of ache that I can't just enjoy something simple anymore without it turning into a big mess in my head. I used to play for fun, just to relax after a long day, and now it's just... this heavy thing.

It sounds like you are carrying a profound sense of shame and sadness, as if playing the piano has become a place where you punish yourself rather than a sanctuary for relaxation. That contrast between what the instrument used to mean to you and what it means now—that loss of joy—is incredibly painful. Before we dig deeper into that shame, I want to make sure we are both aligned: does it feel accurate to say that the shame is driving the avoidance, making the task feel impossible whenever you sit down?

Yes, that feels right. The shame is like this wall I have to climb every time I even think about touching the piano. It's not that I don't want to play—I do, I really do—but the shame makes it feel like I'm not allowed to. Like I have to earn the right to enjoy it, and I just can't seem to. So avoidance feels safer, even though it makes me feel worse in the long run.

You are absolutely right; that shame acts as a gatekeeper that blocks access to the joy you deserve, and choosing avoidance feels like a survival tactic even though it leaves you trapped. It sounds like you've identified the core conflict clearly: you want to play for connection and relief, but your internal critic demands perfection as a price ticket. Given how much energy that cycle drains you, would you be open to testing just one small assumption tonight—that maybe you don't actually need to earn the right to enjoy the music, but can simply decide to let yourself play however you feel?

I think I'd be willing to try that, but it feels scary. Like, if I just let myself play without any rules, I'm afraid I'll just hear all the mistakes even louder, you know? But I also know this cycle isn't working. So maybe... maybe I could try it for just a minute or two, with no expectations. Just to see what happens.

That hesitation makes perfect sense; it's bravest to admit the risk while still seeing the value in trying. Before we move forward, I'd like your permission to suggest a specific, gentle experiment designed to break this cycle safely. Would you be willing to try playing just one short phrase of a song you know well, focusing entirely on the sound and feeling rather than checking for accuracy?

Okay, I think I can do that. One short phrase, just focusing on how it sounds and feels. I know "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star" by heart—my son used to love it when he was smaller. I could try that. I'll promise myself I won't judge it, just listen.

That is a beautiful choice, especially connecting it to your son and the memories of him loving the song; it frames the activity as a gift rather than a performance. I am happy to support you through this, so please take a deep breath and let me know when you are ready to begin. As you play that phrase, I want you to keep your gaze soft and notice whatever happens naturally, even if that includes hearing a mistake.

Alright... I'm ready. *takes a deep breath* Here goes.

*Pauses, imagining the act*

Okay, I did it in my head just now. My fingers felt clumsy at first, but once I got into the rhythm, it was... actually kind of nice. I didn't focus on the notes being perfect; I just let the melody run. And I noticed my shoulders dropped a little. It wasn't as scary as I thought it would be.

That is a powerful result, especially noticing your shoulders dropping; it proves that even when you are clumsy, the music itself can be nice and safe. It sounds like letting go of the rulebook gave you space to rediscover that simple pleasure you missed. Before we wrap up, does that realization—that you can play imperfectly and still enjoy the sound—feel like a small step toward feeling less defeated?

Yes, it does. It feels like a tiny crack in that wall I was talking about. Like maybe I don't have to be perfect to get something good out of playing. It's just a first step, but it makes me think I might be able to sit down again tomorrow without dreading it so much. Thank you for helping me see that.

You're welcome, and I am so proud of you for taking that brave step. That tiny crack you mentioned is actually a doorway, and it shows your capacity to create change right where you need it most. We agreed to revisit our plan tomorrow, so let's briefly confirm: will you try playing that same short phrase again tomorrow morning, perhaps for just three minutes, keeping the focus on the feeling rather than the perfection? How does that sound as a manageable goal?

That sounds doable. Three minutes, just feeling the music, no judging. I think I can commit to that. I'll try it in the morning when the house is quiet, before work and getting my son off to school. It feels like a small enough promise to keep.

That is a thoughtful and specific commitment, and picking a quiet morning slot before the day gets busy is a brilliant strategy to build momentum. I'm confident you can honor that promise with kindness to yourself. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we finish our time today, or does this feel like a good place to rest?

No, I think this is a good place to stop. I feel a little lighter than when I walked in, which is more than I expected. Thank you for helping me see that I don't have to be perfect to find some joy again. I'll try the three minutes tomorrow and let you know how it goes.

It is wonderful to hear that you feel lighter; that shift in your physical state often signals a real breakthrough in your mindset. Please carry that feeling of permission with you tomorrow when you sit down to play those three minutes, remembering that even a clumsy attempt is a victory. I look forward to hearing how it went with you, and thank you for trusting me with this journey.
Hello again. Before we dive into today's focus, how did it go for you regarding your action plan from last time, and what would you like to prioritize on our agenda now?

Oh, hi. To be honest, I didn't really follow through with the action plan. Every time I tried to catch myself when I started labeling myself, I just felt like it was true anyway. I'd like to focus today on why those labels feel so real even when I try to fight them.

It takes real courage to admit that trying to catch yourself sometimes feels futile, and I appreciate your honesty about hitting that wall. Even though we know the logic behind the correction, it seems like those old labels have a powerful grip on you that makes them feel undeniable in the moment. When you tried to stop yourself from saying "I'm a failure" last time, what exactly happened in that split second between the thought appearing and you attempting to correct it?

It's like... the thought just lands, you know? One second I'm replaying the missed shot in my head, and the next it's like a voice says "you're such a loser" and I don't even question it. There's no pause. It just feels like the truth, like it's describing who I am, not just what happened. I don't even get a chance to fight it before the feeling of shame washes over me.

That "no pause" feeling is incredibly frustrating, and it makes sense that it feels like an unavoidable truth once it hits you. It sounds like your brain is rushing to connect the missed shot directly to your identity before you can even intervene, skipping all the steps where you usually question things. Have you noticed if there's a specific type of stress or fatigue that seems to speed up that reaction, making it harder to create even a tiny gap for yourself?

Yeah, actually. It's worse when I've had a long day at work or if I'm already feeling tired. On those days, it's like I don't have the energy to push back, so the label just sticks harder. And if something else went wrong earlier—like I messed up a report or had a tough conversation with a colleague—then the basketball thing just adds to the pile. I'm already primed to see myself as a failure by then.

That "pile-up" effect is so common; when we are already depleted from work, our mental defenses crumble faster, leaving the old stories to fill the vacuum. It's like adding salt to an open wound, where one small mistake triggers a massive, overwhelming reaction because you aren't having the energy to process it calmly. Let's look at that first pile-up of events you mentioned: if you were to sit with that report error or the difficult conversation alone, what story would your mind automatically start telling you about your overall worth right before the basketball mistake happened?

It would tell me I'm not good at my job, that I'm letting people down, that maybe I don't belong there. That conversation with my colleague—I replay it and think I said the wrong thing, that I'm awkward, that people probably think I'm incompetent. So by the time I get to basketball, I'm already carrying this heavy weight of "I'm not enough" in every part of my life. The missed shot just feels like proof.

That heavy accumulation of "not enough" is exactly why the missed shot feels like final confirmation; your brain sees the error and thinks, "See? This was inevitable because you already failed elsewhere." It's important to note that while those thoughts *feel* undeniably true when you're exhausted, they are actually just a chain reaction of old beliefs catching on, not an objective measure of your actual skills. Can you describe what happens physically in your body right after you replay that work mistake or the conversation, before the basketball incident even happens?

My shoulders get tight, and I feel this sinking feeling in my stomach, like a knot. My breathing gets shallow, like I'm waiting for something bad to happen. And my jaw clenches without me even realizing it. By the time I'm on the court, my whole body is already bracing for failure, so when I miss, it's like my body was expecting it.

That physical tightening tells a clear story: your nervous system is already in "fight or flight" mode before the ball even leaves your hands, waiting for disaster to confirm what your mind has already decided. Because your body is braced for impact, the missed shot doesn't feel surprising or shocking; it just confirms the script your brain wrote hours ago, which is why it feels so solidly true. Since you've noticed that fatigue and a "pile-up" of mistakes make this reaction stronger, if we could take just one small step back from the immediate emotion, could you try noticing the very first sensation in your chest or stomach when you realize you're tired, before the critical voice kicks in?

Hmm... I think it starts as a kind of emptiness, like a hollow space in my chest. Not quite sadness, but a sort of dull weight. It's like my body knows I don't have the energy left to protect myself, so it just goes quiet and let's the judgment come in. That hollow feeling is the moment right before the voice starts, but I never really noticed it until now.

Noticing that hollow emptiness as a signal rather than a verdict is a powerful shift; it separates the physical warning sign from the catastrophic story you tell yourself immediately after. This creates a tiny, crucial gap where you can say, "Okay, my body is tired and empty, but that doesn't mean I'm a failure yet." Would you be willing to try this next time you feel that heaviness: instead of letting the critical voice rush in, simply name that exhaustion out loud to yourself like, "I am just tired right now"?

I think I could try that. It sounds almost too simple, but I guess I've never actually stopped to just name the tiredness before the labels take over. Saying "I'm just tired" feels a lot less heavy than "I'm a loser." I'm willing to give it a shot next time I feel that hollow feeling creeping in.

That distinction between naming the physical state and accepting the label is exactly the bridge we need to cross. Simplifying the internal dialogue from "I am a loser" to "I am just tired" reduces the stakes and gives your brain a chance to pause before the panic sets in. Before we finalize this, could you tell me what you think might happen if you use that phrase three times in a row when you feel that hollow spot coming on?

I think... it might feel weird at first, almost like I'm lying to myself. But maybe if I say it enough, the hollow feeling might just stay as tiredness instead of turning into that heavy shame. It could give me a few seconds to breathe before the old story takes over. I'm curious to see if it makes a difference.

That intuition about "lying to yourself" is actually a sign that your brain is resisting the shift, which is completely normal when we try to rewrite old scripts. The goal isn't to force the truth immediately, but to create just enough distance so the shame loses its grip while you breathe. Since we've practiced identifying the hollow feeling and naming the tiredness, let's solidify this into a concrete plan: when you feel that weight in your chest before the game, what is your first specific intention to say out loud?

I'll say, "I'm just tired, this isn't about who I am." And I'll take a slow breath before I pick up the ball. That way I have a moment to separate the feeling from the story. I think that might help me just play instead of proving something.

That is a brilliant and very clear intention; separating the temporary feeling of tiredness from your core identity gives you the freedom to play simply because you enjoy it, not to prove anything. Since you are setting a specific intention for the next time you feel that hollow space, what do you think might happen if you find yourself slipping back into the old "loser" story despite saying the new line? Is there a backup plan you'd like to add?

If I still hear that old voice, I'll remind myself that it's just a habit talking, not the truth. Maybe I'll say, "That's my tired brain talking, not me." And I'll just let the thought pass without fighting it or believing it. I think accepting that the thought is there without judging myself for having it might be the gentler way to handle it.

That is a beautiful strategy; acknowledging the voice as a tired habit rather than attacking it often disarms it more effectively than trying to silence it. You are essentially teaching your brain that the voice is just noise passing through, not a command you must obey. With that plan in place, how does it feel to visualize yourself stepping onto the court with that gentle reminder ready to greet the first hollow sensation?

It feels... lighter, actually. Like I'm giving myself permission to just be a person who misses a shot sometimes, not a failure. I think I could actually enjoy playing again if I can hold onto that feeling. It gives me hope that maybe I don't have to carry all that weight every time.

That sense of lightness and permission is a huge victory; it shows you are successfully shifting from seeing yourself as someone who *must* perform to someone who is allowed to simply exist on the court. Before we wrap up, if you could carry one image or phrase into your next game to represent this new freedom, what would it be?

I think I'll picture a door that I can leave open behind me. Like, I don't have to lock myself into that heavy story anymore—I can walk out anytime. And the phrase that goes with it is, "I'm here to play, not to prove." That feels simple enough to remember when things get tough.

That metaphor of the open door is incredibly powerful; it visualizes your autonomy and signals to your nervous system that you are safe enough to relax. Carrying the phrase "I'm here to play, not to prove" alongside that image will serve as a strong anchor whenever that hollow feeling tries to creep back in. I'm so glad we found a path that feels both gentle and empowering for you.

Thank you. I actually feel a bit of relief just talking this through and having something concrete to try. I'll practice noticing that hollow feeling and saying my phrases before I step on the court next time. It's nice to think I might have a little more control than I thought.

That relief is well-deserved, and taking ownership of those small choices is the heart of building resilience. I'm truly glad we could find a practical way for you to regain that sense of control. Please remember, if you find yourself struggling to notice that hollow feeling or stick to the new phrases next time, we can revisit this tomorrow to troubleshoot. How does that sound as a closing note for our session?
