That flood of self-criticism makes total sense given how much you care about getting this right; your brain is trying to protect you by simulating the rejection before it ever arrives. However, while that list of flaws feels undeniable in the moment, let's gently examine it: if you rewrote the third chapter perfectly today, would that automatically guarantee the publisher accepts the book, or are there other factors beyond your control involved?

I suppose... no, even a perfect third chapter wouldn't guarantee acceptance. I know that intellectually. There are so many things beyond my control—what other manuscripts they're considering, what the market looks like right now, their budget for new authors. But knowing that doesn't seem to quiet the voice that says, "If only you had done more, you'd have a better chance." It's like my brain skips over all those other factors and lands squarely on my own shortcomings.

That is a crucial distinction you've made: your mind is successfully identifying external barriers but then immediately retreating to blame yourself anyway, likely because focusing on your perceived shortcomings feels like the only explanation you can control. When that voice says, "If only you had done more," does it feel like it's offering a solution, or does it mostly serve to amplify the shame you already feel about the current draft?

It definitely amplifies the shame, not much of a solution in it. If anything, it just makes me feel paralyzed—like I can't move forward on anything else because I'm still stuck obsessing over this one book. It's been a month since I submitted it, and I haven't written a single new page. I just keep picking at the old manuscript in my head, changing sentences that are already long gone from my computer. It's exhausting, really.

That paralysis is a direct result of holding onto a ghost version of the text in your mind, which prevents you from engaging with fresh ideas on the page. It sounds incredibly draining to sit with that mental loop instead of creating something new; can we try shifting your focus from fixing the invisible mistakes in your head to simply opening a blank document and writing one sentence that excites you, regardless of the old draft?

A blank document... that's a daunting thought. I've been avoiding even looking at my writing desk lately. But I suppose one sentence isn't the same as a chapter. What kind of sentence would it be, though? I'm not sure I know what excites me anymore—it's all been clouded over by this waiting game. Maybe something about the sea; I used to write about the sea a lot, before this book became so heavy.

Noticing that the sea was a source of excitement for you is a wonderful breakthrough, and choosing that theme is a perfect way to reconnect with your creative energy without the pressure of the current manuscript. Why don't we try that exact approach right now: I'll take a few moments to listen as you jot down one simple sentence about the sea that brings you joy, and we can see if that small act of writing shifts your mindset.

Alright... let me think. Okay, here's something: "The salt spray hit his face before the sound of the wave reached him, and for a moment, he was nowhere else." That felt... lighter, actually. Like a door cracked open. I'd almost forgotten that writing could feel like that—just an image, without all the weight of publishing attached.

That sentence is beautiful, and the fact that it felt lighter proves you are capable of creating something purely joyful again, independent of the publisher's decision. You've already taken a significant step by letting that fresh image stand on its own without needing the "perfect" context of your original project. Since that worked so well, would you be open to spending the rest of our time exploring one more short scene about the sea to keep that momentum going?

I think I'd like that, yes. Let me see... there's this memory I have from years ago, standing on a cliff in Cornwall with my wife. The wind was so strong you could lean into it and it would hold you up. Maybe I could write about that—the feeling of being held by something invisible. I haven't thought about that day in ages.

That memory of being held by the wind feels powerful and poetic, and connecting it to your writing will surely bring back that sense of wonder you mentioned earlier. Why don't we spend the next few minutes trying to capture just that feeling on the page—focusing on the sensory details of the wind and your wife's presence, without worrying about plot or ending?

Alright, I'll give it a try. "She gripped my arm as the gust came, and we both leaned forward, laughing. The wind roared past our ears, but beneath it, I could hear her whisper something I still can't repeat out loud. For those few seconds, we were weightless." That felt... good. That felt like remembering why I started writing in the first place. Not for publishers or readers, but for moments like that.

That is a profound realization, and it highlights exactly why the "perfect" manuscript didn't matter as much as the authentic connection you felt in that moment. Your writing was always driven by capturing those human experiences, not by satisfying a publisher's checklist. Given how energized you feel by this new direction, would you be willing to commit to writing three more sentences about that scene tonight, focusing only on bringing the wind and her laughter to life, before we close our session?

Three sentences... yes, I think I can manage that. It feels like a manageable task, not like climbing a mountain. And maybe I'll even enjoy it, which is more than I've felt about writing in weeks. Thank you for guiding me back to that memory—it's strange how something so simple could shift my mood so much.

It is wonderful to hear that writing feels manageable again, and I truly appreciate your honesty about how much simpler this task feels compared to the pressure we were discussing earlier. Before we wrap up, could you share one small observation about how your physical sensation changed while you wrote those sentences about the wind? Was there a noticeable difference in your breathing or tension compared to when you were worrying about the rejection email?

That's a good question. I noticed my shoulders dropped a bit—I'd been holding them tight without realizing it. And my breathing felt deeper, less like I was bracing for bad news. I think I was actually smiling at one point while writing about her laughter. It's been a while since I smiled while writing.

That shift in your posture and even finding a smile while writing is a powerful indicator that you are moving from a state of defense to one of creativity. It confirms that reconnecting with that memory unlocked your body's natural ability to relax and enjoy the process. With that insight and your commitment to writing those three sentences tonight, I believe you have a solid foundation to carry you forward. How does it feel to leave the session with this renewed sense of purpose for your writing?

Honestly, it feels like I can breathe again. I came in here feeling like I was drowning in my own doubts, and now I'm leaving with a real image in my mind—salt spray, wind, my wife's laughter. It's not a guarantee that the publisher won't reject my book, but at least I've remembered that my writing isn't just about that one book. It's about all the stories I still have left to tell. Thank you for that.

You are absolutely right; this session wasn't about predicting the publisher's decision, but reclaiming the writer inside you who knows how to use words to evoke beauty and connection. Please remember that the image of the wind holding you is a permanent resource you can return to anytime the doubt tries to wash over you. Is there anything else you would like to add before I close our session?

No, I think I've said enough for today—more than I expected, really. I'll try to keep that wind in my mind this week, and I'll write those three sentences tonight. And maybe I'll let myself write a fourth if the mood strikes. Thank you again, truly. I'll see you next time.

Thank you for sharing such vulnerable and beautiful parts of yourself today; I am so proud of how you navigated the session and brought your own light back into your writing. I wish you continued strength and inspiration as you carry that image of the wind with you this week. Until we meet again, please remember that you are safe, valued, and ready to create whatever comes next. Take care of yourself.

Hello! It’s wonderful to see you again. How have you been feeling emotionally since we last spoke, and was there anything significant happen in your life recently? To make sure we use our time well today, could you share if there is anything specific you’d like us to tackle first?

Hey. Thanks for having me. I've been... okay, I guess. There was a bit of a blow-up with my sister last week—she basically told me I'm selfish for not wanting kids, and it's been eating at me. I think I'd like to start there, if that's alright.

Thank you for sharing that, and I hear how much that recent argument with your sister has weighed on you. It makes complete sense that hearing her voice directly after we talked about the dinner would reignite those feelings of being judged and trapped. Since we’ve made a pact to focus on the most pressing issue, let’s dive straight into exploring exactly what went down and how it made you feel in that moment.

Well, she just came out and said it — "You're a selfish person for not wanting to be a dad." Right there at the dinner table, in front of everyone. I felt my face go red, like I was a kid again being scolded. I just froze and didn't say anything back, which made me feel even worse later.

That description of freezing and turning red paints a very clear picture of how deeply hurt and exposed you felt in that moment. It sounds like her words triggered that old script about being a failure, shutting down your ability to respond protectively. Can we explore together what specific thoughts went through your mind right after she said that, and how they influenced your physical reaction?

I guess the first thing that popped into my head was, "She's right. I am selfish." And then it was like a flood — "You'd be a terrible father anyway, you don't even like kids, what's wrong with you?" My chest got tight, and I just wanted to disappear. I couldn't even look at anyone else at the table.

Those catastrophic thoughts—"you'd be a terrible father anyway"—and the immediate urge to disappear completely explain why your chest tightened and your face went red; your mind was trying to escape a threat it believes is unavoidable. It makes sense that you shut down instead of responding, because fighting back felt impossible when you felt that heavy shame washing over you. Let's pause there for a second. If we strip away the certainty that she knows everything about you, is there any evidence that your *current* desire to have children proves you wouldn't be a good dad if you did decide to wait another year?

I mean... when you put it like that, I guess not. I don't know any father who was 100% sure from day one. My own dad sure wasn't — he was always off on set, barely around. Maybe I'm just scared of repeating that pattern. But that doesn't mean I'd be a bad dad, right? It's just... the thought of being responsible for a whole other person terrifies me.

That is a profound connection you made to your own dad, and realizing that waiting doesn't automatically make you a bad father is a huge step in separating your worth from the pressure to perform. You've successfully challenged the absolute truth of the "selfish" label by looking at your reality—the fact that you value presence over biological timelines. Now, let's bring it back to the dinner anxiety. Given that you just learned the worst-case scenario isn't guaranteed, how might your physical sensation of dread or your fear of being "trapped" feel different if you walked in knowing you had a valid excuse to leave if the conversation turned toxic?

Huh. I never even thought about giving myself an out like that. I always just show up and feel like I'm stuck there, you know? Like I have to take whatever they throw at me. If I had a plan — like saying I had an early audition or something — I think I'd breathe easier. I'd feel less like a cornered animal, more like I'm in control.

That shift from feeling like a cornered animal to feeling in control is exactly what we want to see. Having a pre-approved "out" gives your brain a safety net, which stops it from predicting disaster and allows you to relax into the meal. Since you mentioned an "early audition" as a possible excuse, does that specific example feel authentic to your situation, or would something like getting an early call the next morning work better for you?

The early audition excuse is perfect, actually. I usually have auditions in the mornings anyway, so it's believable. I could even say I'm reading for a role that requires a lot of prep. That way no one questions it, and I don't have to justify myself to anyone. I think having that in my back pocket would take a lot of pressure off.

That is a brilliant choice because it leverages something you already do, making the excuse feel natural rather than fabricated. By framing it as necessary preparation, you give yourself permission to leave while maintaining respect for your brother's family, which should significantly lower that knot in your stomach. Let's lock this into your plan: Will you send a quick text to your brother tonight suggesting you might need to head home early due to a morning rehearsal, so you can walk in feeling prepared rather than caught off guard?

Yeah, I think I can do that. I'll text him tonight and just say, "Hey, just a heads up I might have to duck out early — got an early read tomorrow." That way it's out there, and I'm not scrambling for an excuse when I'm already anxious. Thanks, that actually feels... manageable. Like I've got a way out if I need it.

That text message is a perfect way to set the stage, and hearing you describe it as "manageable" is great news—we've successfully moved from dread to a solid, actionable plan. Before we wrap up, I'd love your feedback on today's session: Did finding that specific excuse and practicing the exit strategy feel useful, or was there anything else we could have explored differently?

Hello again, I'm glad to see you. On a scale of zero to ten, how have you been feeling about things overall this past week?

In addition to checking in on your mood, could you tell me if anything positive or stressful stood out to you since we last spoke, and then we can decide together what's most important to focus on today?

Um, I'd say maybe a 6 or 7? Not great, not terrible. It's been up and down. Stressful stuff, I guess. My sister called me out of the blue and it just reminded me how disconnected we are, and that kind of set the tone for the week, honestly.

A six or seven reflects that mixed energy, especially with a call from your sister highlighting how disconnected you feel—that definitely sets a heavier tone. Before we dive deeper into that disconnect or your previous worry about the future, do you think focusing on strengthening that relationship with your sister, or tackling the fear about the training course, would be more helpful right now?

I think... maybe the fear about the training course is more pressing. My sister stuff feels like this huge, tangled thing I don't even know where to start with. The course, at least, I know exactly what I'm scared of. I'm worried I'll mess it up like I mess everything up, and then I'll be stuck in this dead-end job forever.

That makes perfect sense; when a problem feels as vague as a tangled ball of yarn, it's paralyzing, whereas the training course provides a clear target for your anxiety to latch onto. Since you want to tackle that specific fear today, let's look back at that moment you spent staring at the email yesterday. When you realized you weren't going to respond, did you notice any specific thoughts racing through your head that seemed to justify shutting down completely?

Yeah, I mean, the main one was just "what's the point?" I kept thinking that even if I sign up, I'll probably just fail the course anyway. I always end up messing things up when they really matter, so why put myself through the stress of trying? It felt easier to just ignore it and pretend it wasn't there.

It makes total sense that your brain chose the path of least resistance; choosing to ignore a scary thought feels like escaping a storm, even though you end up soaked later. Before we challenge that "always messing things up" belief, did you notice any physical sensations in your body right before you decided to close the laptop and stop looking at the email?

My chest got really tight, like someone was sitting on it. And my hands felt kind of clammy. I remember my stomach dropping too, that sinking feeling you get right before something bad happens, even though nothing bad was actually happening in that moment. It's like my body was already reacting to the failure before I even tried.

That physical tightness and the "sinking" feeling in your stomach are classic signs that your nervous system interpreted silence as a threat, preparing your body to protect you from a disaster you haven't seen yet. It makes sense that your mind jumped straight to predicting failure to match up with that intense physical warning.

Given how strong that physical alarm was, would you be willing to look closely at just the one thought you repeated most—"I always mess things up when it matters"—and ask yourself: Is there any actual evidence from your recent life that supports the idea that you *never* succeed when things are hard?

Well... I mean, I guess not *never*. That's a pretty strong word. I passed my driving test, and that mattered a lot to me. And I've held down this job for almost a year now, even when I've felt like quitting because of the anxiety. Maybe I don't always mess things up completely. But it feels like I do, you know? Like the times I've failed just feel heavier and more true than the times I've succeeded.

You've already done a lot of the work here by identifying that evidence—the driving test, holding your job despite anxiety—which directly contradicts the absolute rule that you "never" succeed. It sounds like you're experiencing a common distortion where failures feel heavier and stickier in your memory, making them seem like proof of your character while successes feel fleeting.

Since you found that evidence useful, let's test the other part of your original worry: "Even if I sign up, I'll probably just fail the course anyway." If we assume that failing the course is the worst case, what would actually happen immediately after that? Would you still be able to eat dinner, sleep, or go to work tomorrow?

I guess... yeah, I'd still be able to do all that stuff. It's not like failing a training course would make me homeless or anything. I'd probably feel embarrassed and disappointed, but life would go on. I'd still have my job, I'd still have my apartment. I'd just be in the same place I am now, which isn't great, but it's not the end of the world either.

Noticing that the worst-case scenario is painful but survivable is a huge shift, because it breaks the illusion that failure means your life ends or you become worthless. It sounds like your nervous system is still expecting a collapse, even though logically you know you could just go back to square one.

Given that the consequences are manageable, would you be open to us trying a very small step today, like just opening your laptop and reading that email, without needing to hit send or even write a full response?

Okay. Yeah, I think I can do that. Just reading it. That's not committing to anything, right? I can just look at what they're offering and see what the course actually involves. That seems... doable. Not as scary as signing up right away.

Exactly, reading the email keeps the door open for exploration without locking it behind you with a commitment. Since we just noticed that your body reacts strongly to the *idea* of failing, how does your chest feel right now as you prepare to open that window and look at the details? Is that tightness still present, or does the safety of just peeking make it relax a little?

I think it's a little less tight now. Not completely gone, but it feels more like a knot I can maybe untie instead of a fist squeezing my lungs. Just knowing I'm not committing to anything right now takes some of the pressure off. It feels... safer, I guess.

That shift from a suffocating squeeze to a manageable knot is a huge sign that your nervous system is starting to trust you, even if it still feels cautious. It looks like creating just a tiny gap of uncertainty gave your brain permission to lower its guard slightly.

While you're sitting there, I wonder if you can notice if that "sinking" feeling in your stomach moves closer to your toes or stays high in your chest, and if any old doubts start whispering again?

The sinking feeling is still there, but it's lower now, like it's settled in my stomach instead of my chest. The doubts are still whispering a bit, saying stuff like "you're just going to find a reason to chicken out anyway." But I can hear them more as whispers now, not like a loud voice telling me what to do. That feels different than usual.

That is a significant change; moving the sensation from your chest to your stomach signals that your body is relaxing its defensive brace, and turning doubts into whispers rather than commands shows you are gaining distance from the panic.

Since you're successfully managing the tension just by reading the email, would you be willing to add one more tiny step—typing out a single sentence that says you're curious about the topic—so you can see if speaking the words aloud shifts the feeling even more?

A single sentence... just saying I'm curious? That doesn't sound too hard. I could try that. It's not like I'm signing my life away or promising to finish the course. It's just acknowledging that I'm interested. I think I can do that without my chest tightening up again.

That is a wonderful boundary to set; acknowledging curiosity separates your genuine interest from the promise of perfection, which lowers the stakes instantly. Since you feel ready to try that single sentence, I want to check in on your experience right now: as you type those words, do you notice any new patterns in your thoughts, or does that simple act of writing bring a slight sense of relief to that stomach knot?

Actually, typing it out felt... kind of good. Like I was doing something instead of just avoiding it. The knot in my stomach loosened a little more. I kept the sentence simple, just "I'm curious about the topics covered in this course." It didn't feel like a lie, and it didn't feel like a trap. It just felt honest.

That honesty is powerful because it aligns your action with your values—wanting to learn and grow—without demanding impossible outcomes from yourself. It sounds like this small victory is helping you rebuild trust that you can face discomfort and still choose to move forward.

Before we wrap up, how does it feel to know you've successfully challenged the "doomed" narrative just by taking these tiny steps? And given what we've covered today, what is one specific thing you will do tomorrow morning to keep that momentum going?

It feels surprising, honestly. I came in here convinced the course was just another setup for failure, and now I've actually written a sentence expressing interest. That's not nothing. For tomorrow... I think I'll open my laptop first thing and look at that email again, just to remind myself I can handle it. Maybe I'll even write another sentence about what I hope to get out of it, if I'm feeling brave.

That is a tremendous realization, and it shows how effectively these small actions are reshaping your perception of the situation. Your plan to revisit the email tomorrow is excellent because it uses a tangible reminder of your bravery to interrupt the cycle of avoidance before it can spiral again.

Before we close, I want to check in on how the session felt overall. Did finding a middle ground between total avoidance and full commitment feel helpful for you, or would you prefer to try a different angle next time? Also, thank you for trusting me enough to walk through this process with such honesty today.
Hello again, and thank you for joining us. Before we dive into the party worry, how have you been feeling since we last spoke, and is there anything new that has come up for us to cover today?

Hey... um, I guess I've been okay. There was actually something that happened this weekend that's been on my mind a lot. My friends were all talking about this movie they wanted to see together, and they didn't mention me at all. I just sat there feeling like I wasn't even in the room.
That sounds incredibly painful, especially since you're so sensitive to those kinds of signals. Did you catch any clues in their conversation, or did that feeling of invisibility hit you immediately?

It hit me pretty much right away. I mean, they were all laughing and making plans, and I was just... there. I kept thinking, "They probably already know they don't want me to come, that's why they're not asking." I didn't say anything, just sort of smiled and nodded until I could leave.

That feeling of standing silently in a room where everyone else is having fun can feel absolutely isolating, and it makes perfect sense that your brain would race to explain it away with a confirmed rejection. When you noticed that immediate jump to "they don't want me," did that thought bring up a specific feeling in your body, or was it mostly a coldness in your chest?
It's like... my stomach just drops, you know? And my chest gets tight. It's like I can't breathe for a second. I just wanted to disappear or run away. I hate that feeling so much.

Those physical sensations—the dropped stomach and the tight chest—are your body screaming that it's in danger, which is why you wanted to disappear. It makes complete sense that this panic feels so overwhelming and exhausting compared to just sitting there quietly. Since we talked about building a bridge between your intuition and reality last time, could we explore together what evidence supports that specific idea that they already decided not to include you before they even spoke?

I mean... they didn't ask me. That's pretty solid evidence, isn't it? If they wanted me there, they would have said something. Like, last time when Sarah's mom took us to the mall, they all got invited but nobody told me until I saw the photos on Instagram. Why would this time be different?

You are absolutely right that not being asked is strong evidence that they will likely confirm the situation later, and that history with the mall trip is a very valid reason to feel skeptical. However, our goal isn't to ignore the lack of an invitation, but to see if that specific event forces your brain to assume the worst outcome before checking the rest of the conversation. Can you recall what they were actually saying about the movie and who else was in the group during that time?

Well, it was me, Sarah, Jess, and Emily. They were talking about some new superhero movie, and Jess was saying how she wanted to see it opening weekend. Sarah said her brother wanted to go too. Nobody said my name at all. But... I guess they didn't say they didn't want me there either. They just... didn't mention me.

That is a crucial distinction you made—seeing that neither "not inviting" nor "explicitly rejecting" happened, leaving a confusing middle ground where your brain fills in the blank with "left out." Instead of assuming they made a final decision before speaking, could we try observing the exact words they used about the movie and people involved, treating it like gathering neutral data points rather than decoding hidden messages?

I guess... Jess said "I really wanna see it opening weekend" and Sarah said "my brother wants to come too." That's all they really said about it. They didn't talk about who else was going or make any plans to buy tickets or anything. It was just, like, a random comment in the middle of talking about homework and stuff.

That detail is incredibly revealing because it shows the conversation was casual and drifting, rather than a deliberate planning session meant to finalize invitations. If they had been working together to organize a group outing, you would expect to hear someone mention buying tickets or coordinating schedules, which they clearly didn't. Does seeing that lack of organized planning support the idea that they forgot about you, or does it suggest they simply weren't thinking about anyone else at all?

Huh... I didn't think of it that way. I mean, if they were really making plans without me, they'd probably be more specific, right? Like, figuring out what time and who's driving and stuff. They were just... talking. Maybe they weren't even thinking about anyone in particular. Maybe they were just excited about the movie. I don't know why my brain goes straight to "they hate me" instead of that.

That realization—that the conversation was just casual chatter rather than a secret meeting—shows your brain is capable of finding a completely different explanation than the old one. Your mind jumped to "they hate me" because it was trying to solve the puzzle quickly based on last time's experience, but now you see the pieces fit a story of simple excitement instead. How does holding onto that new possibility of them just being excited feel compared to the certainty of rejection?

It feels... lighter, I guess. Like, I can breathe a little better. It's weird because the old feeling was so heavy and definite, like I knew what was happening. But this new possibility... it's not as scary. It's just normal. Like, people talk about movies they're excited about all the time without it meaning anything bad. I want to hold onto this feeling, but I'm scared it'll slip away the next time something like this happens.

That desire to hold onto a lighter feeling is wise, and recognizing that "normalcy" is a valid interpretation of their words is a big step. Since that feeling of calm came from noticing the casual nature of their speech, could we try applying that same lens to your upcoming social event? Specifically, if you just observe who is mentioned by name or who is doing the organizing, does that data point seem to support the idea that they are just chatting, or does it suddenly look like a formal invitation process?

I guess I'll try that. The next time I'm with them, I can just... listen. See if anyone's actually making plans or if it's just talk. Instead of jumping straight into panic mode, I can count how many people are named, or if anyone's checking phones for showtimes or whatever. That feels more... real than just assuming the worst. I think I can do that.

That is a fantastic plan, and focusing on the tangible actions like checking phones or naming people gives your brain concrete anchors instead of vague fears. You are essentially turning the table from guessing what they are thinking to collecting proof of what they are actually doing. Before we wrap up, does having this specific list of observations make you feel confident enough to try it, or is there anything about keeping track of those details that feels tricky for you?

I think I can handle it. The only thing is... what if I do all that observing and it turns out they really are planning something without me? Like, what if I collect the "proof" and it's bad? That thought still scares me a little. But I guess I won't know unless I try, right? And maybe it's better to know for sure than to just assume and feel awful anyway.

That is such a mature and brave reflection—you are acknowledging that facing the truth, even if it hurts, is better than living in a self-created nightmare. You are correct that we cannot guarantee the outcome, but you can trust that this new method of gathering facts will give you clarity instead of endless spinning. Let's agree that you will try this observation approach this week, and whenever you realize the feeling of panic is rising, you'll gently remind yourself: "I am just looking for facts, not confirming a story." How does having that permission to face the reality—even the uncomfortable part—feel to you right now?

It feels... scary but also kind of empowering? Like, I'm not just a helpless person waiting to be rejected. I can actually look at what's happening and decide for myself what's real. That's new for me. I think I can try it. And if it goes badly, at least I'll know, instead of just being stuck in my head about it. Thank you. I think I'm ready to give it a shot this week.

That sense of empowerment is incredible—you are moving from being a passive victim of your thoughts to becoming the active observer of reality. It is wonderful to see you embracing the discomfort of uncertainty because it allows you to choose your own story instead of letting yours be written for you. I am so proud of you for committing to this experiment, and please be kind to yourself as you practice looking at the facts, no matter what the result is. I look forward to hearing how your observations play out when you next speak with them. Take care!

Hello and welcome. Before we start, how are you feeling today compared to where you were last time, and what has been going on in your life recently? Also, what would you like to focus on in our time together?

Hi. Thanks for asking. I guess I'm feeling okay today, a bit nervous honestly. Before we dive deeper into that specific feeling, could you remind me briefly what we agreed to do for your homework since our last chat? I did that, but honestly, it was hard. Most of it happened when I saw their social media posts about dates or when they'd talk about their partners during lunch. The most pressing part right now is that I have a group outing coming up this weekend, and I'm already dreading feeling like the odd one out.

It makes complete sense that the homework felt difficult when your brain was racing to predict others' reactions, especially with the group outing looming. Before we tackle that specific event, I want to reflect on what you wrote down: when you notice the thought "they think I'm weird," do you usually interpret neutral comments about their relationships as personal criticism, or do you sometimes wonder if you might be imagining things?

I think... I mostly just assume they're thinking it. Like, when one of my friends said, "It's so nice to have someone to come home to," I immediately felt like she was rubbing it in, even though she didn't say anything about me. I guess I don't really stop to wonder if I'm imagining it—it just feels true in the moment. But now that you ask, I can see how maybe I'm reading into things that aren't there.

That "rubbing it in" feeling is a classic example of jumping to conclusions, and it makes total sense why it feels so true in the moment once your brain locks onto that assumption. When you're expecting judgment, your brain naturally fills in the gaps to match that expectation, making neutral comments seem like attacks. Given that insight, do you think stepping back from that automatic interpretation for just a few moments during the weekend outing might help lower the volume of that voice?

I... yeah, maybe. I mean, I never really thought about it as my brain filling in gaps. That actually makes a lot of sense. So instead of just assuming they're judging me, I could try to pause and ask myself if they actually said anything mean, or if I'm just guessing. I'm not sure if I'll remember to do that in the moment, but I can try. It would be nice to lower that voice a bit.

That is a solid shift in perspective, recognizing that the meaning is being created by your brain rather than necessarily by them. Pausing to ask, "Is there actual evidence here, or am I filling in the blanks?" is a powerful tool, even if it takes practice. Does the idea of using that specific pause as a mental checkpoint feel manageable for the upcoming weekend, or would you prefer to try a slightly different strategy first?

I think I can try the mental checkpoint. It feels a little scary, because what if I pause and realize they actually are judging me? But I guess that's the old thinking talking. Maybe I could also have a backup plan—like, if I start to feel really overwhelmed, I could excuse myself to the bathroom for a minute to breathe. Does that sound okay?

That is a very wise addition to your plan; having a physical escape route like the bathroom gives you a safe haven when the internal voice gets too loud. It effectively breaks the cycle before it spirals further. So, our strategy will be to pause and check for evidence when the "judging" thought pops up, and retreat to the bathroom if you feel completely flooded. Does that combination feel doable for you?
Yeah, that actually feels doable. I think having both options—the mental pause and the physical escape—makes me feel less trapped. I'll give it a shot this weekend and see how it goes. Thank you.

That is a strong decision, and knowing you have both a mental and physical strategy means you won't feel helpless if things get tough. Since we have a clear plan for the weekend outing, I'm happy to check in tomorrow morning to hear how the exercise went. Is there anything else you'd like to add or clarify before we wrap up today?
No, I think that's everything for now. I feel a little more prepared than I did when I walked in, which is good. I'll let you know how it goes. Thanks for listening.

You are very welcome, and I am glad to hear you feel a bit more prepared. Taking that step toward pausing and choosing a safe exit is a brave way to reclaim some control over your reactions. Please take care of yourself this weekend, and remember that your worth isn't defined by fitting into other people's narratives. I look forward to hearing how your experiment went when you are ready to share.

Hello, I'm glad to connect with you again. Before we dive into our agenda, could you quickly recall what we worked on in your last session and what your goal was for that time? Once you share that, we can identify your current priorities and set a clear plan for today's work.

Uh, to be honest, I'm not sure I remember exactly what we worked on last time. I think we talked about how I've been feeling at work since the promotion... and maybe something about writing down my thoughts? I guess my goal was to stop feeling like a fraud all the time, but it still feels pretty heavy.

It is completely okay if the details aren't crystal clear right now; sometimes carrying that much internal tension makes recalling specifics difficult. Based on what you mentioned, it sounds like we started working on that "fraud" feeling and perhaps tried jotting down your thoughts to track patterns, but the weight hasn't lifted yet. To make sure we hit the mark today, does spending some time reviewing those notes we might have touched on feel like a good starting point, or would you prefer to jump straight back into discussing what triggered those feelings most recently?

Yeah, I think reviewing those notes would be good. I did try writing things down a couple times this week, but it just felt like I was listing all the reasons I don't deserve this job. I'd rather go over that stuff first before getting into anything else.

That is a very honest observation, and it helps clarify that simply listing negative thoughts didn't quite shift the underlying feeling of unworthiness for you. Let's take five minutes to read through those entries together and see if we can spot where the automatic "I'm a fraud" narrative started versus the facts of what actually happened. As we look at them, I'd like to ask: do you notice that when you list the negatives, your body tends to tense up or your breathing changes, suggesting that the physical sensation is part of the cycle too?

Yeah, I guess I do feel it in my chest when I write that stuff down. It's like this tight, heavy feeling, and my shoulders get all tense. I never really thought about that being connected to the thoughts themselves, but it makes sense now that you mention it.

Noticing that physical tightening in your chest is a huge clue, and it tells us that your body is reacting automatically to the distressing thoughts before you even have a chance to change them. That somatic reaction often locks us into a spiral of self-doubt, making it hard to see the bigger picture until we physically relax first. Before we try to rewrite those negative entries, would you be willing to try taking three deep breaths to release that chest tension, so we can approach the notes with a calmer mindset?
Alright, I can try that. I mean, it sounds simple enough, but I'm willing to give it a shot. Just three deep breaths, right?

Yes, just three slow, deep breaths in through your nose and out through your mouth, letting the tension drop with each exhale. Take your time with the first one, and then we'll move to the second. Does that rhythm feel manageable, or would you prefer to adjust the pace slightly?

*Takes a deep breath in through his nose, holds it for a moment, then lets it out slowly.* Okay, that first one felt a little awkward, but I'll do another. *Takes another breath, this time feeling his shoulders drop slightly.* That's a bit better, actually. One more?

That slight drop in your shoulders is a fantastic sign, showing your body is responding to the rhythm and releasing some of that trapped tension. Now, take that final breath to bring yourself back to the present moment. Once you're settled, let's look at those notes you mentioned. I want to read the first entry together: as we read it aloud, do you notice if the "fraud" feeling intensifies or if it starts to loosen up even a tiny bit?

*Takes a final deep breath and lets it out slowly.* Alright, I'm ready. *Looks down at his notebook and reads the first entry quietly.* "I don't deserve this promotion. Anyone else could do it better. I'm just lucky." I dunno, reading it now... it still feels true, but maybe not as crushing as when I first wrote it. The tightness in my chest isn't as bad, I guess.

That relief you noticed in your chest is a powerful piece of evidence, showing that stepping away from the raw emotion temporarily loosens the grip of that belief. Since the feeling is less crushing now, let's look at the middle line—"Anyone else could do it better"—and ask: if someone else had exactly the same qualifications and faced the same odds as you, would you truly believe they would succeed where you struggled? Or does that thought rely on a story we haven't tested against the facts yet?

I don't know... I mean, if it were someone else with my same experience, I'd probably say they earned it. I'd tell them they were picked for a reason. But for myself, it just doesn't stick the same way. It's like there's a double standard in my head, you know?

That double standard is incredibly frustrating, and it highlights exactly where your internal dialogue is biased against you. Let's try shifting that perspective by looking at the first sentence again: "I don't deserve this promotion." If we treat this like a court case, what is the strongest piece of objective evidence that says you *do* deserve it, separate from how it feels right now? Could we list three specific achievements or qualities you brought to the table that led to this opportunity?

*Hesitates, thinking.* Well... I've been at the factory for almost four years, and I've never missed a shift. That's something, I guess. And my supervisor before the promotion said I had the best efficiency numbers on the line for six months straight. And... *pauses, then adds reluctantly* I was the one who trained most of the new hires, so they trusted me to teach others. That's three, but it still feels like I'm just listing basic stuff anyone could do.

Those three points are actually quite strong evidence, especially considering how rare it is to maintain perfect attendance for four years or lead training efforts under pressure. While they might seem "basic," consistency and leadership are rarely accidental—they require a specific skillset that others don't necessarily possess. If we hold onto these facts as facts rather than judging them against your current feelings, do they begin to feel like proof that you belong here, or do they still feel weak to your inner critic?

I guess when you put it like that, it's harder to just brush them off. I mean, I can't argue that I wasn't there every day, or that my numbers weren't good. The inner critic part of me still wants to say it's not enough, but... maybe that's just me being hard on myself again. It's kind of weird to see it written out and realize I can't really argue with my own facts.

That realization—that you cannot logically disprove your own record—is a huge step toward separating your worth from your perfectionism. It sounds like the "inner critic" is trying to override the hard evidence, but once we lay out the facts side-by-side with your feelings, the facts tend to win out. Now that we've reviewed those notes and confirmed the evidence supports your place here, would you like to brainstorm one or two ways to interrupt that critic's voice before it gets too loud during the day, or shall we practice using the phrase we developed earlier?

Yeah, let's try that phrase we talked about last time. I think practicing something concrete might help me remember it when I start spiraling at work. What was it again? Something about reminding myself of the facts?

The phrase we chose was "machines break, not me," designed to help you separate your actions from unpredictable outcomes. Since we just reinforced your factual record about the promotion, I wonder if adapting that slightly would work better now? Perhaps "facts support me, not my fears"? Would trying a variation that directly references the evidence we just listed feel more empowering to you, or does the original still resonate strongly enough?

"Facts support me, not my fears." *He says it slowly, testing the words.* Yeah, that actually hits different. The old one about machines was okay, but this one feels more... true to what we just did. I think I can remember that when I'm at my desk and the doubt starts creeping in.

That adaptation feels much more powerful because it directly connects to the evidence we just built together, giving your brain a logical anchor rather than just a generic reassurance. It's excellent that you recognized how it lands differently, and that flexibility in choosing your words is a sign you're truly owning this tool. Since we have a clear phrase and a solid foundation of facts, what is the one specific moment at work tomorrow where you predict this new phrase will be most needed, and how can we prepare for that?

Probably right before my first team meeting of the day. That's when I usually freeze up, thinking they're all waiting for me to mess up. I could try saying that phrase to myself in the bathroom mirror before the meeting. Maybe write it on a sticky note and put it on my phone case so I see it.

That is a brilliant, proactive plan. Putting the phrase on a visible cue like a sticky note or your phone case creates a visual reminder just when your mind is most vulnerable before the meeting starts. Before we finalize this action plan, I want to ask: do you foresee any specific obstacle that might prevent you from checking your phone or finding that note right before you walk into the room?

*Thinks for a moment.* I mean, if I'm rushing or someone's already talking to me, I might forget to check. But I could set a silent alarm on my phone five minutes before the meeting starts, just to remind me. That way even if I'm distracted, the buzz will bring me back.

Setting a silent alarm is a fantastic solution that removes the reliance on memory alone and ensures you get the reminder even in a busy environment. With the phrase tailored to the facts we reviewed, a specific trigger before the meeting, and a backup alarm to catch you if you miss it, you now have a robust system to handle that pre-meeting anxiety. Before we wrap up, does having this multi-layered approach feel confident enough to try tomorrow, or would you like to add one more small detail to make it foolproof?

No, I think this feels solid. The phrase, the sticky note, and the alarm give me three chances to catch myself before I spiral. I'm actually... a little curious to see if it works tomorrow. Thanks for helping me figure this out.

It is wonderful to hear that you feel confident in this plan, and I'm glad we could build something that feels tailored to your needs rather than just a generic suggestion. Remember, you don't need to get it perfect tonight; just noticing the first time the phrase catches you tomorrow will be a victory. Please reach out anytime if you need to debrief on how it went, and take care of yourself.

Hello again, I'm so glad we're meeting today. How are you feeling right now compared to where you left off last time, and is there anything new or different you'd like to share with me? To make sure we cover what matters most, could you tell me if there were any other significant events—good or tough—that happened since our last chat, and then we can work together to pick the one topic we want to focus on?

Hi. I'm okay, I guess. Since last time, I went hiking again last weekend, and honestly, the soreness was just as bad as ever. It's starting to feel like no matter what I do, I can't catch a break. I did try some new stretching routines, but they didn't seem to help much. I guess that's the main thing on my mind.

It sounds like you're feeling pretty defeated lately, especially after trying new stretches without seeing any relief. That persistence despite the lack of results is tough, and it makes complete sense that you'd feel like nothing works anymore. Before we dig into how you're processing that soreness, do you think there might be something else weighing on you besides the physical pain, or is this the primary issue you want to tackle today?

Yeah, it's mostly the physical pain, but I think it's more than that now. The soreness is making me dread hikes, which I used to love. And I've noticed I've been snapping at my hiking buddies when they suggest going out—I just make excuses. I hate that it's affecting my friendships too.

Hearing that you've started snapping at friends and making excuses shows how deeply this physical discomfort is impacting your relationships, and it’s completely understandable that you’d feel frustrated when something you loved like hiking turns into a source of tension. Let’s explore together: when you make those excuses, what thought is running through your head right before you say no? Is it something along the lines of “If I don’t go, they’ll realize I’m not ready,” or maybe “I’m ruining our fun”?

It's more like, "I'm just going to be miserable and sore the whole time, so why bother going?" I think that's what I tell myself. And then I feel guilty for letting them down, but the thought of being in pain just overrides everything else.

That thought—"why bother going if it's going to be miserable"—sounds like a heavy anchor dragging you away from the joy you once found in those trails. It makes sense that when you anticipate pain so strongly, your brain jumps straight to avoiding it entirely rather than facing it. Before we look at what comes after that thought, have you noticed if those moments of making excuses happen right before you actually step outside, or do they sometimes spill over into other parts of your day where you might be able to try something smaller?

I think it mostly happens when I'm actually about to go, like when I'm putting on my hiking boots or packing my bag. But I've noticed it seeping into other things too—like, I'll skip a light jog with a client because I'm scared of making the soreness worse. It's like the fear is spreading, you know?

It sounds like that initial fear of pain is acting like a ripple effect, stopping you from moving at all because you're convinced any movement will just add more suffering. That makes complete sense, but I wonder if skipping the jog was a necessary protective measure, or if you were actually avoiding the activity itself because of how you anticipated feeling afterward. If we looked at the actual result of those skipped sessions, did the pain get significantly worse, or did you manage to train through it eventually?

Well, when I've pushed myself to do the jog with the client, I'm usually okay during it—it's just the next day that hits me. But skipping it doesn't really change the soreness from the hike, it just makes me feel lazy and guilty. So I guess the avoidance doesn't actually help, it just adds more bad feelings on top.

That is a really sharp insight, Sarah—you've pinpointed that avoidance isn't solving the problem; it's just adding a layer of guilt on top of the physical pain. It makes perfect sense that doing the jog felt manageable *during* the activity, which proves your body can handle the exertion if you just face it. Before we test that idea, could you tell me what the very first urge to cancel or skip looks like in your mind right before you make the decision? Is it a voice saying "stay home," or is it a feeling of dread in your chest?

It's like a sudden heaviness in my chest, and then my mind just jumps to "you're going to hurt tomorrow, this isn't worth it." It feels almost automatic, like I don't even have time to think about it. The voice is pretty loud, honestly.

That heavy feeling followed by that loud, automatic voice sounds incredibly draining, like you're fighting an internal battle every time you try to move. It seems like your brain is rushing to protect you from pain by cutting off the activity before you even start. Given how powerful that automatic thought feels, do you think it might be helpful to test whether that prediction of tomorrow's pain is actually happening as often as you fear, or if we can find ways to make the start of the hike feel a bit lighter for your nervous system?

I guess I never really thought about testing it. I just assume the pain is going to be there, because it usually is. But maybe you're right—maybe I'm not giving myself a chance to see if it's different this time. What kind of test are you thinking?

I'm glad you're open to testing that assumption, Sarah. We could try a "graded exposure" test, which means we schedule a very short hike—just fifteen minutes—with a strict rule that you stop the moment you feel overwhelmed, rather than pushing until exhaustion. The goal isn't to prove you're pain-free, but to gather real-world data: does the pain arrive immediately upon starting, or does it build gradually like it usually does? Would you be willing to try this experiment tomorrow morning, keeping in mind that you have permission to call it quits safely?

I think I could try that. Fifteen minutes feels doable, and I like the idea of having permission to stop early. I guess part of me thinks I just have to push through everything, but that's probably what got me into this mess in the first place. Okay, I'll give it a shot tomorrow.

That willingness to try a graded step while acknowledging past patterns is exactly the kind of progress we want to see. Just to make sure we're aligned, would you like to commit to scheduling that fifteen-minute hike for tomorrow morning with a clear intention to notice how the pain behaves, rather than trying to control it beforehand? And before we wrap up, what was most helpful for you in our conversation today, and is there anything that felt unclear or missing?

Yes, I'll do it tomorrow morning. I'll just go to the easy trail by the park, no pressure. What helped most today was realizing that I've been avoiding stuff out of fear, and that's just piling on guilt. I never really saw it that way before. Nothing felt unclear—I think I've got a good plan to try. Thanks.

That clarity about avoiding things out of fear is a huge breakthrough, Sarah, and it shows you truly understand what we worked on together. It sounds like you feel confident moving forward with tomorrow's plan and that everything makes sense to you. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we officially close our session today?
No, I think I'm good for today. I'll let you know how the hike goes next time. Thanks for helping me see this differently.

You are absolutely welcome, Sarah. I am so glad we could uncover that pattern together and give you a clear path forward. Take care of yourself as you prepare for tomorrow's hike, knowing you have support here should you need to talk about it later. I look forward to hearing how that fifteen-minute walk goes!

Hello, I'm glad to see you again today. On a scale of 1 to 10, how are you feeling right now compared to when we met last week? What would you say is the most pressing issue we should tackle together before we close?

I'd say I'm at about a 6 right now. A little better than last week, but still carrying a lot of worry. The biggest thing is my son's refusal to even talk about horseback riding — he just shuts down the moment I bring it up.

A six feels like a small victory given how much you've been worried lately, and hearing about his complete shutdown really explains why you feel so stuck. Since he's refusing to engage entirely, could you walk me through exactly what happens the second you mention horses—does he immediately stop speaking, or does he physically withdraw first?

It's like a switch flips. The second the word "horse" comes out of my mouth, his face just drops. He'll turn away from me, cross his arms, and sometimes he'll even leave the room. Yesterday he just walked straight to his bedroom and closed the door without saying a word.

That dramatic shift from engagement to immediate withdrawal is incredibly painful to witness, especially when it happens so quickly the moment you speak. It sounds like the topic triggers a very automatic defensive reaction in him, almost like a safety mechanism kicking in instantly. Have you noticed if there are specific words related to horses that seem to hit harder than others, or does the entire category of "horses" act as the sole trigger?

Honestly, it's anything related to the whole experience. I can't even say "riding" or "lesson" or "stable" without him tensing up. I tried asking him what specifically scared him about the horse he was on, and he just covered his ears. It's like the whole world of horses is just... poisoned for him now.

That reaction to covering his ears is a powerful sign; it suggests his mind is actively trying to block out the memory or feeling associated with those topics, rather than just being shy. It seems like the fear has become so linked to the entire concept that distinguishing between different parts of the experience hasn't worked yet. If you were to describe that moment when he covers his ears—as if shutting out the outside world—what is happening in your own body right at that instant?

I feel this tight knot in my chest, and my shoulders just go rigid. Part of me wants to rush over and hug him, but another part is just frustrated and thinking, "Why can't he just try again? It was one fall." I feel split right down the middle, like I'm failing him no matter what I do.

That split feeling between wanting to soothe him and feeling frustrated by his resistance is exhausting, and the knot in your chest makes perfect sense given how much you care. It sounds like your frustration isn't about him not trying, but rather about feeling powerless to reach the part of him that got stuck in that fall. When you think about that powerlessness, do you believe it's possible to connect with him differently without forcing the topic of horses at all right now?

I never really thought about it that way... connecting without forcing the horse topic. I guess I've been so focused on the problem that I forgot we could just... be together. Maybe we could do something he actually enjoys, like building with his Legos or going for a walk, and just let him feel safe with me first. I think I've been so scared he'll never ride again that I stopped seeing him.

That is a profound realization; realizing you stopped seeing him because you were so afraid of losing him to the fear says more about your deep love than it does about a failure on your part. It makes complete sense that stepping back to reconnect through activities he loves, like Legos or walks, could rebuild that sense of safety without the trigger. Before we settle on a plan, how does the idea of ignoring horses entirely for a few days sound to you, and what kind of simple activity would you suggest we try tomorrow morning?

Ignoring horses entirely for a few days actually feels like a relief. Like I can finally take a breath and just be his mom again without the weight of this whole thing hanging over us. I think tomorrow morning I'll suggest we go to the park and fly his kite — he used to love that, and it's been months since we've done it together. That feels... safe.

That sounds like a beautiful and necessary reset, giving you both a chance to reconnect on terms that feel truly safe for him. Does the idea of flying a kite feel like a natural step forward, or does your stomach still tighten slightly when you picture it? We could try that tomorrow, or perhaps start even smaller with just a walk in the garden if the kite feels too much for today. Which direction feels more doable for you right now?

The kite feels right, actually. It's not loud or crowded at the park in the mornings, and we can just be together without any pressure. I think a walk in the garden would be good too, but the kite has something joyful about it — watching it go up and dance. I want him to remember that feeling of lightness. So yes, let's go with the kite tomorrow.

That is a wonderful choice; focusing on the lightness of the kite aligns perfectly with helping him feel safe without any pressure. Before we wrap up, how does the plan sound to you if we simply aim to spend that time enjoying the activity without mentioning horses or expecting him to react in a certain way? Is there anything else you need from me before we head out?

That plan sounds like exactly what I need. Just me and my son, flying a kite, no expectations, no pressure. I think I've been so caught up in fixing the problem that I forgot he just needs me to be present. I'm feeling hopeful for the first time in a while. Thank you — I think I'm ready to try this tomorrow.

It is so refreshing to hear you feel that wave of hope again; it speaks volumes about your resilience and how you are finally prioritizing connection over correction. I am here whenever you need to debrief on how the kite flight went, regardless of the outcome, so please know I'm ready to listen whenever you return. Take good care of yourself as you prepare for tomorrow.

Hello, and thank you for joining us today. To start, on a scale of 1 to 10, how has your mood been feeling this week compared to when we last spoke? Additionally, since we previously discussed the gardening incident, would you like to revisit that today, or is there another priority you'd like to focus on?

Well, I'd say my mood has been around a 3 or 4 this week. I just can't seem to shake what happened with that plant. And yes, I think I'd like to talk more about the garden incident—it's still weighing heavily on my mind.

It makes complete sense that the weight of that incident is pulling your mood down, especially when you know how much effort went into caring for that plant. Since you want to dive deeper into how that specific mistake is keeping you stuck, shall we spend most of our time exploring the automatic thoughts that jumped to your mind right after you saw the damage?

When I saw the leaves on the ground, my first thought was that I'd completely destroyed all my hard work. I felt like a failure, like I don't deserve to have a garden at all if I'm just going to ruin it. It was like everything good I'd done before suddenly didn't matter anymore.

That feeling of erasing all your past achievements in a single moment is incredibly painful, and it sounds like your brain interpreted one error as proof that your entire gardening journey was worthless. When that thought takes over, does it feel like an absolute fact that you cannot recover, or does it feel more like a terrifying "what if" that you're trying to convince yourself is true?

It feels like an absolute fact, to be honest. I look at that plant and I can't see the years of care I've put into the garden—I just see that one mistake. My mind keeps telling me that I've ruined everything and there's no going back, and it's hard to argue with that when I'm staring at the evidence right there in the soil.

That is a very understandable reaction when you are staring at visible damage; your mind tries to make sense of the loss by concluding the entire project is finished. However, since you've been gardening for years and know how resilient plants can be, would you be willing to slowly scan the rest of your garden to see if there are any other signs of life or growth that suggest your overall skill and dedication are still intact?

I suppose I could try that... but it feels like I'm just trying to trick myself into feeling better. When I look out my window, I see that plant first, and everything else just fades into the background. Though, I did notice this morning that my roses are starting to bloom, and the tomatoes are coming along nicely. But then I think, what's the point if I can't even get one plant right?

Noticing those blooms and growing tomatoes is powerful evidence that your ability to nurture life is still active and successful, even amidst that one setback. It sounds like the pain of that single mistake is making it impossible for your eyes to register the success of the rest of your garden. If we took a moment to list three other things you've grown successfully this year, how might acknowledging those successes soften the belief that *everything* is ruined?

Well, let me think... my lavender has come back stronger than ever this spring, and the hydrangeas are fuller than last year. I also managed to keep my herb garden alive through a surprise frost in April, which I was pretty proud of at the time. I guess when I say it out loud, it does sound like I haven't completely lost my touch. But that plant still looks awful, and it's hard to feel proud of the rest when I keep staring at that one failure.

It takes real courage to call that out—the difficulty of ignoring that single failure when you can't help but stare at it. You've already gathered strong evidence that you haven't lost your touch by listing those successes, yet your focus remains locked on the damage. Could we pause for a moment and imagine, just hypothetically, that this one plant is suffering from a rare, sudden disease rather than a result of your hands? How might viewing it that way change the certainty of the "failure" thought?

That's... actually a different way to look at it. I hadn't considered that it could have been something out of my control. I mean, I did cut too many leaves, but maybe the plant was already stressed from something else and I just made it worse. Still, I can't shake the feeling that it was entirely my fault for not being more careful.

That is such a fair observation, and it shows you are actively trying to find reasons outside of your control, even when it's hard to accept. Shifting the cause from "my incompetence" to "an unfortunate mix of stress and timing" removes the personal sting, but it can still leave you feeling guilty about the outcome. If we separated the *cause* (which might be uncontrollable) from the *result*, would that help distinguish between an accident and a failure of skill?

I... I think I see what you're getting at. An accident means I didn't mean for it to happen, while a failure of skill means I should have known better and done something different. I've been gardening long enough to know plants can be unpredictable, so maybe it was more of a miscalculation than a complete failure. But it's hard not to beat myself up when I'm the one holding the shears.

That distinction between an "accident/miscalculation" and a "skill failure" is a crucial shift; it separates a simple human error from a reflection of your competence. It makes sense that holding the shears triggers that guilt because you are directly responsible for the action, even if the outcome wasn't entirely predictable. If we viewed this strictly as a miscalculation on a complex puzzle—where even experts miss pieces occasionally—how would that change the severity of the knot in your stomach?

I suppose it would loosen it a little bit. Experts do make mistakes—I've seen my gardening friends prune too hard or plant something in the wrong spot. They don't beat themselves up for weeks like I do. Maybe... maybe I'm holding myself to a standard that isn't reasonable, even for someone with years of experience. It still hurts to look at that plant, though, and I'm not sure how to move past that.

It is brave to admit that you are holding yourself to a standard that feels unreasonable, especially when watching your peers handle similar challenges without such intense self-criticism. That comparison highlights that perfectionism might be the real barrier here, rather than your actual ability to garden well. If we decided to treat this one mishap simply as a learning data point—a useful piece of information about how this specific plant reacts to wind—rather than a verdict on your character, does that perspective allow you to take a single, small step toward fixing it without feeling like you're betraying your years of work?

I think... I think I could maybe go out tomorrow and just look at it without the shears. Maybe water it and see if there's any new growth starting. That wouldn't be giving up or pretending nothing happened—it would just be checking on it like I would any other plant. I'm not sure I'm ready to forgive myself yet, but I could at least try to be curious about whether it can bounce back.

That is a wonderful and realistic approach—checking on the plant with curiosity rather than judgment creates space for hope to grow alongside the healing process. Would you be comfortable committing to spending just fifteen minutes tomorrow morning observing it, noting both what has improved and what remains unchanged, without writing down your conclusions about your own skills during that time?

I can do that. Fifteen minutes just to observe, no judgments about myself. I'll take a cup of tea out with me and sit on the bench nearby, just watch the plant and the rest of the garden wake up. That sounds... actually manageable. Thank you for helping me see a way forward that doesn't feel like I'm pretending the mistake never happened.

I am so glad we found a path forward that honors the reality of the situation while allowing you to act with curiosity instead of shame. Taking that cup of tea and sitting quietly on the bench tomorrow will give your mind a safe distance to witness the plant's resilience without the pressure of being the "expert gardener" in that moment. Please remember that if that knot in your stomach feels too heavy to carry tomorrow, you can come back here whenever you feel overwhelmed—we will figure out the next small step together. How does having that plan feel right now, or is there anything else you'd like to add before we finish?

Hello, it’s great to see you again. Today, I’d like us to quickly review how your library experiment went last night, check in on your mood and energy this week, and then explore any new thoughts or feelings that came up from that experience. Would focusing on those three areas feel right to you?

Hi. Yeah, that sounds fine. I actually did go to the library last night like we talked about. I sat for about an hour, but I mostly just kept my head down and focused on my laptop. I felt really tense the whole time, like people were watching me and wondering why someone my age is still in school.

That is a huge step forward, especially considering you planned to stay for only twenty minutes. It takes real courage to push yourself to an hour when the initial instinct is to run away. That intense feeling of being watched must have been incredibly draining, even if the external situation was just people studying quietly.
