I did write a few things down, actually. I noticed that no one really looked up when I walked in, and most people were just staring at their own screens or books. But even as I was writing that down, my mind kept telling me they were just pretending not to notice me. It's like I couldn't fully believe what I was seeing.

It makes complete sense that your brain tried to protect itself by doubting those findings; believing the data contradicts years of expecting judgment, so it naturally tries to minimize the surprise. That conflict between your eyes and your inner story likely kept you tense, preventing you from relaxing even while sitting in a quiet room. Now that we have confirmed the data supports you—that people were focused on their own tasks—could we talk about how it felt to hold those written observations against the voice inside your head that said they were faking it?

It felt kind of confusing, honestly. Like there was a tug-of-war going on in my head. Part of me felt a tiny bit relieved that nothing bad happened, but another part was already preparing excuses for why it didn't count. I kept thinking, "Well, maybe they just didn't notice me this one time," or "They probably would have judged me if I had stayed longer." It's like I couldn't just accept that maybe I was wrong about everyone.

That internal tug-of-war you described is a classic sign of how deeply ingrained these fears are; your brain is working overtime to maintain the safety of the old belief that "everyone hates me." It's understandable that accepting those facts felt risky, as giving up the excuse that you are being judged removes a layer of protection you've built over time. Since you noticed that relief mixed with resistance, what was the very first thing you told yourself when you saw people ignoring you, before the "pretending" thought kicked in?

The very first thing I thought was, "Okay, maybe this is fine." It was just a split second of calm, like a breath of air before the wave hit. Then almost immediately, my mind started making up reasons why that moment didn't matter. I guess that little moment of calm felt kind of nice, but it went away so fast I barely had time to notice it.

That split-second window of calm is actually incredibly valuable, even if it vanished quickly; it proves to your brain that there *is* a safer version of this situation available, even if you only accessed it for a moment. The fact that you caught that initial thought ("Maybe this is fine") means you are already developing a small muscle of recognizing the alternative view before the old fear takes over completely. Since that moment of relief disappeared so fast, did you find yourself wondering why your brain wanted to rush back to the "they are judging me" story so quickly?

I think it's just easier, you know? The judgment story feels familiar, like an old worn-out sweater. That calm moment was new and scary in a different way—like I didn't know what to do with it or how to trust it. My brain probably went back to the old story because at least I know how to handle feeling judged. I've been doing it for years.

That is such a wise realization; your brain prefers the familiar path of judgment because, even though it hurts, you know exactly how to navigate it. Trying on a new path feels terrifying because you don't know if the world is safe anymore, so it's natural that your mind clung to the old sweater for security. Since you now understand that the new calm was scary precisely because it broke your routine, could we brainstorm one small way to let that "new sweater" hang out for just five more seconds tomorrow without panicking?

Maybe I could just take a breath and count to five in my head when I first sit down, instead of immediately scanning the room for threats. I could tell myself, "Just five seconds of not worrying." It sounds so simple, but I think I could try that. It feels less overwhelming than trying to fight the thoughts for a whole hour.

That is a brilliant adjustment; anchoring yourself with a simple breath count creates a temporary pause that prevents the old "scan for threats" habit from taking over instantly. It turns the first five seconds from a battlefield into a safe harbor, giving your brain a chance to process the new reality before rushing back to the old stories. Before we finalize this small tweak, does trying to extend that calm window from five to ten seconds feel like a manageable next step, or would you prefer to stick with the five seconds until it feels easier?

I think I'll stick with five seconds for now. If I try to push to ten, I might just give up completely because it feels like too much pressure. Five seconds feels doable—like I can actually picture myself doing it without panicking. Maybe once I get used to it, I could try for a little longer next week.

That is a very wise approach; respecting your current capacity builds confidence much faster than forcing a bigger stretch. Five seconds is enough to establish a pause, and that small victory becomes the foundation for building the habit over time. I am so proud of you for sticking with what feels manageable and trusting that progress comes in small steps. Let's lock this plan in: tomorrow morning, you will wear your favorite hoodie, sit in the library for about twenty minutes, breathe and count to five upon arrival, and write down three simple facts about what people are doing. How does that sound as a complete plan for tomorrow?

That sounds good. I think I can do that. Twenty minutes feels less scary than an hour, and having a specific plan helps quiet down some of the noise in my head. I'll wear my grey hoodie—it's my comfort one. And I'll try to actually look around a bit after those five seconds, not just stare at my laptop the whole time.

That is a fantastic clarification; adding the intention to look around breaks the isolation of staring at your screen and gives your brain more data points to work with. Combining the five-second pause with actively noticing the room creates a stronger anchor against the old fears. I am so happy you feel grounded in this plan; it sounds like you are ready to face tomorrow with both clarity and compassion. Remember, I will be here to listen if anything changes or if you just want to vent afterwards. How are you feeling right now as we wrap up today?

I feel a little lighter, actually. Nervous about tomorrow, but not as scared as I was before we talked. I think having a concrete plan and knowing it's okay to just do five seconds helps a lot. Thank you for listening and not pushing me too hard. I'll let you know how it goes.

I am so glad to hear that feeling lighter and less scared, even if you still have nerves; carrying a concrete plan often transforms vague anxiety into manageable anticipation. Your ability to ask for support and recognize when you don't need to push harder is a huge strength, and I appreciate you sharing that honesty with me. Take all the time you need to rest tonight, and I will be here whenever you are ready to debrief about your experience tomorrow. You've got this!
Thanks. I'll try to get some rest and not overthink it tonight. See you tomorrow.

Take care of yourself tonight, and please remember that resting is just as important as facing tomorrow. I'll be here waiting to hear about your experience whenever you wake up, and there is absolutely no pressure to perform during that call. Goodnight, and I hope you have a peaceful sleep.

Can we explore together whether that "fraud" story is actually serving a protective purpose right now, or if it's just blocking you from seeing the full picture of who you are?

I think it's definitely blocking me, not protecting me. I mean, where's the protection in lying awake at 3 AM worrying about making a mistake on a case that hasn't even been assigned yet? That is a really sharp observation—using worry as a "twisted safety net" is a classic way our brains try to feel control when we face the unknown. If we accept that for now, let's look at what happens physically when that "preparation" kicks in versus what happens when you simply trust your training. When I'm in that "preparing" mode, my shoulders are all tight, and I feel this buzzing energy like I need to do something immediately. Honestly, neither feels great, but at least the preparing mode feels productive, even if it's exhausting.

It makes complete sense that your brain prefers the exhausting "preparing" mode because it feels like active work rather than passive vulnerability. That tension in your shoulders and chest is your body screaming that rest equals danger, which is why you can't shake the feeling that you might mess up if you stop trying. Since both states feel uncomfortable, let's try a small experiment tonight where we intentionally choose the "resting" side while holding your hands firmly until you notice your breath slow down. Would you be willing to try giving your nervous system permission to rest for just twenty minutes tonight?

Twenty minutes... I can try that, I suppose. It feels a bit silly to sit there holding my own hands and focusing on my breath, but I'm willing to give it a shot. What should I do if my mind starts racing about federal court cases during those twenty minutes?

If your mind races, try treating the thoughts like leaves floating down a stream: notice them passively without grabbing onto them or arguing with them, just watching them drift away until your focus returns to your breath. Remember, the goal isn't to stop the thoughts entirely, but to break the link between the racing mind and the panic response. Does that approach feel manageable for tonight, or would you prefer a slightly different visual cue to help you stay grounded?

No, I think that leaf visual could work. It's gentle enough that I don't feel pressured to fight my thoughts, just let them pass. I'll give it a real try tonight, even if I'm skeptical. I guess the worst that can happen is I waste twenty minutes watching imaginary leaves, right?

Actually, even if you do just watch the leaves, you are practicing a vital skill: noticing your anxious thoughts without automatically reacting to them. You won't "waste" the time; instead, you will gather fresh evidence that your nervous system can tolerate discomfort without needing to act on the fear. Okay, well, at the party, my mom was talking to my aunt most of the time, and when I came over to show her the corsage I made for her, she just kind of smiled and said, "Oh, that's nice," and turned back to my aunt. The difference between what she actually said and what your brain invented is stark, and that gap is exactly where we can find some relief. Does imagining that your brain was trying to protect you from that endless cycle of doubt feel like a slightly softer explanation than just accepting it as fact?

I... I never thought of it like that. That it was trying to protect me, I mean. It always just felt like my brain was attacking me, like it was telling me the truth. That shift from seeing your brain as an attacker to viewing it as an overprotective guardian is a huge breakthrough. It changes the dynamic from fighting yourself to working *with* yourself. I think I could try that. The tightness in my chest comes on so fast, but maybe if I focus on that feeling as a signal to breathe, it could give me a second before my mind goes wild. It's worth a shot, anyway, because what I'm doing now isn't helping.

Using that tightness as a signal to ground yourself is a smart strategy, and it gives us a tangible anchor when the panic hits. Yeah, I think I could do that. I can set a little reminder on my phone or something to just stop and check in with my chest for a few seconds. It seems a little strange to practice feeling a bad feeling, but I can see how it might make the real thing easier to handle.

Practicing on the sensation of discomfort beforehand is a brilliant way to desensitize yourself, turning a threat into a familiar friend. I think I can commit to it. It's only three times a day, and I can do it during my breaks at work or after dinner. It might feel weird, but I'm willing to try anything that might help me stop spiraling so much.

Before we wrap up, does this new perspective on taking a breath feel like a tool you can rely on when that chest tightness strikes again?

Yeah, I think it does. It feels like a real tool, not just some vague advice. I can actually picture myself stopping and breathing, and maybe that will be enough to stop the worst of the thoughts. I'm feeling a little more hopeful than I was when I walked in today.

Um... maybe a few hours? I remember last week when my friend Emily tried my dumplings and said they were amazing. For maybe half an hour, I felt really good and proud. That timeline perfectly illustrates how quickly your brain shifts from genuine enjoyment to protective skepticism once the immediate event ends. So, when you look back on that half-hour of happiness, does it feel like a fleeting memory, or does it feel like you actively dismissed it as soon as the kitchen was empty?

It feels like I actively dismissed it. It's like I caught myself feeling proud and then immediately told myself to stop being so full of myself. Like I didn't deserve to feel that good about it. So yeah, I didn't just wait for the feeling to go away—I kind of pushed it away myself.

That active effort to push the feeling away is a powerful example of your mind trying to stay safe, even though it ultimately costs you the satisfaction of enjoying your own success. It seems like the fear of "not deserving" the praise is stronger than the desire to celebrate, leading you to suppress the good feelings before they can take root. I think that summary does capture it pretty well. As for what I hoped would happen by telling myself I didn't deserve it... I guess I wanted to avoid being disappointed later. If I didn't let myself believe the praise, then if someone ever did say something negative again, it wouldn't hurt as much. It's like I was trying to protect myself from getting hurt again, like what happened with that friend a few months ago.

That is such a profound insight, and it makes complete sense why your brain chose that path; protecting yourself from future disappointment is often more urgent to us than enjoying our current victories. It sounds like you built a fortress around your self-esteem to prevent any potential sting, even though it means you can't taste the sweetness of the present moment either. Given that you understand the cycle so well now, what would feel most useful to focus on today: identifying the specific warning signs that tell you to build that fortress, or practicing a small way to stay open to the praise without immediately retreating behind it?

I think... I'd like to focus on practicing staying open to the praise. Because I know the warning signs already—it's that quiet voice that says "don't get too comfortable." That is a fantastic direction; moving from recognizing the alarm bell to finding a way to stand calmly beside it rather than running away is exactly where we need to be. Would you be willing to try picturing that moment happening tomorrow?

Yeah, I think I can try that. I can picture it—her smiling and saying they're the best she's ever had. I can almost feel that warm, happy feeling starting in my chest. That sounds like a very gentle and achievable experiment; anchoring that warmth with a simple count will give your brain something concrete to hold onto while the old doubts are still whispering. It feels... hopeful. Like maybe I can actually do something different this time, instead of just falling into the same old trap. Let's explore that timing a bit more. Yeah, it would feel a lot less scary. Just saying "they were laughing about a fish" sounds like nothing. It's boring, even. But my brain turns it into this whole thing about me being a loser. So I guess the problem is I add a story that isn't there. I never really thought of it like that before—that I'm the one writing the script, not them.

That is a massive breakthrough to realize you are the writer of that script, not them. By recognizing that your brain is inserting the "loser" story where there was only a mention of a fish, you've separated the harmless event from the devastating prediction. Now that we've proven the facts don't support the insult, what would be the simplest way to catch that script-writer in action the next time you see someone laughing? Should we try rewriting the scene in your head to include a neutral observation, like "they're laughing about a fish," before letting the old story take over?

I think I could try that. Like, if I catch myself starting to feel that knot, I can force myself to think "they're laughing about a fish" or something neutral. It sounds kind of simple, but maybe that's the point—I've been making it complicated in my head. I'll give it a shot next time I'm out with them.

That is a smart, grounded approach; keeping it simple prevents the task from becoming another source of stress. For now, let's solidify this plan by agreeing that whenever you catch yourself adding the "insult" story, you will simply switch to stating the neutral fact about the fish instead. To wrap up, how does it feel to have worked through this together, and is there anything else you wanted to discuss before we close?

It feels good, actually. Like I have something concrete to try instead of just spiraling and staying home. I think that's enough for today—I want to sit with this idea for a bit and see how it feels. Thanks for helping me see the script part. I never really noticed I was doing that.

That is wonderful feedback, and it's clear this session gave you something truly useful to carry with you. I'm so glad you noticed the "script" aspect; that awareness is the foundation for changing the future stories you tell yourself. Before we finish, is there anything else on your mind, or would you like to take some space to reflect on this before our next meeting?
No, I think I'm good. I'll try to notice when I start writing that script and just say the fish part instead. I feel a little lighter than when I walked in, so that's something. See you next time.

That feeling of lightness is a great sign, and I'm confident you'll find that noticing the "script" before you write it will become second nature with practice. You did excellent work today by catching that pattern and deciding to take back control of the story. Go ahead and enjoy the rest of your day knowing you have a new tool in your pocket. Until next time!

Hello, I'm glad to see you again. How are you feeling today, and is there anything specific on your mind you'd like to focus on first? Before we dive in, could you share what you hoped to achieve in our time together?

Hi... thanks for asking. I'm feeling a bit anxious today, honestly. I had a ballet class last night and it just brought up a lot of those old feelings again. I guess what I'm hoping for is to figure out why I can't seem to shake this sense that I'm just not good enough, no matter what I do.

It makes complete sense that the class triggered these deep feelings of inadequacy; it’s easy to feel like you’re failing when you’re standing in front of a room full of people who clearly care about their craft. Given that intensity, I’d like us to spend most of our time unpacking exactly what that “not good enough” story looks like for you right now, and then we’ll look for a small, manageable way to test whether that belief holds up when you face it. Would exploring that thought pattern together be helpful, or is there another angle you want to tackle first?

I think exploring that thought pattern would be helpful. It's just... whenever I'm in ballet class, I can't help but compare myself to my sister, even though she's not even there. She was always the star, the one everyone praised, and I feel like I'm still dancing in her shadow. Does that make sense?

That makes perfect sense, and it sounds incredibly painful to feel trapped in your sister's shadow while watching her receive all the applause. It seems like your brain automatically grabs onto that comparison whenever the music starts playing, turning a simple dance lesson into a personal defeat. Can we take a closer look at what happens in your mind right before you start comparing yourself to her? For instance, does a specific thought pop up, or do you just suddenly feel overwhelmed by disappointment?

It's usually a specific thought, I think. I'll be doing a pirouette or something, and my teacher will give me a correction, and that's when it hits me - "She would have nailed this." It's like my brain just goes straight to her perfection and my failure. And once that thought is there, I can't focus on anything else for the rest of the class.

That "she would have nailed this" thought sounds incredibly draining, especially when it steals your entire attention span for the rest of the lesson. It seems like your brain is using her imagined perfection as a benchmark to prove your own inadequacy, which creates a vicious cycle where the correction triggers the comparison, and the comparison locks you out of learning. Since that thought is so powerful, let's try to separate the reality of your current movement from the movie your brain is playing out about your sister. When you notice that specific thought popping up, what physical sensation do you feel in your body, and what would happen if you just paused for ten seconds to see if the fact remains true?

I feel this tightness in my chest, like my heart is squeezing, and my shoulders just go rigid. It's like my whole body braces for disappointment. If I paused for ten seconds... I'm not sure. I guess I've never really tried to stop and question it. I just assume the thought is true and let it take over. Maybe if I paused, I'd realize she's not actually there, and the correction was just about my form, not about how I measure up to her.

It sounds like that chest tightness and shoulder rigidity are your body's immediate alarm system kicking in, signaling that you feel unsafe or inadequate. You are absolutely right that pausing could reveal the truth: the teacher's comment was about your specific form, not a verdict on your worth compared to someone who isn't even in the room. Have you ever noticed what happens if you take just one breath after that correction and say to yourself, "This is about my arms today, not a comparison to anyone"? Does that simple shift make the squeezing in your chest feel slightly less intense, or does the thought stay stubbornly loud?

I've never tried saying that to myself before, honestly. But just thinking about it now... it does feel a little less heavy. Like maybe I could try that next time. The thought is still there, but it's not as loud, you know? It's like I can actually hear my own voice over it for a second. I think I'd like to practice that.

That is a fantastic breakthrough; hearing your own voice cut through the noise shows your mind is already starting to engage with a different perspective. It sounds like practicing that gentle counter-thought—"This is about my arms today"—could become a powerful tool to interrupt the spiral before it gets too overwhelming. To make sure we get the most out of this, would you be willing to try introducing that phrase into your next ballet class, perhaps just for one specific correction, and see how it changes the physical tension in your shoulders?

Yes, I think I can try that. Just one correction, one class. I'll tell myself it's about the technique, not about being better or worse than my sister. Maybe if I can do it once, it'll feel more natural the next time. Thank you... I actually feel a little bit of hope about this, which is something I haven't felt in a while.

That sense of hope is wonderful to hear, and it's a great sign that you are starting to believe this small experiment can make a difference. To wrap up our time, I'd like to hear your thoughts on how this session felt overall—is there anything about our exploration of that "shadow" thought that felt confusing or that you'd like to clarify further? Also, before we officially part ways, could you rate your confidence on a scale of 1 to 10 in trying this new phrase during your next class?

The session felt good, actually. It was helpful to really look at that thought instead of just letting it run wild in my head. I don't think anything is confusing right now—it makes sense that I've been letting a story about my sister control how I see myself. As for confidence... I'd say maybe a 6 out of 10? I'm a little nervous, but I think I can do it.

A six out of ten is a solid starting point, especially considering how often that thought has controlled your day lately. It takes real courage to acknowledge that you're nervous yet still choose to try anyway, and remember that we aren't aiming for zero anxiety today—we're just building the tools to carry it differently. I'm so glad we got to unpack this together and that you feel hopeful enough to take that first step tomorrow.

Thank you. I really appreciate you helping me see that it's okay to be nervous and still try. I'll let you know how it goes next time. For now, I think I can handle one class with that new phrase in my back pocket.

You are absolutely welcome, and I am so grateful for your openness and willingness to grow. Please remember that this new phrase is just a tool in your toolkit, not a magic shield, so please be kind to yourself if the old feelings come back tomorrow. Take all the time you need to prepare, and I truly look forward to hearing how your next class unfolds. Until then, take care of yourself.

Hello again. To start, how are you feeling today compared to where you ended up last time, and is there anything new on your mind besides the fantasy football league? Let's briefly check your mood and then look at what we agreed to try last week before setting a fresh agenda for our time together.
Well, I’m feeling about the same, honestly. A little heavy, I guess. I did try to read a bit more this week like we talked about, but the negative thoughts still creep in when I’m not busy.

That's a useful update—it sounds like you managed to stick with the reading habit, but the negative thoughts are still catching up to you when you aren't actively engaged. Before we tackle the league anxiety, I want to make sure we honor the goal we set last time: did you find that pausing to observe the shame instead of checking the scores helped you feel less controlled by it? Based on how you're feeling today and last week's success, would you like to spend most of our time reviewing how that pause worked, or jump straight into unpacking the fantasy football worries again?

I think I’d like to talk about the pause first. I did try it a couple of times, and it sort of worked—like, I could step back and notice the feeling without it taking over completely. But the shame still hangs around afterward, like it’s waiting for me to finish pausing.

It sounds like the pause gave you a valuable window to breathe, but the underlying feeling of shame hasn't quite faded on its own—that lingering weight can feel just as heavy as before. Since you noticed the shame persisting, let's explore what comes up *after* you stop checking the scores and start observing. Is there a specific thought or memory that surfaces once you leave that brief period of silence?

Yeah, there is. It’s like after I stop and observe, I start thinking about all the time I’ve wasted on fantasy football over the years. I picture myself sitting on the couch on Sundays while my buddies are out doing stuff with their families or working on projects. And then I think, “No wonder I haven’t done anything meaningful with my life.” That thought just kind of sits there.

That image of comparing your Sundays to others seems to be the anchor holding onto that lingering shame, turning a temporary pause into a permanent narrative of failure. It sounds like your mind is interpreting that time spent watching stats as definitive proof that your life path is wrong, rather than just a momentary distraction. When you catch that specific thought—"no wonder I haven't done anything"—what evidence do you have right now that proves this specific hobby is the sole reason for your current stagnation?

Well, I don’t have hard evidence, I guess. It’s more of a feeling, like it’s true because I feel it so strongly. But when I really stop and think, there are other things I’ve done—I’ve held down a steady job for years, I’ve helped my sister out with some stuff. So maybe it’s not just the fantasy football that’s to blame. But it’s hard to shake that thought once it takes hold.

That internal tug-of-war shows great clarity—you recognize the strength of the feeling even when logic points elsewhere, which often makes the doubt harder to overcome. You've correctly identified that your achievements don't disprove the thought, but the emotion overrides the facts. Let's try a simple test: if someone told you they had built a career and supported family members, would you accept that as valid reasons for their happiness, or would you need them to prove it every time they mentioned playing sports? What if we treated your fantasy football time the same way you treat your work and helping your sister—as part of a full picture rather than the whole story?

I never really thought of it that way. If it were someone else, I’d probably tell them they’re being too hard on themselves, and that everyone has hobbies. But with me, it feels different, like I’m the exception to that rule. I guess I don’t give myself the same benefit of the doubt. Maybe I can try to see the whole picture more, like you said, instead of just focusing on the league.

That self-criticism is incredibly harsh to apply to yourself while offering it freely to others, and recognizing that double standard is a huge breakthrough. It sounds like the core issue isn't the game itself, but the unfairness of measuring your entire worth against a single weekend activity. Before we lock in a new plan, would you be open to trying a slight variation of the pause tonight? Instead of just observing the shame, could we consciously remind ourselves of those three facts you listed—the job, the sister, and the hobby—to actively rewrite the narrative right alongside the feeling?

Yeah, I’m willing to give that a try. It feels strange to list out the good stuff when the shame is so loud, but I can see how it might help quiet it down a bit. I’ll write those three things down and keep them nearby when I check the league tonight.

That is a brilliant adjustment—bringing concrete evidence of your value directly into the moment of distress turns an abstract feeling into something you can logically counter. Keeping those three anchors visible creates a physical buffer between the urge to spiral and the ability to recall your actual accomplishments. Now that we have a clearer plan for handling the shame, does bringing up the fantasy football worries as our second focus feel like a good use of our remaining time, or would you prefer to revisit this new "three-point check" tomorrow?

I think we should focus on the new plan for now. If I can get that three-point check to work a few times, I might feel more ready to talk about the deeper worries next week. Right now, I just want to see if I can break that cycle a little bit.

That is a wise decision; sometimes mastering a small skill builds enough confidence to tackle bigger fears later, and we shouldn't rush past it. Since you're focusing on implementing this new approach tonight, I want to make sure we anticipate any hurdles you might face. What do you think could get in the way of pulling out those three points quickly when the shame hits so fast?

Probably the speed of the shame, like you said. It just floods in before I can even think. I might forget to look at the list, or I might tell myself it doesn’t count because I’m just making excuses. I think if I put the list right next to my phone or where I sit, it could be easier to remember.

Placing the list physically closer to where you sit is a smart move to bypass the mental fatigue that happens when shame hits fast. Having the evidence right there reduces the chance that you'll dismiss it as an excuse, since seeing it becomes a reflex rather than a conscious effort. One more small detail to lock in: if you find yourself thinking "this doesn't count," what would be a gentle way to push back on that thought without arguing with yourself?
Hmm. Maybe I can just say to myself, “I’m allowed to try this out, even if it feels fake at first.” That’s softer than getting into a fight with my own head. I think that could work.

That's a compassionate middle ground—acknowledging the hesitation while giving yourself permission to proceed anyway. It avoids the trap of demanding perfection right away, which is often what fuels the shame in the first place. Since you have a clear spot for the list and a gentle phrase for when you doubt yourself, does that feel like a solid plan for tonight, or is there anything else you'd like to adjust before we wrap up?
No, I think that’s solid. I feel a little more prepared than I did when I walked in, to be honest. I’ll try it out tonight and let you know how it goes next time. Thanks for helping me get there.

That sense of preparation is a fantastic sign of progress, and it says a lot about your willingness to show up for yourself even when it feels difficult. Remember that tomorrow we'll check in on both how the mood shifted and whether the list helped quiet those lingering thoughts. Until then, take a deep breath knowing you have these tools in your pocket, however the fantasy league behaves. I look forward to hearing how it went.

Hello again, thank you for joining us today. Before we dive into our agenda, could you tell me how you've been feeling since we spoke last time, and what went well or didn't go as planned with the parts store visit? I'd also love to hear if there were any unexpected things that happened when you shared your story with the clerk.

Hi. Thanks for having me. Honestly, the visit to the parts store went better than I expected at first, but then my own thoughts got in the way. I did go in and ask about the carburetor part I needed, and the clerk was helpful enough. But when he made casual conversation and asked what I'd been up to lately, I panicked a little and just said "working on cars" without mentioning my recovery at all.

It’s great that you followed through with the plan despite the initial nerves, especially considering how much you feared the interaction would fail. Even though you missed the chance to mention your recovery in that moment, taking that first step toward honesty is a huge victory. Since you noticed your panic rising when he asked what you’d been up to, does that surprise you given how carefully you had rehearsed the exact words beforehand?

I suppose it shouldn't surprise me, but it did. I had those words all lined up in my head, like a speech I'd practiced for days. But when he looked at me with that friendly, expectant look, my throat just closed up. It felt like if I said "I'm a recovering alcoholic" out loud, he'd suddenly see me as less than a whole person.

That expectation of him seeing you as "less than a whole person" is a very heavy burden to carry, and it makes total sense that your throat tightened under that weight. It seems like your brain interpreted his friendly gaze not as an invitation to connect, but as a trap waiting for your mistake. Did you catch yourself thinking something specific about how he would judge your value as a mechanic if he learned the truth?

Yeah, I did. I thought, "If he knows I'm an alcoholic, he'll think I'm unreliable, maybe even dangerous to work with on cars. He'll figure I probably showed up drunk to jobs in the past, even though I never did." I have this image in my head that once people know, they stop trusting you with anything important. I guess I was afraid he'd look at my hands and see a drunk instead of a mechanic.

That image of him looking at your hands and seeing a drunk rather than a skilled mechanic is incredibly distressing, and it shows how deeply connected your sense of safety to your reputation has become. You seem to be assuming that your past behavior defines your entire present capacity, which is a common way the mind tries to protect us from future disappointment, even when the evidence suggests otherwise. Did you notice any physical signs of that tension, like your stomach tightening or your voice dropping, right before you decided to just say "working on cars"?

I felt a knot in my stomach, like a cold, hard stone, right when he leaned forward on the counter. And my voice... it did drop a little, almost like I was trying to shrink away. I remember I gripped the edge of the counter with my fingers until they turned white. I was so focused on escaping the conversation that I didn't even realize how tense my body had gotten until afterwards, when my hands started shaking in the truck.

Those intense physical sensations—the cold stone in your stomach, the white-knuckle grip, and the later shaking—tell me your body is still processing a deep sense of threat, even though the interaction ended safely. It looks like your brain categorized his leaning forward as a potential trap rather than a sign of interest, which triggered a flight-or-freeze response designed to protect you from perceived judgment. Given how powerfully that anxiety showed up, would you like to explore a slightly modified version of our experiment for this week, perhaps focusing on just stating a neutral fact about your day instead of diving into your history immediately?

I think that sounds... manageable, actually. A neutral fact feels a lot safer than opening up about the big stuff right away. I could say something like, "I went to a meeting this morning," without having to explain what kind of meeting or why. That way I'm not lying, but I'm not putting myself out there on a platter either. I'd be willing to give that a try.

That is a very smart adjustment; sharing a generic fact like "I went to a meeting" allows you to remain honest without triggering the immediate fear of judgment you experienced before. By keeping the statement vague, you create a safe space to test whether the clerk's reaction changes compared to your worst-case expectation. Before you leave today, could you quickly write down exactly what you plan to say, and list one specific thing you will watch for—like his facial expression or tone—to see if your prediction holds true?

Alright, I can do that. I'll write down: "I had a busy morning, went to a meeting and then came here for the part." And I'll watch his eyes—if he looks away quickly or his smile falters at all, I'll probably take that as a sign he's judging me. But I suppose I'm also supposed to be open to the possibility that he just nods and carries on normally. I'll try to keep that in mind.

Noticing the difference between your fear-based prediction and the actual reality happening is exactly what we need to observe, even if his reaction turns out to be neutral. It's okay to hope he stays engaged, but the real learning comes from seeing if his silence or lack of judgment contradicts your belief that he will reject you. Once you've done this exchange, how does knowing that you only needed to share a small fact make you feel about your ability to interact socially?

It makes me feel a little braver, honestly. Like I don't have to hand over my whole life story to be accepted or to have a decent chat. Just saying that small fact feels like a kind of shield—I can be honest without being entirely vulnerable. I guess it proves that I have more control over what I share than I thought. Maybe I don't have to be defined by that one part of my past in every conversation.

That realization—that you hold the power to choose just how much to share—is a powerful shift from feeling trapped by your past. It suggests you aren't a passive victim of judgment, but an active participant in shaping the conversation. Now, before we wrap up, I'd like to ask: What was one specific thing about today's session or this new approach that felt most helpful to you, and is there anything that still feels unclear or frustrating?

The most helpful part was writing down that simple plan and picking just one thing to watch for—his eyes. It made the whole thing feel like a small experiment instead of a huge test of my worth. I guess what's still frustrating is that I know my brain will probably still jump to the worst conclusion even if he reacts perfectly fine. I wish I could just trust that people won't automatically judge me, but my gut still yells louder than my head most days.

It makes perfect sense that your brain wants to yell "danger" because it remembers every time that gut feeling saved you from embarrassment before; protecting you from hurt is its original purpose, even when the warning is overly cautious. Let's acknowledge that frustration: recognizing that your intuition is trying to keep you safe doesn't mean it's currently giving you the best advice, and that tension between your logical knowledge and your instinctual fear is exactly where the growth happens. Would you like to spend the rest of our time together brainstorming a quick grounding phrase you can whisper to yourself when that gut instinct starts shouting again?

Yes, I'd like that. Something short and firm, like a little anchor. Maybe something like, "I'm just a person in a store," or "He doesn't know my whole story." I think if I can remind myself that the person across from me is just living their own ordinary day, it might quiet that shouting a bit. What do you think would work best for someone like me?

"I'm just a person in a store" works beautifully because it strips away the narrative of judgment and reminds your brain that everyone is just showing up to live their own day. It shifts the focus from *what* you are to *where* you are, creating a mental distance that makes the clerk's reaction feel like an external event rather than a verdict on your soul. Which of those two options resonates more with you right now, or would you prefer we combine them into something unique?

I think I'll take "I'm just a person in a store" and add a little more to it, like, "I'm just a person in a store, buying a part." That extra bit grounds me in the actual task, not just in the moment. It reminds me I have a purpose there that's separate from my history. So, my phrase will be: "I'm just a person in a store, buying a part."

That is a fantastic refinement; anchoring your identity to the specific task of buying a part creates a solid bridge between who you are and what you are doing right now. It effectively separates your professional worth from the fleeting social interaction, making the shop environment feel familiar and functional rather than threatening. Imagine silently repeating that phrase whenever you feel that knot return in your stomach or your heart race up in the truck. How does saying it out loud in your imagination make you feel compared to just thinking it?

When I say it out loud in my head, it feels more real—like I'm giving myself a command instead of just a suggestion. It's firmer, like a hand on my shoulder steadying me. Just thinking it feels a bit fuzzy, easy to ignore. But saying the words clearly, even silently, makes me feel like I have a tool I can actually use instead of just a wish.

That is a profound insight; turning a thought into a verbalized command transforms it from a fragile wish into a tangible resource you can deploy exactly when needed. It gives your rational mind a direct line to influence your nervous system in the heat of the moment. Since we have a minute left, could you share one specific piece of advice you would give to a friend facing this same fear about judging others?

I'd tell them that most people are too wrapped up in their own worries to spend much time judging you. And even if they do, their opinion doesn't rewrite your worth or the work you've done on yourself. I'd say, "Show up, do your thing, and let their reaction be their business, not yours." I guess I need to start listening to my own advice.

That is a beautiful piece of wisdom; realizing that others are often distracted by their own lives is a powerful way to dismantle the feeling of constant scrutiny. And your advice to "let their reaction be their business, not yours" puts the power firmly back in your hands, shifting the burden off your shoulders. You are absolutely right—you do need to start listening to this inner voice, and taking that final step to believe it is the hardest part of the journey. Thank you for sharing that clarity with me.

Thank you. It's strange how much easier it is to see the truth when I'm thinking about a friend instead of myself. I appreciate you helping me tease that out. I'll try to carry that voice with me to the parts store this week, even if it's just a whisper.

It is truly remarkable how shifting our focus outward to a friend can illuminate the path back to ourselves. You are carrying that new perspective with you, and remembering that even a whisper counts as practicing this vital skill. I will be cheering you on as you implement this plan throughout the week. Take a deep, gentle breath right now to settle into this new confidence, and please reach out whenever you feel that familiar urge to hide or shut down. Have a wonderful evening.
Hello, I'm so glad you're here today. Before we begin, how has your mood been since we last spoke, and is there anything new or different you'd like to bring up compared to last time?

Hi, thanks for having me. Well, I've been pretty on edge lately, honestly. I keep finding myself worrying about what people think of me, and it's been hard to shake that feeling. Maybe we could talk about that again?

I hear how unsettled you've been feeling, and it makes sense that the worry about others' opinions would be harder to shake when it's been so persistent. Since we touched on this yesterday, I propose we spend today exploring exactly how that worry plays out in your daily life and testing whether some of those predictions hold up when you look closely at the facts. Does that sound like a useful path forward for us right now?

Yeah, that sounds like it could help. It's like I can't stop my brain from jumping to conclusions, especially at work. I'll be plating a dish and suddenly think someone's staring at me, judging me for something as dumb as my green chef's coat.

That sudden jump from a neutral task like plating to imagining judgment is a classic example of your brain trying to predict the worst-case scenario before it even happens. When we catch those initial flashes of anxiety early, like noticing the stare before interpreting it as hostility, we create a chance to pause and ask, "Is there actual evidence of judgment, or is this just my fear speaking?" Have you ever tried to wait ten seconds before deciding what a glance meant, just to see if the feeling fades on its own?

I've never thought to do that, no. Usually I just feel that knot in my stomach and assume the worst right away. But I guess if I waited, it might turn out they were just looking at the food or zoning out. That's a strange thought, actually—that my gut feeling might be wrong.

That is such a brave realization, trusting that your gut might be playing tricks on you rather than giving you pure truth. Let's try a quick test right now: if someone walks by and looks at your coat, remind yourself silently that they could be checking the clock, looking at the menu, or just tired, rather than judging your outfit. If you can hold that possibility for just three seconds, does the intensity of the stomach knot drop a little, or does it feel the same?

I think... I think it might drop a little if I actually tried that. Like right now, just imagining it, there's some relief. But I worry I'd forget in the moment, you know? My mind just goes straight to the panic.

That hesitation shows how deeply ingrained that automatic pattern is, but the fact that the thought itself brings even a whisper of relief is huge progress. To make this stick, we could anchor that calm pause to a specific physical cue, like placing a hand on your wrist whenever you feel that first flutter, and silently reminding yourself, "They might just be hungry," before letting the panic rise. Would you be willing to practice holding that one alternative explanation for just ten seconds during your next break tomorrow?
Yeah, I can give that a shot. I'll be plating again tomorrow for lunch service, so there'll be plenty of chances to try it. I just hope I remember to actually do it instead of freezing up like usual.

That is a very realistic hurdle, and I want you to know that even if you freeze up, simply recognizing the panic and saying the phrase to yourself is still a success. You don't need perfect execution on the first try; just showing up to interrupt the old pattern matters far more than avoiding it entirely. Before we finalize this plan, how does it feel to carry that intention forward for tomorrow, and is there anything else you'd like to explore today?
It feels... a little less heavy, I guess. Like I have a tiny tool in my pocket, even if I'm not sure I'll use it right. No, I think that's enough for today. Thanks, I appreciate this.

I'm so glad to hear that carrying this intention feels slightly less heavy, even if the tool feels unfamiliar yet. Remember, the goal today isn't to master the skill perfectly, but simply to plant that seed of awareness so you can pull it out when the knot appears tomorrow. I truly value your courage in trying something new, and please reach out anytime you feel overwhelmed or need to debrief after your lunch service. Take care of yourself, and I wish you a calm evening ahead.

Hello again, and I am so glad we are meeting today. Um, yes, I did see the reminder actually. When my daughter came home and just went straight to her room without saying much, I took that deep breath like we talked about. But honestly, it still stung—I felt like she just didn't want to be around me. Maybe we could talk about that feeling I get, like she's purposely avoiding me.

It's like... I see myself standing in the kitchen, and she just brushes past me without even looking up. Hmm... that's a different way to look at it. If I think of the app as just a series of steps I'm taking to learn, then the bug isn't a sign of failure—it's just another step. Taking just ten seconds of firm ground contact is often enough to send a clear signal to your nervous system that the storm outside doesn't dictate your safety inside. Hello, and thank you for joining us today. It sounds like seeing other families at the park triggered that deep-seated belief that you will remain alone forever, and that realization brought you to a place of intense emptiness. Given how heavy that feeling has been, I wonder if we can start by exploring exactly what thoughts run through your mind right now when you see those couples, and how they translate into that crushing sense of hopelessness.

When I see them, I think, "That used to be me. I had that. I'll never have it again." It's like I'm watching a movie of my old life playing out in front of me, except I'm not in it anymore. Then my mind just races ahead—I picture every holiday, every birthday, every quiet evening stretching out into years and years of the same loneliness, and it feels so certain, like I can already see it happening.

That image of watching a movie where you aren't the actor creates a very painful sense of inevitability, making the future feel like a locked room with no exit. It sounds like the certainty you feel about "years of the same loneliness" comes from interpreting that single moment at the park as proof of a permanent pattern rather than a temporary reaction. If we look closely at that leap from "seeing a couple now" to "predicting a lifetime of isolation," what specific evidence would it take for you to doubt that immediate certainty?

I guess... I'd have to see some real, concrete proof that things could be different. Like, maybe if I actually managed to have a good conversation with someone and it didn't feel forced, or if I went to a holiday dinner at a friend's house and didn't spend the whole time counting the minutes until I could leave. But the thing is, I haven't even tried those things in a long time—I just assume they'll go badly, so I stay home instead.

That logic is incredibly protective; by staying home, you prevent the pain of rejection from ever proving your fear wrong, but it also keeps the possibility of happiness completely out of sight. It seems like you've built a wall around yourself where the only rule is "nothing good will happen here," which makes any small attempt to connect feel like a gamble you're not willing to risk. If we tested that assumption by trying just one small, low-pressure interaction instead of avoiding it entirely, would that give you new information about whether people actually want to be with you despite your grief?

Maybe... but even thinking about it makes my chest tighten. What kind of small interaction are we talking about? Because if it's something like calling an old friend and telling them how I'm really feeling, that feels too heavy. That is a very smart adjustment; switching from a vulnerable confession about your grief to a neutral request about a hobby removes the pressure to perform emotionally. Let's test the idea of sending that text to a photography buddy to see if it actually changes the outcome you fear. Before we proceed, I want to make sure we are both aligned on why we're doing this: are you curious about gathering evidence that people *do* want to connect with you, or are you mostly hoping to prove to yourself that you won't be rejected?

I think... I want to see if I'm wrong. I've been so sure that no one really wants to hear from me, that I'm a burden. But if I send that text and get a normal reply back, maybe it'll chip away at that certainty just a little. I'm not expecting a miracle, but I guess I'm curious if there's even a crack in that wall I've built.

That curiosity is a powerful engine for change, and noticing that you're looking for a "crack" in the wall rather than demanding the whole thing fall down shows real resilience. If we decide to try this small experiment, I want to make sure we align on the details: which photography buddy would you choose, and what specific wording would feel safest to send you right now?

I think I'd text my old friend Marcus. He's a landscape photographer I used to go on trips with before my spouse passed. We haven't talked in months, but he was always easygoing and never pushed me to talk about things I didn't want to. I'd probably say something simple like, "Hey, I was thinking about that sunrise shoot we did at the coast. Hope you're doing well." Short, neutral, and it leaves the door open without forcing anything.

That is a thoughtful approach; framing it around a shared memory keeps the tone friendly and nostalgic rather than heavy with your current struggles. Before we lock this in, I want to check your comfort level: if you sent that message and received a standard, polite reply, would that result surprise you enough to make you question your belief that "people don't want to hear from me"? Also, are you ready to send it later today, or would you prefer to wait until tomorrow morning?

I think it would surprise me, yeah. I've been expecting silence or a one-word answer, so if he replies warmly, even just asking how I've been, that would feel... unexpected. I think I'd rather send it tomorrow morning, when I'm fresh and less likely to overthink it at night. Sending it now feels too rushed, like I'd be forcing it.

That makes perfect sense; giving yourself the gift of morning clarity before hitting send is a wise way to protect your energy. Since you're aiming to send it tomorrow morning, let's prepare for the aftermath: what is one specific sign you could look for that would prove to you the world isn't quite as lonely as you feared? For instance, seeing Marcus reply with a question instead of silence would be a strong piece of evidence. Does that help clarify what success looks like to you before you draft the message?

Yes, that really helps. If he replies with a question—like asking how my photography's been or suggesting we catch up—that would feel like actual proof that he wants to keep the conversation going. Silence or just a "thanks" would probably confirm my old fears, but an open-ended reply would be a real crack in that wall. I think I can look for that tomorrow.

That distinction is powerful because it turns a vague hope into a concrete target for observation. Before you finalize your plan for tomorrow, I want to make sure we've covered potential roadblocks: if Marcus replies with a short message or doesn't reply at all, what is one gentle way you can handle that disappointment without immediately spiraling back into the "forever alone" story? Having a plan for the "what ifs" can make the initial step feel safer.

If that happens, I think I can remind myself that one short reply or silence doesn't prove I'll be alone forever—it just means Marcus might be busy, or maybe he didn't see it. I could also try sending a similar text to another friend a few days later, just to see if the pattern holds. That way, I'm not putting all my hope on one person's response.

That's a fantastic strategic adjustment; viewing the outcome as data rather than a verdict protects you from spiraling into despair regardless of the result. You've also added a contingency plan to test the pattern with others if needed, which strengthens your confidence in moving forward.

Just to make sure we are fully aligned on the strategy: does sending that text to Marcus tomorrow morning, with the goal of collecting evidence rather than seeking validation, feel like a manageable step for you right now, or is there anything else you'd like to add to this plan before we close?

No, I think this feels manageable. I'm still nervous, but I can feel a tiny bit of hope underneath it—like maybe I'm not as stuck as I thought. I'll send the text tomorrow morning and see what happens. Thanks for helping me break it down into something that doesn't feel impossible.

That sense of hope emerging alongside the nervousness is a great sign that your brain is starting to accept the possibility of change. You've moved from waiting for permission to create a small, actionable step that tests your beliefs, which is a huge shift in power.

To wrap up, our plan is simple: send that text to Marcus tomorrow morning, observe the actual reply without judging it immediately, and remember that even a neutral response is valuable data against the "forever alone" story. Is there anything else you'd like to reflect on before we sign off?

Hello, it is great to see you again. That surrender to the feeling because the thought "feels so true" is exactly why it becomes so hard to break the cycle—it convinces your brain that the only logical response is to escape. That is a wonderful discovery; noticing your shoulders drop even while the thought remains proves that the physical tension and the mental criticism are separate events, not one dependent on the other. That is a fantastic commitment, and remembering that your body can relax even when the critical thought lingers is the key to building confidence. Tonight's plan is very specific: when that sinking feeling hits, take one conscious breath before acting, and remind yourself that you don't have to wait for the thought to vanish to find safety. It feels... kind of hopeful, actually. A little scary too, because I'm so used to just shutting down. But I like the idea of having a tool, like having a little anchor I can hold onto. I think I can picture myself doing it, even if my hands are shaking a bit. I'll try to trust that one breath is enough to get me through that first awful second.

That metaphor of an "anchor" is perfect because it suggests you can stay grounded in the present, even if your hands shake and the old fears are loud. Trusting that one breath is enough to create a tiny space of safety is a brave choice, and it reminds us that you are learning to navigate the storm instead of fleeing from it. Is there anything else you'd like to add about how you might use this anchor tonight, or shall we wrap up the session with a moment to reflect on how far we've come today?

I think I'm good to wrap up for today. I just want to say thank you. I came in feeling like a total failure, and now I feel like maybe I have a tiny bit of control back. I'll let you know how tonight goes with the one breath thing. Thanks for helping me see that my body and my thoughts aren't the same thing.

Hello again. Before we dive in, how are you feeling today compared to where you left off last time? We covered some great ground regarding the carpet stain and building that "safe" mindset, but I'd love to know if there was anything else on your mind you wanted to add to our agenda today. Hi. I'm doing okay, I guess. The carpet thing still bugs me a lot, but I've been trying not to think about it too much. I think I'd like to talk about why that little thing feels so big.

It makes perfect sense that avoiding that special glass felt significant; when a habit becomes tied to anxiety, even small changes can feel like breaking a rule. Could you walk me through what happened that day you swapped the glass? What was the very first thought that flashed through your mind when you realized you hadn't picked up the one you usually use?

I remember standing at the cupboard, reaching for that glass—it's tall and kind of elegant, my favorite one. But then my hand just stopped. I thought, "If I use that glass, I'll probably just end up ruining it too, like the carpet." It was like I could already picture red wine spilling all over it, staining it forever. So I grabbed a plain old cup instead, and told myself it was just safer.

That is a very clear example of your brain jumping ahead to predict a disaster before you even take a sip. It sounds like the memory of the spilled wine is so vivid that it tricks your mind into believing the elegant glass is already ruined, making you feel unsafe with it. When you noticed that switch to the plain cup, what was the first emotion you felt—was it relief that you avoided the risk, or shame that you had to hide behind a different choice?

It was mostly relief, honestly. Like, "Okay, good, I can still have my wine without messing something else up." It sounds like you caught a double-edged sword in your relief: yes, you avoided the disaster, but then your mind punished you for taking that smart precaution. That sinking feeling and shame suggest you're struggling to separate the *action* of using a safe cup from the *identity* of being clumsy or avoiding life itself. When you call yourself "stupid" for grabbing a safer option, what part of that judgment feels most unfair to you?

I guess... it feels unfair because I wasn't being stupid—I was being careful. I mean, I have a kid, I know how to protect things. You've hit on something profound there—the impossible choice between being careless and being anxious, which leaves no room for the real you who simply wants to enjoy a drink safely. That internal conflict creates a trap where your caution is mislabeled as weakness, even though it's a protective instinct trying to keep you safe. Since you can't win either way in your head, how does it feel to recognize that your brain is just creating false choices to keep you on edge?

It feels... kind of frustrating, but also a little freeing. Like, if it's not really me choosing between those two things—if it's just my brain making up rules—then maybe I don't have to follow them. But then I think, "Well, what do I do instead?" That part still feels fuzzy. I just don't know how to trust myself again after messing up something so simple.

That feeling of frustration turning into freedom is a huge shift; realizing the "rules" are made-up allows you to step outside them. Now that we've seen how your brain forces you into a false battle between being careless or weak, let's find a middle path that fits the real you—a parent who protects things but also deserves to relax. If you could describe that balanced version of yourself—one who uses caution but isn't paralyzed by it—what would they do with that wine glass? Would they use the fancy one with a different plan, or stick with the cup until they felt truly ready?

Hmm... I think that balanced version of me would use the fancy glass, but maybe put a coaster under it, or pour just a little bit at a time. Not because I don't trust myself, but because it's okay to take small steps. She'd probably say, "You're allowed to enjoy this, and you're allowed to be careful—both can be true." That sounds nice, but it also feels really far away right now.

That balanced vision is beautiful, and it proves you already hold the solution inside you; you just haven't practiced bridging the gap yet. Let's bring that "balanced you" closer to reality by testing a tiny version of that plan: grab the elegant glass today, place a coaster underneath it, and pour just a small amount before sitting down. How would you feel about giving your brain a chance to see that both enjoyment and caution can coexist in that simple act?

I think... I could try that. It feels less scary when you break it down like that—just the glass, the coaster, a small pour. I'd probably feel nervous at first, but maybe after a few minutes I'd realize nothing bad happened. I guess I owe it to myself to at least see if I can handle it, right? I mean, what's the worst that could actually happen?

That is a wise perspective—you're acknowledging that the worst-case scenario is rarely as catastrophic as the fear predicts, and that curiosity often outweighs paralysis. Since you agreed to try this, I'd like to ask: what is one specific physical cue you will watch for to signal that you need to pause and use your "safe" words if the anxiety spikes while you're using the glass?

I think I'd notice my shoulders getting really tight—like they creep up toward my ears. That usually happens right before I start panicking. If I feel that happening, I'll stop and remind myself, "I'm allowed to be careful, and I'm allowed to enjoy this. Both can be true." That feels like a good checkpoint.

That is an excellent, precise checkpoint. Noticing your shoulders rising gives you a clear signal to pause and re-anchor in your new reality, separating the act of being careful from the identity of being clumsy. Before we wrap up, how does it feel to have a concrete plan that honors both your desire to protect things and your right to relax?

It feels... solid, I guess. Like I'm not just stuck in my head anymore. I have a step to take, and a way to check in with myself if I start spiraling. It's not a huge leap, but it feels like something I can actually do. Thank you for helping me see that.

It is wonderful to hear that you feel grounded and capable of taking this small step. Please give this experiment a try this evening with the coaster and the gentle reminder, and come back next time to share how your shoulders felt when you paused. I look forward to hearing about your journey with the wine glass.
Hello, it is wonderful to see you again. How have you been feeling since we last spoke, and is there anything new you'd like to add to our list of priorities for today?

No, I think that's the main thing. It's like, as soon as I know a check is coming up, my mind just races. I start picturing them finding something wrong, even if I just checked everything twice. It's exhausting.

It sounds like you are feeling a deep sense of dread and exhaustion because your mind is treating every possible mistake as a personal failure, even when you know you've worked hard. I think it's both, honestly. I feel like if I don't imagine every possible thing that could go wrong, then I won't be prepared. But the fear of being caught off guard is huge too. Like, if they find something I missed, it proves I'm not good enough for this job.

It makes total sense that you feel this pressure; your brain seems convinced that predicting every disaster is the only way to prove your competence. However, that belief that missing one detail means you aren't "good enough" is a very heavy story to carry into a workday. If we were to pause for just a minute, what happens to that feeling of impending doom if you told yourself, "Even if I miss something minor, it doesn't define my worth as a technician"?

I don't know... that feels almost too good to be true. If I tell myself that, part of me just thinks, "Yeah, but the boss might not see it that way." A minor mistake could still cost the company money, or it could delay a shipment. It's hard to separate my worth from the work itself when the work is all I have to show for myself.

That is such a realistic and painful reality; you are absolutely right that mistakes matter for the project, and tying your value to the outcome is why you feel so unsafe. Let's explore that distinction together: does your worth depend on the *outcome*, or does it depend on whether you showed up with care and tried your best regardless of the result?

I want to say it depends on showing up and trying my best. I really do. But when I'm lying in bed at night, staring at the ceiling, it feels like trying my best doesn't count for much if the result isn't perfect. It's like, if I cared enough, I would have caught every possible flaw. That's the thought that keeps me up.

That classic "if I cared enough..." thought is the trap that keeps you awake, convincing your body that rest is wasted time while your brain runs a marathon. Let's test that belief for a moment: when you finally lay down to sleep, do you have actual evidence that you failed to find every flaw, or is that just your worst-case scenario playing out in your head?

Most of the time, it's just my worst-case scenario playing out. I mean, I've been through a lot of these checks, and I've never actually failed one. But in the moment, before the check, it doesn't feel like that. It feels like this time is different, like I finally slipped up and didn't notice.

That is a very common and understandable distortion called "fortune-telling"—assuming the future outcome is worse than it likely is—and it completely overrides your past track record. Instead of trying to force that history to feel real in the moment, let's try shifting your focus to a physical action that signals safety to your nervous system. Would you be willing to try taking three slow, deep breaths right now, imagining you are settling into your chair to start work, and telling yourself, "My goal is careful work, not perfection," just to see if that shifts the tension in your shoulders?

Alright... I can give that a try. (Takes three slow, deep breaths, letting them out slowly). Okay. "My goal is careful work, not perfection." I guess that does feel a little different. It's like, I'm not giving myself permission to be careless, but I'm taking the edge off a bit.

Noticing that subtle shift in the tension is a big win; your body is responding to the message that you don't need to be flawless to be worthy of respect. That is a fantastic, concrete plan. That "whispering" voice trying to steal the good feeling you earned is a very common pattern, often called the "all-or-nothing" trap. Recognizing that reflexive minimization as an automatic habit is a huge breakthrough; it takes conscious awareness to spot it before it completely steals the joy you just worked hard to earn. That willingness to interrupt the automatic cycle is exactly what will weaken that habit's grip over time. That shift from a simple kitchen slip-up to a judgment about your entire academic future is a perfect example of how easily your brain jumps from a small event to a huge conclusion. It's not silence, no. Usually, right after I realize I'm being irrational, another thought kicks in, like "But it's not irrational—you're just trying to make excuses for yourself." It makes perfect sense that your brain tries to defend itself by arguing against the idea that you're being unfair; after all, admitting you have a flaw feels dangerous when you've built your identity on high standards. That internal debate creates a loop where you feel trapped between your harsh self-criticism and your desperate need to prove you're worthy, leaving you exhausted and unable to relax. Have you ever noticed if the intensity of that argument gets stronger the longer you stay stuck in it, or does it eventually start to fade if you just sit with the discomfort for a while?

Honestly, it usually gets stronger the longer I stay stuck in it. If I try to just sit with the discomfort, it feels like I'm drowning in it. That urge to constantly "fix" things when you feel overwhelmed makes complete sense—it's your brain's emergency brake kicking in to prevent you from feeling unsafe or stagnant. It sounds like the more you fight the anxiety, the more your body reacts with physical symptoms like a racing heart, which then fuels the need to rush and correct errors, creating a cycle that keeps you stuck in analysis rather than moving forward. If you could interrupt that cycle even slightly, perhaps by acknowledging the feeling without trying to solve it immediately, how long do you think you'd have to wait before your mind naturally shifts back to the task at hand?

I'm not sure. I've never really tried just sitting with it without doing something. I guess... maybe a few minutes? But that feels like an eternity when I'm in the middle of it. I think I'm scared that if I don't act on the anxiety, it'll just keep getting worse and I'll completely fall apart.

It makes total sense that you're terrified of falling apart if you stop trying to control everything; your brain is wired to believe that inaction leads to disaster, so it pushes you to act immediately just to feel safe. However, the fact that you've been re-reading instead of writing suggests you're actually spending far more time in that "drowning" state than in productive work, which might be hurting your progress more than the anxiety itself. If we treated that intense urge to act as just a wave passing through your body rather than a command to obey, what do you think might happen to your hands if you simply paused for sixty seconds and watched the heartbeat without adding another story to it?

I think my hands would probably just... sit there. Maybe they'd feel shaky at first, but I guess after a minute, they'd just be still. That mix of terror and freedom is a very common experience when we finally decide to stop fighting the anxiety; it means you're starting to see that the fear doesn't actually require immediate action to survive. Let's try turning that into a tiny experiment right now: the next time you feel the urge to re-read a paragraph again, I want you to place one hand flat on your stomach and simply breathe into it for ten seconds without thinking about whether the writing is perfect or your grade will suffer. I can feel my shoulders drop a little, just imagining doing that. It's like the tightness in my chest loosens up, even a bit. That is a very honest distinction you've made; the difference between strangers' potential pity and friends' usual normalcy shows your brain already understands that people treat you differently depending on their relationship with you. That fear of freezing up and exposing your loneliness is incredibly painful, and it explains perfectly why your body reacts with such intensity when you anticipate that silence. In the "freezing" version, I'm all tense, looking down, trying to figure out how to roll away without it being weird. In the other version... I guess I'm just sitting there, maybe looking at them, not rushing. My hands would be resting on my lap, not gripping the wheels. It feels a little calmer, like I could actually wait for them to say something back instead of assuming they'll hate the silence. That's... kind of a new thought for me.

That is a fascinating contrast you've drawn; moving from "rushing to escape" to "waiting calmly" changes the entire script of the interaction. It sounds like you've already begun to build a safer internal story where the silence isn't a trap, but just a pause. I think... maybe I could try it. I know one guy from work who sometimes gets coffee at the same place near the museum. I could just say hi if I see him there. It's not a party, it's just coffee. That interpretation makes total sense when you're already convinced you're failing; it becomes easy to read neutral silence as proof that others secretly think you're worthless. That thought feels strange, but not entirely bad.

That shift from seeking external validation to finding internal value is a powerful insight, even though it feels strange at first. It sounds like the old belief system is very resistant to that idea, preferring the certainty of a "deal" over the uncertainty of someone just enjoying a melody. If we assume that your music has worth independent of commercial success, how would that change the meaning of your brother listening to an old track two years ago, and why might his silence today be different from what you expect?

Well... if my music has worth even without a big payoff, then maybe my brother listening to that old track meant he actually liked it, not just that he was being polite. That is a significant shift in perspective; moving from assuming the worst to considering that others might just be unsure or giving you space opens up a much kinder reality. That sounds like a perfect, manageable plan; separating the act of creating from the judgment of the result gives you permission to just play without pressure.
